t: Synchronization: race conditions, mutexes, semaphores, monitors, condition variables, spinlocks
sum: How locks are actually built: why software alone struggles, the atomic instructions hardware provides, spinlocks versus sleeping mutexes and the futex that joins them, semaphores, condition variables and monitors, and what contention costs.
prereq: os2
Threads of one process share memory, so two threads can read and write the same variable at the same time.
os3
The scheduler can preempt a thread between any two instructions and decides who runs when a thread blocks.
swe12
A race condition is a bug where the result depends on how steps from different threads interleave; read-modify-write and check-then-act are the classic shapes.
why:
Two threads of a web server each handle a purchase and each run the same line: stock = stock - 1. Stock was 1. Both threads read 1, both compute 0, both write 0, and both tell their customers the purchase succeeded. You have sold one item twice, and if you run the same test a thousand times it might only happen once. This is a race condition, and the swe12 lesson traced it line by line. Its fix is familiar: put a lock around the code that touches stock.

But that fix hides a puzzle. A lock is itself a piece of shared state that two threads try to change at the same moment. How can a lock be built without already having a lock? If you try to write one with an ordinary variable (wait until locked is 0, then set it to 1), you have the same race as the stock counter, one level down. The answer involves the hardware: special atomic instructions, memory barriers, and an operating-system mechanism that lets waiting threads sleep without missing their wake-up call.

This is the layer interviewers probe in OS rounds. "Mutex versus semaphore" and "what is a spinlock" are standard campus questions; "how is a mutex implemented on Linux", "why must a condition-variable wait be in a while loop" and "why does this service stop scaling beyond 8 threads" are senior questions. Getting them right requires knowing what happens below the lock() call.

The lesson goes from the problem to the tools: what a correct lock must guarantee, why software-only solutions such as Peterson's algorithm break on real CPUs, the atomic instructions hardware provides, spinlocks, how Linux mutexes combine user-space atomics with the futex system call, semaphores, condition variables, monitors, and finally what all of this costs when many threads contend.
primer:
The single-key bathroom

A café has one bathroom and one key on a hook. To use the bathroom you take the key; while you have it, nobody else can get in; when you leave you hang it back. The bathroom is a critical section, a piece of code that must not be run by two threads at once because it touches shared data, and the key is a lock that gives mutual exclusion. Everything in this lesson is a variation on this idea: how to make taking the key a single indivisible act, what to do while waiting for it (stand at the door checking, or sit down and ask to be called), and how to wait for things other than the key, such as "wait until the coffee is ready".

The analogy breaks in an important way. In the café, taking the key is obviously one action: two people cannot both grab it. In a computer, "check if the lock is free, then take it" is at least two steps, a read and a write, and another CPU can slip in between them. Making those steps indivisible requires hardware help.

Why "check then take" fails

Here is the naive lock, and the interleaving that breaks it:

while (locked == 1) { }   // wait until free
locked = 1;              // take it

Thread A: reads locked == 0, leaves loop
Thread B: reads locked == 0, leaves loop      <- before A writes
Thread A: locked = 1, enters critical section
Thread B: locked = 1, enters critical section  <- both inside

Any lock built from separate reads and writes has some interleaving like this. The cure is an atomic instruction: a single CPU instruction that reads a memory location and writes it in one step that no other CPU can interleave with. With an atomic "set to 1 and tell me the old value", a thread that gets back 0 knows it is the one that took the lock.

Two ways to wait

Once a thread finds the lock taken, it can spin: keep retrying in a tight loop (a spinlock). That is fast if the lock is released within a few hundred nanoseconds, and wasteful if not. Or it can sleep: ask the kernel to take it off the CPU and wake it when the lock is released (a mutex). Sleeping wastes no CPU but costs a system call and two context switches (os1), several microseconds. Real locks combine both.

Waiting for a condition, not just a lock

Locks solve "only one at a time". Many problems are instead "wait until something is true": a consumer waiting until a queue is non-empty, a worker waiting until a job arrives. Two tools handle this. A semaphore is a counter that threads decrement (blocking at zero) and increment (waking a waiter). A condition variable is a waiting room attached to a lock: a thread holding the lock can say "release the lock and sleep until someone signals me", atomically. Wrap shared data, its lock and its condition variables in one object that locks automatically, and you have a monitor.
body:
1. The race, at instruction level

On x86-64, counter++ on a shared integer compiles to something like three instructions: load the value into a register, add one, store it back. Two threads, counter = 5:

StepThread AThread Bcounter in memory
1load → reg = 55
2load → reg = 55
3add → reg = 65
4add → reg = 65
5store 66
6store 66 (should be 7)

The interleaving can come from two CPUs running truly in parallel or from one CPU being preempted (os3) between the load and the store. Both are possible on every modern machine, which is why "it works on my laptop" means nothing for concurrent code.

2. What a correct solution must guarantee

The textbook "critical-section problem" asks for three properties. Mutual exclusion: at most one thread inside at a time. Progress: if no thread is inside and some want to enter, one of them must get in; the decision cannot be postponed forever. Bounded waiting: once a thread asks to enter, only a bounded number of others may enter before it, so nobody starves. In practice we add two engineering requirements: don't waste CPU, and perform well with many CPUs.

One early solution, used by single-CPU kernels, was to disable interrupts during the critical section: no timer interrupt means no preemption, so nothing else can run. It cannot work for user programs (disabling interrupts is privileged, os1, and a program could simply never re-enable them) and it does nothing on a multiprocessor, where other CPUs keep running. Kernels still disable interrupts locally for very short sections that interrupt handlers also touch, always combined with a spinlock for other CPUs.

3. Peterson's algorithm, and why it fails on real CPUs

In 1981 Gary Peterson published a famously short software-only lock for two threads, using only ordinary reads and writes:

bool flag[2] = {false, false};   // flag[i]: thread i wants in
int  turn;                        // whose turn it is to wait

void lock(int i) {                // i is 0 or 1
    int j = 1 - i;
    flag[i] = true;               // I want in
    turn = j;                     // but you go first if you also want in
    while (flag[j] && turn == j) { }   // wait while you want in and it's your turn
}
void unlock(int i) { flag[i] = false; }

Why it works: if both threads want in, both set their flags and then both write turn. Whichever wrote turn last has given priority away, so it waits, and the other enters. If only one wants in, the other's flag is false and it enters at once (progress). And a waiting thread enters after at most one entry by the other (bounded waiting).

The proof assumes that memory operations happen in program order and that every CPU sees writes in the same order, a model called sequential consistency. Real hardware does not provide it. An x86 CPU puts each store into a per-core store buffer and lets later loads proceed before the store reaches the cache. So thread 0 can write flag[0] = true into its buffer, then read flag[1] from cache as false; thread 1 does the same; both enter. Compilers may also reorder or cache these plain accesses. The algorithm works again only with a full memory barrier (fence) between the writes and the read, or with sequentially consistent atomics. The lesson for interviews: Peterson's algorithm shows how to reason about mutual exclusion, and its failure shows why real locks are built on hardware atomic instructions with explicit ordering.

4. The atomic instructions hardware provides

Every modern CPU offers read-modify-write instructions that are atomic across all CPUs. The CPU achieves this by taking exclusive ownership of the cache line for the duration of the instruction, using the cache-coherence protocol, so no other CPU can read or write that line in between.

  • Test-and-set: write 1, return the old value. (x86's xchg with memory is atomic and does this.)
  • Compare-and-swap (CAS): "if the location still holds expected, write new and report success; otherwise report failure and the current value". x86 lock cmpxchg; ARM uses load-linked/store-conditional pairs (ldxr/stxr) or, on newer chips, a cas instruction.
  • Fetch-and-add: add to a location and return the old value (x86 lock xadd). Ideal for counters.

These are exposed in languages as atomics: C11's atomic_fetch_add, C++'s std::atomic, Java's AtomicInteger, Go's sync/atomic. An uncontended atomic operation costs a few to about 20 nanoseconds; when many CPUs hammer the same location, each operation has to pull the cache line from another core, which can cost 50-100+ nanoseconds and serialises everyone.

5. Spinlocks

With test-and-set, a lock is three lines:

void spin_lock(atomic_int *l)   { while (atomic_exchange(l, 1) == 1) { /* spin */ } }
void spin_unlock(atomic_int *l) { atomic_store(l, 0); }

The thread that gets back 0 owns the lock; everyone else loops. This is correct (the exchange is atomic) but has two practical problems. First, every failed attempt is a write, so waiting CPUs fight over the cache line and slow down the lock holder's release. The standard fix is test-and-test-and-set: spin on a plain read (which can be served from each CPU's own cache) and only attempt the atomic exchange when the lock looks free; also add a CPU pause hint in the loop. Second, it is unfair: whichever CPU happens to win the race gets the lock, and an unlucky thread can wait indefinitely. A ticket lock fixes fairness like a deli counter: each arriving thread takes a ticket with fetch-and-add, then waits until a "now serving" counter equals its ticket; unlock increments "now serving".

When is spinning right? When the critical section is very short, the holder is guaranteed to be running on another CPU, and sleeping is either impossible or more expensive than the wait. That describes the inside of the kernel: interrupt handlers cannot sleep, and many kernel critical sections are tens of nanoseconds. Linux kernel spinlocks also disable preemption while held, so the holder cannot be switched out. In user space, a spinning thread has no such guarantee: if the holder is preempted, the spinner burns its entire time slice. On a single-CPU machine, spinning is pointless, since the holder cannot run while you spin.

6. Sleeping locks and the futex

A mutex should cost almost nothing when uncontended (the common case) and sleep when contended. Early Unix mutexes made a system call for every lock and unlock, which is wasteful when nobody else wants the lock. Linux solved this in 2002 with the futex ("fast user-space mutex"), a system call with two main operations on an integer in the program's own memory:

  • FUTEX_WAIT(addr, expected): "if *addr still equals expected, put me to sleep on addr". The kernel checks the value and queues the thread atomically, so a wake-up between the program's check and its sleep cannot be missed.
  • FUTEX_WAKE(addr, n): wake up to n threads sleeping on addr.

Ulrich Drepper's paper "Futexes Are Tricky" gives the classic mutex built on it, with three states: 0 = unlocked, 1 = locked with no waiters, 2 = locked and maybe waiters.

lock:
    c = CAS(&m, 0, 1)                 // fast path: 0 -> 1, no syscall
    if c == 0: return
    if c != 2: c = exchange(&m, 2)    // mark "there are waiters"
    while c != 0:
        futex_wait(&m, 2)             // sleep while it is still 2
        c = exchange(&m, 2)
unlock:
    if fetch_sub(&m, 1) != 1:         // was 2: someone may be waiting
        m = 0
        futex_wake(&m, 1)             // only now pay for a syscall

glibc's pthread_mutex_t, Java's monitors when contended, Go's sync.Mutex parking, Python's threading.Lock and the GIL itself all bottom out in futexes on Linux. Most implementations also spin briefly before sleeping (adaptive mutexes), betting that a lock held by a running thread will be released within a microsecond or so.

7. Semaphores

Edsger Dijkstra introduced the semaphore in the 1960s: an integer with two atomic operations, originally P and V after Dutch words, now usually wait/acquire and post/signal/release. wait decrements the count, blocking while it is zero; post increments it and wakes one waiter. Three common uses:

  • As a lock (initial count 1, a "binary semaphore"): wait to enter, post to leave.
  • To bound concurrency (initial count N): at most N threads hold a "unit" at once, such as N database connections or N concurrent downloads. Python's threading.BoundedSemaphore(10) and asyncio's Semaphore are used exactly like this.
  • As a signal (initial count 0): one thread waits until another posts, for example "wait until the worker has finished initialising".

The important difference from a mutex is ownership. A mutex is locked and unlocked by the same thread, and the system can check that (error-checking mutexes), support recursion, and apply priority inheritance (os3) because it knows who holds it. A semaphore has no owner; any thread can post, which is what makes it useful for signalling and also what makes misuse undetectable. POSIX provides sem_wait/sem_post, built on futexes too.

8. Condition variables

Suppose a consumer must wait until a shared queue is non-empty. Spinning on while queue.empty() wastes CPU. Sleeping with a plain futex risks a lost wake-up: the consumer checks (empty), the producer adds an item and signals (nobody is asleep yet), then the consumer goes to sleep forever. A condition variable solves this by being tied to a mutex. The rules:

  1. The waiter takes the mutex, then checks the condition.
  2. While the condition is false it calls wait(cv, mutex), which atomically releases the mutex and puts the thread to sleep, so no signal can slip in between. When woken, wait reacquires the mutex before returning.
  3. The signaller takes the same mutex, changes the state, and calls signal (wake one waiter) or broadcast (wake all), then releases the mutex.
import threading
items, lock = [], threading.Lock()
nonempty = threading.Condition(lock)

def consumer():
    with nonempty:                    # take the mutex
        while not items:              # WHILE, not if
            nonempty.wait()           # release + sleep, reacquire on wake
        return items.pop(0)

def producer(x):
    with nonempty:
        items.append(x)
        nonempty.notify()             # wake one waiter

Why while and not if? Two reasons. POSIX and Java allow spurious wake-ups, returns from wait without any signal, because it simplifies implementations on some platforms. More importantly, every common library uses Mesa semantics (named after the Xerox Mesa language): signal merely makes the waiter runnable. Between the signal and the waiter reacquiring the mutex, a third thread can grab the mutex and take the item. Under the original Hoare semantics, the signaller handed the mutex directly to the waiter, so the condition was guaranteed true, but that requires extra context switches and nobody implements it. With Mesa semantics, the condition is a hint, and the loop rechecks it.

Signal or broadcast? Signal wakes one waiter, which is enough when any waiter can use the change and the change only helps one (one item added). Broadcast wakes all, needed when the change may let several proceed or when different waiters wait for different conditions on the same variable. Broadcast is always correct but can cause a thundering herd, many threads waking only to find nothing to do and go back to sleep. os5 uses condition variables to build a bounded producer-consumer buffer and shows the bug that a single condition variable with signal can cause.

9. Monitors

Locks and condition variables are easy to misuse: forget to lock before touching data, forget to unlock on an error path. A monitor, proposed by Hoare and Brinch Hansen in the early 1970s, makes synchronisation a property of the object. All the shared data is private to the monitor; every operation automatically takes the monitor's lock on entry and releases it on exit; and condition variables inside it let operations wait. Java is the best-known example: every object has an intrinsic lock and one condition queue, synchronized methods take the lock, and wait()/notify()/notifyAll() are the condition operations (with Mesa semantics, so the same while loop applies). C#'s lock and Monitor, and a Python class that takes self._lock in every method with a Condition, are monitors by convention.

10. What synchronisation costs

OperationRough cost on a modern x86 server
Uncontended atomic or mutex lock+unlock~10-25 ns
Cache line moving between cores (contended atomic)~50-100 ns; more across sockets
Contended mutex handoff via futex (sleep and wake)several µs, including two context switches
Spinning while holder is preemptedup to a whole time slice (milliseconds)

The lesson in that table is that locks are not slow; contention is. A lock taken a million times a second by one thread is cheap. The same lock wanted by 32 threads becomes a queue: only one thread makes progress, the rest sleep and wake, and throughput stops scaling (Amdahl's law: the serialised fraction caps the speed-up). The remedies, in roughly the order to try them: hold locks for less time (do the slow work outside), split one lock into many (per-bucket locks in a hash map, per-CPU counters), use reader-writer locks when reads dominate (os5), and redesign to share less (message passing, per-thread state).
deep:
Memory ordering is part of every lock

CPUs reorder memory operations (store buffers, out-of-order loads) and compilers reorder code, as long as a single thread cannot observe the difference. Locks must stop this at their boundaries: taking a lock has acquire semantics (no read or write after it may move before it) and releasing has release semantics (no read or write before it may move after it). Together they guarantee that everything the previous holder wrote inside the critical section is visible to the next holder. On x86, locked instructions are full barriers and ordinary stores already have release semantics, so the costs are low; on ARM, which reorders more aggressively, acquire and release map to dedicated instructions (ldar, stlr). This is why the advice "use a lock or a proper atomic, never a plain flag" is not pedantry: code that "works" on x86 can break on ARM servers and Apple silicon. swe12 covers the language-level memory models.

Scalable spinlocks: MCS and Linux's qspinlock

With a ticket lock, all waiters spin on the same "now serving" word, so every release invalidates that cache line in every waiting CPU, and the release takes longer the more waiters there are. The MCS lock (Mellor-Crummey and Scott, 1991) gives each waiter its own queue node and has it spin on a flag in its own node; the releaser writes only the next waiter's flag, so each handoff touches one remote cache line regardless of how many wait. Linux's default spinlock since 4.2, the qspinlock, packs an MCS-style queue into a 32-bit word, spinning normally when uncontended and queueing when contended. The general idea, have each waiter spin on its own cache line, also shows up in user-space locks and in Java's AbstractQueuedSynchronizer.

Adaptive spinning and lock handoff policy

Whether to spin or sleep depends on whether the holder is running. Linux kernel mutexes do optimistic spinning: a waiter spins as long as the lock owner is currently running on another CPU, and sleeps as soon as the owner is not. User-space glibc offers PTHREAD_MUTEX_ADAPTIVE_NP with a bounded spin. A second policy choice is fairness. If an unlocking thread immediately tries to lock again, it often wins against the sleeping waiter, which still has to be woken and scheduled; that maximises throughput but can starve waiters. Strict FIFO handoff is fair but makes every handoff pay a context switch, causing lock convoys where throughput collapses to one handoff per wake-up latency. Many implementations compromise: allow barging, but switch to handoff mode after a waiter has waited too long (Go's sync.Mutex starvation mode after 1 ms is a documented example).

Read-mostly data: reader-writer locks, seqlocks and RCU

When reads vastly outnumber writes, mutual exclusion among readers is wasteful. Reader-writer locks (os5) allow many readers or one writer, but every reader still writes to the lock's counter, so on many cores the counter's cache line becomes the bottleneck. Two kernel techniques avoid reader writes entirely. A seqlock has the writer increment a sequence number before and after its update; readers read the number, read the data, read the number again, and retry if it changed or was odd. Readers never block the writer, which suits small data such as the kernel's clock. RCU (read-copy-update) lets readers proceed with no locks or atomic writes at all: writers make a new copy, publish it with a single pointer update, and free the old copy only after a grace period in which every CPU has passed through a point where it cannot hold an old reference. RCU is used throughout Linux (routing tables, file-descriptor tables, module lists) and has user-space versions (liburcu).

Lock-free structures and their traps

A lock-free stack pushes with CAS on the head pointer, retrying if another thread changed it. Such structures guarantee that some thread always makes progress, even if others are preempted, which matters in real-time and signal-handler contexts. They are notoriously subtle. The ABA problem: a thread reads head = A, is preempted; others pop A, pop B, push A back; the CAS sees A and succeeds, linking to the freed B. Fixes are tagged pointers (a counter alongside the pointer, checked with double-width CAS) or safe memory reclamation such as hazard pointers or epochs. And lock-free code still contends on the same cache line, so it is not automatically faster than a well-sharded locked design.

Kernel locking rules that explain user-visible bugs

Inside the kernel, code holding a spinlock must not sleep (the CPU cannot be given up while others spin on you), and data shared with interrupt handlers needs spin_lock_irqsave so an interrupt on the same CPU cannot try to take a lock its own CPU already holds, which would deadlock instantly. Linux's lockdep validator records the order in which every class of lock is taken and warns about any cycle the first time it could occur, rather than waiting for the deadlock to happen. The same idea (a global lock order, checked by tools) is the main defence against deadlocks in user space too (os6).
prod:
Recognising contention

Symptoms of lock contention: throughput that stops rising (or falls) as threads or cores are added; CPU that is either low with idle threads (they are sleeping on locks) or high in system time (futex calls) or high in user time with a spin function on top of the profile; and tail latency that grows with load. The tools: perf trace -s -p <pid> or strace -c -f on a short sample to count futex calls; off-CPU flame graphs (bcc's offcputime) showing the stacks where threads block; perf lock contention on recent kernels for both kernel and user locks; Java thread dumps (jstack) showing many threads BLOCKED on the same monitor with the owner's stack; Go's mutex and block profiles in pprof; and py-spy dump for Python threads.

Common culprits

A global lock around a cache or connection pool that every request takes; a logging library that serialises all threads on one file handle; the memory allocator (older glibc versions with many threads and few arenas, one reason services switch to jemalloc or tcmalloc, which use per-thread caches); a synchronised singleton such as a random-number generator or date formatter; and metrics counters incremented by every request on one shared atomic. The fixes follow the cost table: move slow work (I/O, serialisation, logging) out of the critical section, shard (striped locks, per-CPU or per-thread counters summed on read), use read-mostly structures, and avoid locks on the hot path entirely where possible.

False sharing

A classic performance bug with no lock in sight: an array of per-thread counters, each thread incrementing only its own slot. It looks embarrassingly parallel, but eight 8-byte counters fit in one 64-byte cache line, so every increment steals the line from the other cores, and the program can get slower as threads are added. perf c2c finds cache lines with heavy cross-core modification. The fix is to pad or align each thread's data to its own cache line (alignas(64) in C/C++, @Contended in Java, used in the JDK's own LongAdder). The LMAX Disruptor, a well-known low-latency Java queue, owes much of its speed to careful padding of its sequence counters.

Hangs: deadlock, lost wake-ups and stuck owners

A process whose threads are all asleep on futexes with no CPU use is usually deadlocked (os6) or waiting for a wake-up that was lost. Thread dumps give the lock graph: who holds what, who waits for what. Lost wake-ups come from waiting on a condition outside the mutex or with if instead of while; they show up as rare hangs under load. A third hang: a thread that died or was cancelled while holding a lock. POSIX robust mutexes (PTHREAD_MUTEX_ROBUST) report EOWNERDEAD to the next locker for locks in shared memory between processes, so the survivor can repair the data.

Python specifics

In CPython with the GIL, only one thread runs Python bytecode at a time (py8), so contention for the GIL itself looks like a lock problem: CPU-bound threads plus I/O threads produce poor latency for the I/O threads. Your own threading.Lock objects are still needed, since the GIL does not make compound operations atomic. In the free-threaded build (officially supported from 3.14), threads really run in parallel and the costs in this lesson apply directly, including contention on reference counts of shared objects, which the runtime mitigates with biased and deferred reference counting.
myths: A semaphore with a count of one is the same thing as a mutex.

They block the same way, but a mutex has an owner: only the thread that locked it may unlock it, which lets the system detect misuse, support recursive locking and apply priority inheritance (os3). A binary semaphore has no owner; any thread can post it, which makes it suitable for signalling between threads but loses those protections.
if (!ready) cond.wait() is enough when waiting on a condition variable.

It must be a while loop. Condition variables allow spurious wake-ups, and with the Mesa semantics every common library uses, a signalled thread only becomes runnable; by the time it reacquires the mutex another thread may have consumed the item or changed the state. Rechecking the condition after every wake-up is the only correct pattern.
Spinlocks are always faster than mutexes because they avoid system calls.

Spinning is only cheap when the lock will be released within roughly the time a sleep and wake-up would take, a few microseconds, and the holder is actually running on another CPU. If the holder is preempted, a spinning thread burns its whole time slice doing nothing. Modern mutexes spin briefly and then sleep, which captures most of the benefit without the waste.
Using volatile (or a plain boolean flag) is enough to synchronise threads.

In C and C++, volatile stops the compiler caching a value in a register but provides no atomicity and no ordering across CPUs, so a flag-then-data handoff can still expose stale data on weakly ordered hardware. Correct code uses atomics with acquire/release ordering or a real lock, which include the needed memory barriers. Java's volatile is different and does give ordering, which adds to the confusion.
Locks are slow, so lock-free code is always faster.

An uncontended mutex costs one atomic instruction to take and one to release, around 20 nanoseconds. What is slow is contention: many threads fighting over the same lock or cache line. Lock-free structures still contend on the same cache lines with compare-and-swap retries, and they are far harder to get right. Reducing sharing usually beats removing locks.
lab:
See a race, fix it three ways, and compare costs. Use Linux, WSL or macOS with gcc or clang.

  1. Save as race.c: 
    #include <pthread.h>
#include <stdatomic.h>
#include <stdio.h>
#include <string.h>
#define N 10000000
volatile long plain = 0; long locked = 0; atomic_long at = 0;
atomic_int spin = 0; long spun = 0;
pthread_mutex_t m = PTHREAD_MUTEX_INITIALIZER;
const char *mode;
void *work(void *_) {
    for (long i = 0; i < N; i++) {
        if (!strcmp(mode, "plain"))  plain++;
        else if (!strcmp(mode, "mutex")) { pthread_mutex_lock(&m); locked++; pthread_mutex_unlock(&m); }
        else if (!strcmp(mode, "atomic")) atomic_fetch_add(&at, 1);
        else { while (atomic_exchange(&spin, 1)) ; spun++; atomic_store(&spin, 0); }
    }
    return 0;
}
int main(int argc, char **argv) {
    mode = argv[1]; pthread_t t[4];
    for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++) pthread_create(&t[i], 0, work, 0);
    for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++) pthread_join(t[i], 0);
    printf("%s: %ld (expected %d)\n", mode, plain + locked + at + spun, 4 * N);
}
  2. Build and time each mode: gcc -O2 -pthread race.c -o race, then for m in plain atomic spin mutex; do /usr/bin/time -f "%e s, %S sys" ./race $m; done (on macOS use time ./race $m).
  3. Count futex calls in the mutex run: strace -f -c -e trace=futex ./race mutex.

What to look for. plain prints a total well below 40,000,000 and different each run: lost updates from the load-add-store race. The other three print exactly 40,000,000. atomic is usually fastest, since each increment is one locked instruction, though still much slower per operation than a single-threaded loop because the cache line bounces between cores. spin and mutex are slower still; the mutex run shows some system time and many futex calls (contended handoffs entering the kernel), while the spin run shows almost no system time but burns user CPU waiting. Try changing the thread count to 1: every correct version becomes fast, which is the point of the lesson: the cost is contention, not the lock.
recap: A race condition happens when threads access shared data concurrently and at least one writes, so the outcome depends on timing; the code that touches the shared data is a critical section that needs mutual exclusion.
Correct mutual exclusion needs exclusion, progress and bounded waiting; software-only algorithms such as Peterson's satisfy them on paper but break on modern CPUs that reorder memory operations.
Hardware provides atomic read-modify-write instructions such as test-and-set, compare-and-swap and fetch-and-add, which are the foundation of every lock.
A spinlock loops on an atomic instruction until it gets the lock; it suits very short critical sections on multiprocessors and kernel code that cannot sleep, and wastes CPU otherwise.
A mutex puts waiting threads to sleep; on Linux it is built on the futex system call, so the uncontended case is a single atomic instruction in user space and only contention enters the kernel.
A semaphore is a counter with wait (P) and post (V); counting semaphores bound concurrency, and unlike mutexes they have no owner.
A condition variable lets a thread sleep until some state changes; wait atomically releases the mutex and sleeps, and the condition must be rechecked in a while loop.
A monitor bundles shared data, a lock and condition variables so that every access is automatically synchronised, as in Java's synchronized methods.
Locks also act as memory barriers, making writes inside the critical section visible to the next holder.
In production, the cost of synchronisation is contention: measure lock wait time and futex activity, shrink critical sections, shard locks and avoid false sharing.
glossary: ABA problem
A lock-free bug where a value changes from A to B and back to A, so a compare-and-swap wrongly concludes nothing changed.
Acquire / release ordering
Memory-ordering guarantees attached to taking and freeing a lock or atomic: reads and writes after an acquire cannot move before it, and those before a release cannot move after it.
Atomic instruction
A CPU instruction that reads and writes a memory location as one indivisible step that no other CPU can interleave with.
Bounded waiting
The guarantee that a thread waiting to enter a critical section will get in after a bounded number of other entries.
Busy waiting
Repeatedly checking a condition in a loop while using CPU, instead of sleeping.
Cache line
The unit, typically 64 bytes, in which CPUs move data between caches and memory; two CPUs writing the same line force it to bounce between them.
Compare-and-swap (CAS)
An atomic instruction that writes a new value only if the location still holds an expected value, and reports whether it succeeded.
Condition variable
A queue of threads waiting for some condition on shared state, always used with a mutex; wait releases the mutex and sleeps, signal or broadcast wakes waiters.
Contention
Several threads wanting the same lock or cache line at the same time, forcing them to wait.
Critical section
Code that accesses shared data and must not be executed by more than one thread at a time.
False sharing
Threads writing different variables that happen to sit on the same cache line, causing the line to bounce between CPUs as if they shared data.
Fetch-and-add
An atomic instruction that adds to a value and returns the old value; used for counters and ticket locks.
Futex
Fast user-space mutex: a Linux system call that lets threads sleep on and wake waiters of an integer in user memory, used to build mutexes and condition variables.
GIL
CPython's global interpreter lock, which lets only one thread execute Python bytecode at a time (py8).
Lock convoy
A pattern where a contended lock is handed from thread to thread with a context switch each time, so throughput collapses to one handoff per wake-up.
Lost wake-up
A bug where a thread checks a condition, decides to sleep, and misses a signal sent between its check and its sleep.
MCS lock
A queue-based spinlock in which each waiter spins on its own cache line, so handoffs stay cheap however many threads wait.
Memory barrier (fence)
An instruction that stops the CPU and compiler from reordering memory operations across it.
Mesa semantics
Condition-variable behaviour where signal only makes a waiter runnable, so the waiter must recheck the condition; used by POSIX, Java and Python.
Monitor
A language-level construct that combines shared data, a mutex that every method takes automatically, and condition variables.
Mutex
A lock with an owner that allows one thread at a time into a critical section and puts other threads to sleep while they wait.
Mutual exclusion
The property that at most one thread is inside a critical section at a time.
Peterson's algorithm
A classic software-only lock for two threads using two flags and a turn variable; correct only with sequentially consistent memory.
Race condition
A bug where the result depends on the timing of concurrent operations on shared state.
RCU (read-copy-update)
A technique where readers take no locks and writers publish a new copy, freeing the old one only after all readers that might see it have finished.
Semaphore
A non-negative counter with two atomic operations: wait (P) decrements or blocks at zero, and post (V) increments and wakes a waiter.
Seqlock
A lock where the writer bumps a sequence number around each update and readers retry if the number changed while they read.
Spinlock
A lock that waiting threads acquire by looping on an atomic instruction until it succeeds.
Spurious wake-up
A return from a condition-variable wait without a matching signal, which the standards permit.
Test-and-set
An atomic instruction that sets a memory location to 1 and returns its previous value.
Ticket lock
A fair spinlock where each arriving thread takes a number with fetch-and-add and waits until the 'now serving' counter reaches it.
drill:
Review: the job queue that sometimes hangs

A teammate wrote this worker pool in Python. Under load tests it occasionally hangs with all workers asleep and items still in the queue; at other times a worker crashes with IndexError: pop from empty list. Find every bug, explain the interleaving behind each symptom, and fix it.

jobs = []
lock = threading.Lock()
cv = threading.Condition(lock)

def submit(job):
    jobs.append(job)
    with cv:
        cv.notify()

def worker():
    while True:
        if not jobs:
            with cv:
                cv.wait()
        with lock:
            job = jobs.pop(0)
        run(job)
Answer

Bug 1: lost wake-up (the hang). The worker checks if not jobs without holding the lock, then takes the lock and waits. Interleaving: the worker sees an empty list; before it reaches cv.wait(), submit appends a job and calls notify(), which wakes nobody because no one is waiting yet; the worker then waits and sleeps forever with a job in the queue. If every worker hits this, the pool hangs. The check and the wait must happen under the same lock, so that the notify cannot slip between them.

Bug 2: if instead of while (the IndexError). When a worker wakes from wait(), it assumes a job is there. But with Mesa semantics another worker that was not waiting can grab the lock first and pop the job, or the wake-up can be spurious; the woken worker then pops from an empty list. The condition must be rechecked in a loop after every wake-up.

Bug 3: the append is outside the lock. jobs.append in submit modifies shared state without the lock. In CPython the GIL happens to make a single list append atomic, but the code relies on that accident, breaks on a free-threaded build, and is the reason bug 1 is possible at all: state changes and notifications must both happen under the mutex.

Fix:

def submit(job):
    with cv:
        jobs.append(job)
        cv.notify()

def worker():
    while True:
        with cv:
            while not jobs:
                cv.wait()
            job = jobs.pop(0)
        run(job)                     # run outside the lock

Running the job outside the lock keeps the critical section short so workers do not serialise on it. In real code use queue.Queue, which implements exactly this pattern (plus a bound and timeouts), and use collections.deque rather than list.pop(0), which is O(n).
qa: E
What is a race condition? Give the classic example.

A race condition is when the result of a program depends on the timing of threads accessing shared data, with at least one writing. The classic example is two threads doing counter++ a million times each: the increment is a load, an add and a store, and if both load the same old value before either stores, one increment is lost, so the final count is less than two million and different on every run.
E
What is a critical section, and what properties must a solution to the critical-section problem have?

A critical section is code that accesses shared state and must not run in two threads at once. A correct solution needs mutual exclusion (at most one thread inside), progress (if nobody is inside and some want in, one of them gets in without indefinite postponement) and bounded waiting (a waiting thread gets in after a bounded number of others). Good solutions also avoid wasting CPU and work on multiprocessors.
E
What is the difference between a mutex and a semaphore?

A mutex is a lock with an owner: one thread locks it, the same thread unlocks it, and others sleep meanwhile. A semaphore is a counter: wait decrements it and blocks at zero, post increments it and wakes a waiter, and any thread can post. Use a mutex to protect shared data, and a counting semaphore to limit how many threads use a resource at once, such as ten concurrent database connections, or to signal events between threads.
Follow-up: Why does ownership matter? — It allows error checking (unlocking a mutex you do not hold), recursive locks and priority inheritance, none of which a semaphore can offer.
M
Why can't you implement a lock with an ordinary flag variable: while (locked) {}; locked = 1;?

Because the check and the set are separate steps. Two threads can both see locked == 0, both exit the loop, and both set it to 1 and enter the critical section. The check-and-set must be one indivisible operation, which is what atomic instructions such as test-and-set or compare-and-swap provide. On top of that, the compiler and CPU may reorder ordinary loads and stores, so even a clever algorithm with plain variables can fail.
M
How does a spinlock work, and when would you use one instead of a mutex?

A spinlock is an integer that a thread acquires with an atomic instruction such as test-and-set or compare-and-swap, looping until it succeeds, and releases by storing 0. Waiters never sleep, so handoff is very fast, but they burn CPU while waiting. Use one when critical sections are a few hundred nanoseconds, threads run on different CPUs, and sleeping is impossible or too slow, which is mainly inside the kernel, especially in interrupt handlers. In user space, a mutex that spins briefly and then sleeps is almost always better, because a spinning thread cannot know whether the lock holder has been preempted.
M
How is a mutex implemented on Linux?

With a futex. The mutex is an integer in user memory: 0 unlocked, 1 locked, 2 locked with waiters. Locking tries a compare-and-swap from 0 to 1; if it succeeds, no system call happens. If not, the thread sets the value to 2 and calls futex(FUTEX_WAIT, addr, 2), which sleeps only if the value is still 2, avoiding a lost wake-up. Unlocking sets the value to 0 and, if it had been 2, calls futex(FUTEX_WAKE) to wake one waiter. So the uncontended case costs one atomic instruction each way and only contention enters the kernel.
M
Explain how a condition variable is used, and why the wait is inside a while loop.

A thread takes the mutex, checks the condition on shared state, and while it is false calls wait, which atomically releases the mutex and sleeps; on wake-up it reacquires the mutex before returning. Another thread changes the state under the same mutex and calls signal or broadcast. The loop is needed because wake-ups can be spurious, and because with Mesa semantics the woken thread only becomes runnable: another thread can take the mutex first and change the state again, so the condition must be rechecked.

Follow-up: When do you use broadcast instead of signal? — When the change might let several waiters proceed, or when waiters wait for different conditions on the same variable, so a single signal might wake the wrong one.
M
What is a monitor?

A monitor is a language construct that packages shared data with the operations on it, and guarantees that only one thread executes inside any of those operations at a time, by taking an implicit lock on entry and releasing it on exit. Condition variables inside the monitor let threads wait for state changes. Java's synchronized methods with wait and notify, and C#'s lock with Monitor.Wait, are monitors. They reduce errors because the programmer cannot forget to take the lock.
M
What is false sharing and how do you detect it?

False sharing is when threads on different CPUs write different variables that sit in the same 64-byte cache line. Each write requires exclusive ownership of the line, so it bounces between CPU caches as if the data were shared, and a loop that should scale linearly with threads can slow down. Typical culprits are per-thread counters stored in one array. perf c2c on Linux reports cache lines with heavy cross-CPU modification; the fix is padding or aligning per-thread data to separate cache lines.
H
Explain Peterson's algorithm and why it fails on modern hardware without fences.

For two threads, each sets its own flag to say it wants in, then sets turn to the other thread, then waits while the other's flag is set and turn is the other's. If both want in, whoever wrote turn last waits, so exactly one proceeds, giving mutual exclusion, progress and bounded waiting under sequential consistency. Modern CPUs have store buffers: a thread's write to its flag can sit in its buffer while it reads the other flag from memory, so both threads can read the other's flag as false and both enter. Compilers may reorder the plain accesses too. A full memory fence between the writes and the reads, or sequentially consistent atomics, restores correctness.
Follow-up: Why learn it then? — It shows the structure of mutual-exclusion arguments and why real locks rely on atomic instructions and memory ordering rather than plain loads and stores.
H
Implement a counting semaphore using a mutex and a condition variable.

Keep an integer count, a mutex and a condition variable. wait: lock the mutex; while count is zero, wait on the condition variable; decrement count; unlock. post: lock the mutex; increment count; signal the condition variable; unlock. The while loop handles spurious and stolen wake-ups, and doing the check and decrement under the mutex makes them atomic. Signal rather than broadcast is enough because each post makes one unit available.

Follow-up: How would you add a timeout? — Use the timed wait variant and return failure if the deadline passes while count is still zero, remembering to recompute the remaining time on each loop iteration.
H
Why do locks need memory barriers, and what goes wrong without them?

CPUs and compilers reorder memory operations for speed, as long as a single thread cannot tell. Another thread can. If a thread writes data and then releases a lock with a plain store, the release could become visible before the data, so the next holder reads stale data. Lock acquire therefore has acquire semantics (later operations cannot move before it) and release has release semantics (earlier operations cannot move after it). Correctly using a lock gives you visibility for free; hand-rolled flags without atomics do not.
H
A service's throughput stops increasing beyond 8 threads on a 32-core machine and CPU shows high system time. How do you investigate lock contention?

High system time with flat scaling suggests threads blocking and waking through the kernel. Count futex system calls with perf trace -s or an eBPF tool; heavy futex wait and wake activity means contended locks. Find which lock: perf lock or lock-contention tracing on newer kernels, off-CPU flame graphs that show where threads block, or language tools such as Java thread dumps showing BLOCKED threads and the monitor owner. Also check for spinning in user space (perf top), cache-line bouncing with perf c2c, and allocator locks. Fixes are shrinking the critical section, sharding the lock or data (per-core counters, striped locks), using reader-writer locks or RCU-style read paths for read-mostly data, or redesigning to pass messages instead of sharing.

t: Classic synchronization problems: producer-consumer, readers-writers, dining philosophers
sum: The three problems every OS course and many interviews use to test synchronization: the bounded buffer with semaphores and condition variables, readers-writers and its starvation trade-offs, and dining philosophers with four ways to avoid deadlock, plus where each shows up in real systems.
prereq: os4

Mutexes give mutual exclusion; semaphores are counters with wait and post; condition variables let a thread release a mutex and sleep until signalled, and the condition must be rechecked in a while loop.
why:
The tools in os4 (mutexes, semaphores, condition variables) are like a box of woodworking tools: knowing what each one does is not the same as knowing how to build a chair. Synchronization bugs rarely come from not knowing what a mutex is. They come from combining correct primitives in the wrong order, waking the wrong thread, or letting one kind of thread starve another. To learn how to combine them, computer scientists distilled the recurring shapes of concurrent programs into a handful of classic problems.

Three of them cover most of what you will meet. Producer-consumer is the shape of every pipeline: one part of a system makes work, another part does it, and a buffer sits between them. Your web server's request queue, your logger, the pipe between grep and wc, and a Kafka topic are all producer-consumer. Readers-writers is the shape of shared data that is read constantly and changed occasionally: configuration, caches, routing tables. Dining philosophers is the shape of tasks that each need several shared resources at once: a bank transfer locking two accounts, a transaction locking two rows. It is the smallest example of deadlock.

These problems are interview staples for a reason. At campus and SDE level you will be asked to write the semaphore solution to the bounded buffer or explain why the naive philosophers deadlock. LeetCode's concurrency set (print in order, FooBar, H2O, dining philosophers) turns them into coding questions. At senior level the same ideas appear disguised: "why did this queue hang", "why do config updates cause latency spikes", "how would you prevent deadlock between these two services".

This lesson solves each problem properly, shows the tempting wrong versions and exactly how they fail, explains the trade-offs between solutions, and connects each one to the production systems where it lives.
primer:
Three scenes

A bakery counter. Bakers put trays of bread on a rack with ten shelves; shop staff take trays off to sell. If the rack is full, bakers must wait; if it is empty, staff must wait; and two people should not shove a tray onto the same shelf at once. That is producer-consumer with a bounded buffer: two kinds of waiting (full, empty) plus mutual exclusion on the rack itself.

A museum noticeboard. Any number of visitors can read the board at the same time without bothering each other. But when the curator changes a notice, nobody should be reading half of an old notice and half of a new one, and two curators should not edit at once. That is readers-writers: many readers or one writer. The hard part is fairness: if visitors keep arriving, does the curator ever get a turn? If the curator is always first, do visitors wait too long?

A dinner with too few forks. Five philosophers sit around a round table. Between each pair lies one fork, five in all. A philosopher alternates between thinking and eating, and needs both the fork on the left and the fork on the right to eat. If every philosopher picks up the left fork at the same moment, each then waits forever for the right one, which their neighbour holds. That is dining philosophers, and the frozen table is a deadlock.

Which tool fits which need

Before solving anything, it helps to map each need onto the os4 toolbox. "Only one at a time may touch this" is mutual exclusion, so a mutex. "Wait until there are some of these" (free slots, filled slots, seats at the table) is counting, so a counting semaphore, or a mutex plus a counter plus a condition variable. "Wait until this particular thing becomes true" (the queue is not empty, no writer is active, both my forks are free) is a condition, so a condition variable with a while loop. Most solutions in this lesson are just careful combinations of these three answers, and most bugs come from mixing them up: blocking on a condition while holding the lock that someone else needs to make the condition true, or using one waiting room for two different conditions. Keep asking two questions as you read: what exactly is each thread waiting for, and who is responsible for waking it?

What makes these problems hard

Each scene combines two needs. One is safety: nothing bad happens (no two writes to the same shelf, no reading a half-written notice, no fork used by two philosophers). The other is liveness: something good eventually happens (every tray eventually gets sold, the curator eventually updates the board, every philosopher eventually eats). It is easy to get safety by locking everything, and easy to get speed by locking nothing. Getting both, plus fairness, is the skill. The rest of this lesson builds each solution in steps, showing the wrong turns because interviewers ask about them.
body:
1. Producer-consumer: the setup

The buffer is usually a ring buffer: an array of N slots with an index where the next item goes (tail) and an index where the next item comes from (head), both wrapping around modulo N. Three things must be synchronised:

  1. A producer must not insert when all N slots are full.
  2. A consumer must not remove when no slot is full.
  3. Two producers (or two consumers) must not update tail (or head) at the same time, or they would write the same slot.

Requirements 1 and 2 are waiting for a condition; requirement 3 is mutual exclusion. The classic solutions use semaphores for the first two and a mutex for the third, or one mutex plus condition variables for all three.

2. The semaphore solution

Use three semaphores. empty counts free slots and starts at N. full counts filled slots and starts at 0. mutex starts at 1 and protects the indexes.

producer:                         consumer:
  item = make()                     wait(full)      # wait for a filled slot
  wait(empty)    # wait for a slot  wait(mutex)
  wait(mutex)                       item = buf[head]; head = (head+1) % N
  buf[tail] = item                  post(mutex)
  tail = (tail+1) % N               post(empty)     # one more free slot
  post(mutex)                       use(item)
  post(full)     # one more item

Trace it with N = 2, one producer and one consumer, starting empty (empty = 2, full = 0):

EventemptyfullBuffer
Consumer: wait(full) → blocks20[ , ]
Producer puts A: wait(empty), insert, post(full) → wakes consumer10 (consumed by the wake-up)[A, ]
Producer puts B01[A, B]
Producer tries C: wait(empty) → blocks (buffer full)01[A, B]
Consumer (woken earlier) removes A, post(empty) → wakes producer0 (consumed by the wake-up)1[ , B]
Producer inserts C in the freed slot02[C, B]

The counting semaphores carry the "how many" information, so nobody needs to look at the buffer to decide whether to wait. The mutex is only needed when there are several producers or several consumers; with exactly one of each, they always touch different indexes.

The famous bug: order of waits. Suppose the producer does wait(mutex) first and then wait(empty). When the buffer is full, the producer takes the mutex and then sleeps on empty while still holding it. The consumer, to make a slot free, must wait(mutex), which never succeeds. Deadlock. The rule: never block on a condition while holding a lock that the thread who would satisfy the condition needs. Waits on counting semaphores go outside the mutex. (The order of the posts at the end does not matter for correctness.)

3. The condition-variable solution, built in two attempts

Most production code uses a mutex and condition variables instead. First attempt, with a single condition variable:

def put(x):                          def get():
    with cv:                             with cv:
        while len(q) == N: cv.wait()         while not q: cv.wait()
        q.append(x)                          x = q.popleft()
        cv.notify()                          cv.notify()
                                             return x

It has correct while loops, the check and the wait are under the mutex, and it still hangs. Take N = 1, one producer P and two consumers C1 and C2:

  1. C1 and C2 call get, find the queue empty and wait.
  2. P puts an item and notifies; C1 is woken (made runnable). P loops to put again, finds the queue full and waits.
  3. C1 runs, takes the item, and calls notify(), meaning to wake P. But both C2 and P are waiting on the same condition variable, and the notify happens to wake C2.
  4. C2 rechecks (good), finds the queue empty, waits again. C1 comes back, finds it empty, waits.
  5. Now P, C1 and C2 are all asleep. Nobody will ever notify. Hang.

The bug is that one condition variable serves two different conditions ("not full" for producers and "not empty" for consumers), so a signal meant for one kind of waiter can be absorbed by the other kind. Two fixes: notify_all() (correct but wakes everyone, the thundering herd), or the proper design with two condition variables sharing one mutex:

import threading, collections
class BoundedQueue:
    def __init__(self, n):
        self.q, self.n = collections.deque(), n
        self.lock = threading.Lock()
        self.not_full = threading.Condition(self.lock)
        self.not_empty = threading.Condition(self.lock)
    def put(self, x):
        with self.lock:
            while len(self.q) == self.n:
                self.not_full.wait()
            self.q.append(x)
            self.not_empty.notify()        # wakes a consumer, never a producer
    def get(self):
        with self.lock:
            while not self.q:
                self.not_empty.wait()
            x = self.q.popleft()
            self.not_full.notify()         # wakes a producer, never a consumer
            return x

This is almost exactly how Python's queue.Queue is written (it has a third condition for join()), and how Java's ArrayBlockingQueue works with its notEmpty and notFull conditions. Go's buffered channels give the same semantics as a language feature.

4. Readers-writers: the first solution (reader preference)

The goal is to let any number of readers in together but give a writer the resource alone. The classic 1971 solution by Courtois, Heymans and Parnas counts active readers:

readers = 0
mutex = Semaphore(1)     # protects the readers counter
room  = Semaphore(1)     # held by a writer, or by the readers as a group

reader:                               writer:
    wait(mutex)                           wait(room)
    readers += 1                          ... write ...
    if readers == 1: wait(room)  # first reader locks writers out
    post(mutex)                           post(room)
    ... read ...
    wait(mutex)
    readers -= 1
    if readers == 0: post(room)  # last reader lets writers in
    post(mutex)

It is correct: a writer holds room alone, and readers hold it collectively from the first in to the last out. Its flaw is fairness. While at least one reader is inside, new readers walk straight in without touching room. If reads overlap continuously (a popular cache under load), readers never drops to zero and a waiting writer starves. This is reader preference.

5. Writer preference and fair versions

The second classic solution reverses the preference: once a writer is waiting, newly arriving readers must wait too, so the writer gets in as soon as the current readers finish. Now continuous writes can starve readers. The usual practical answer is a fair lock that serves arrivals roughly in order. A simple way, from Downey's Little Book of Semaphores, adds a turnstile: every reader passes through the turnstile (wait then immediately post) on arrival, and a writer holds the turnstile while it waits for the room. A writer that has arrived therefore blocks readers who come after it, while readers who arrived before it finish normally.

Real libraries choose differently, and it is worth knowing which you are using. glibc's pthread_rwlock_t prefers readers by default (a non-portable attribute selects writer preference). Go's sync.RWMutex blocks new readers once a writer is waiting, which also means a reader that recursively takes the read lock can deadlock if a writer arrives in between. Java's ReentrantReadWriteLock has a non-fair default and an optional fair mode. Linux kernel rwlock_t favours readers; its sleeping rw_semaphore is fairer.

6. Dining philosophers: four ways out

Edsger Dijkstra posed this as an exam problem in 1965 (with computers and tape drives), and Tony Hoare gave it the philosophers. The naive code, each philosopher i doing lock(fork[i]); lock(fork[(i+1) % 5]); eat(); unlock both, deadlocks as the primer's figure shows. Deadlock requires four conditions at once (os6 covers them formally): resources held exclusively, held while waiting for more, not taken away, and a circular chain of waits. Each solution removes one of them.

Solution A: order the resources. Number the forks 0-4 and make every philosopher pick up the lower-numbered of their two forks first. Philosophers 0-3 still pick left then right, but philosopher 4, whose forks are 4 and 0, picks fork 0 first. Now suppose everyone reaches for their first fork at once: philosopher 0 and philosopher 4 both reach for fork 0, and only one gets it. Whoever loses holds nothing, so the chain is broken and at least one philosopher (philosopher 3, whose second fork 4 is free) can eat. This breaks circular wait. It is cheap, needs no coordinator, and is the technique databases, kernels and careful application code use: a global lock order.

Solution B: limit who may try. A semaphore seats initialised to 4 (one fewer than the philosophers): wait(seats) before reaching for forks, post(seats) after eating. With at most four reaching for five forks, by the pigeonhole principle at least one of them can get both. This is the arbitrator or waiter solution. It is simple but caps concurrency and puts a central gate in front of every meal.

Solution C: take both or neither. Pick up both forks atomically, under one mutex, only when both are free; otherwise wait. Tanenbaum's textbook version gives each philosopher a state (THINKING, HUNGRY, EATING) and a condition variable; a hungry philosopher eats when neither neighbour is eating, and a philosopher who finishes checks both neighbours and signals any who can now eat. This breaks hold and wait. Its weakness is starvation: two neighbours who alternate eating can keep the philosopher between them hungry forever.

Solution D: back off. Take the left fork, try to take the right one (trylock or a timeout), and if that fails, put the left one down and retry later. This breaks no preemption by having threads release voluntarily. It avoids deadlock but risks livelock: all five pick up, fail, put down and retry in lockstep forever. Random back-off makes livelock vanishingly unlikely, which is exactly what Ethernet and many distributed protocols do.

SolutionBreaksCostStarvation?
Resource orderingCircular waitNeed a global orderPossible without fair locks
Arbitrator (N−1 seats)Circular wait (by limiting)Less concurrency, central gateAvoided with a FIFO semaphore
Both-or-neither (monitor)Hold and waitOne global lock for checksYes, neighbours can alternate
Try and back offNo preemptionWasted work, retriesLivelock risk without randomness

7. Two more patterns you will meet: barriers and rendezvous

A barrier makes N threads wait until all have reached a point, then releases them together, as in parallel simulations where every thread must finish step k before any starts step k+1, or data-parallel training where workers synchronise gradients each step. With a mutex, a counter and a condition variable: each arrival increments the count; if it is the last, it resets the count, increments a "generation" number and broadcasts; otherwise it waits until the generation changes (checking the generation, not the count, is what makes the barrier reusable). Python has threading.Barrier, Java CyclicBarrier. A rendezvous is the two-thread version: two semaphores at 0, each thread posts its own and waits on the other's, and neither proceeds until both have arrived.

8. Interview coding versions

LeetCode's concurrency problems are these patterns in disguise. "Print in order" (three threads must run first, second, third) is a chain of signals: two semaphores or events initialised to 0. "Print FooBar alternately" is two semaphores passing a turn back and forth, foo starting at 1 and bar at 0. "Building H2O" is admission control plus a barrier (see the questions). "The dining philosophers" is solution A or B. In all of them, state the invariant first ("at most two H in the current molecule"), choose the primitive that encodes it, and check the two failure modes: can a thread wait forever (liveness), and can two threads be inside something together that should be exclusive (safety)?
deep:
Why the semaphore bounded buffer needs no buffer inspection

A subtle strength of the semaphore solution is that the counting semaphores encode the invariant empty + full + (items in transit) = N. A producer that returns from wait(empty) has reserved a slot even before taking the mutex, so the mutex only orders index updates, and producers and consumers never have to look at the buffer to decide whether to wait. This is also why a lock-free single-producer single-consumer ring buffer is possible: with one producer and one consumer, the producer only writes tail and the consumer only writes head, each reads the other's with acquire semantics, and no mutex is needed at all. That design powers kernel network-card rings, audio buffers and io_uring's submission and completion queues (os11).

Choosing a condition-variable signalling strategy

Three refinements matter in high-throughput queues. Signal only on transitions that can unblock someone (put only needs to signal when the queue was empty, get only when it was full), which avoids futile wake-ups at the cost of more delicate code. Signal after updating state but before or after releasing the mutex? Signalling while holding the mutex is always correct; signalling after releasing it can save a wake-then-block bounce, and with modern futex "requeue" optimisations the difference is small. And for many consumers, batch: a consumer that drains up to k items per lock acquisition cuts lock traffic by k. Java's LinkedBlockingQueue goes further by using two locks, one for the head and one for the tail, so a producer and a consumer never contend unless the queue is nearly empty.

The cost model of reader-writer locks

A reader-writer lock looks like free concurrency for readers, but each reader acquisition atomically increments a shared counter and each release decrements it. On a 64-core machine with short read sections, that counter's cache line moves between cores on every operation, so readers serialise on cache traffic even though they never block each other logically. Benchmarks often show a plain mutex beating an rwlock for sections under a microsecond. Scalable alternatives distribute the reader count: per-CPU reader counters that writers must sum (Linux's percpu-rwsem; "big-reader" locks), seqlocks where readers write nothing, and RCU or copy-on-write publication where readers just load a pointer. The rule of thumb: an rwlock helps when read sections are long (microseconds or more) and writers are rare; for tiny reads of rarely-changed data, publish immutable snapshots.

Starvation-free dining: Chandy-Misra

For a distributed version (philosophers are processes that communicate only by messages), Chandy and Misra's 1984 solution makes forks "clean" or "dirty". Initially each fork is dirty and held by the lower-numbered neighbour, which makes the precedence graph acyclic. A philosopher who wants a fork asks its holder; the holder keeps a clean fork but must give up a dirty one, cleaning it before sending. After eating, both forks become dirty. Because a philosopher who has just eaten always yields to a hungry neighbour, nobody starves, and the graph stays acyclic so nobody deadlocks. The idea of ordering by recent use, so the one who waited longest wins, reappears in fair lock designs and in wound-wait and wait-die schemes in databases (os6).

The kernel's own bounded buffer: the pipe

Every shell pipeline is a producer-consumer system built by the kernel. A Linux pipe is a ring of page-sized buffers, 64 KiB in total by default (adjustable with fcntl(F_SETPIPE_SZ)). A writer that fills it blocks in write() until the reader drains some; a reader of an empty pipe blocks in read() until data arrives or every writer has closed its end, at which point read() returns 0 (end of file). Inside, the kernel uses exactly this lesson's design: a mutex on the pipe and two wait queues, one for readers and one for writers. That is why producer | slow_consumer automatically slows the producer down: backpressure for free (os12).

The sleeping barber and admission control

Another classic, Dijkstra's sleeping barber, models a server with a waiting room of fixed size: customers who find the waiting room full leave immediately rather than block. Its solution is a bounded buffer whose producers use a non-blocking try on the free-slot count instead of waiting. That is exactly load shedding: a web server that returns 503 when its request queue is full, rather than queueing indefinitely. Recognising when a producer should block (backpressure within a process or pipeline) versus give up immediately (shedding load from external clients who will retry) is a real design decision in every queue you build.
prod:
Bounded queues are your backpressure

Every production pipeline has queues: thread-pool task queues, in-process buffers before a database writer, socket buffers, broker topics. The most common failure is an unbounded queue between a fast producer and a slow consumer. Java's Executors.newFixedThreadPool uses an unbounded LinkedBlockingQueue, and Python's ThreadPoolExecutor also queues without limit, so a traffic spike or a slow downstream silently turns into gigabytes of queued tasks, then minutes of latency, then an out-of-memory crash. Bound the queue, decide what happens when it is full (block the producer, reject with an error, drop the oldest), and expose its depth as a metric. Queue depth that trends upward at constant input is the earliest warning that consumers are falling behind.

Thundering herds

Broadcast-style wake-ups appear in real systems beyond condition variables. Historically, many processes blocked in accept() or epoll_wait() on the same listening socket would all be woken by one incoming connection, and all but one would find nothing to do; Linux added EPOLLEXCLUSIVE and SO_REUSEPORT (net13) to wake only one. Cache stampedes are the distributed version: a popular cache entry expires and a thousand requests all recompute it at once (sc2's request coalescing and early refresh are the fixes). The common cure is to make one waiter do the work while the rest wait for its result.

Reader-writer locks in services

Read-mostly shared state (feature flags, routing tables, model registries, in-memory caches) is often protected with a reader-writer lock. Watch for three production problems: writer starvation under reader preference (config updates that never apply under load), reader stalls under writer preference (a slow writer stops all requests), and upgrade deadlocks (two readers each try to upgrade to a writer lock and wait for each other). The robust pattern is copy-on-write publication: build the new version privately, swap an atomic reference, and let readers use whichever version they loaded. Go's atomic.Value/atomic.Pointer, Java's volatile references to immutable maps, and Python's plain attribute rebinding (atomic under the GIL) all support it.

Deadlock in real systems looks like the philosophers

A bank transfer service that locks the source account then the destination deadlocks when transfers A→B and B→A run together; the fix is solution A, locking accounts in ID order. Databases see the same thing between transactions that update rows in different orders, detect the cycle, and abort one (os6, sc5); applications that order their updates avoid most of those aborts. In microservices, two services that each hold a connection or a lock while calling the other recreate the table at a larger scale. In each case, look for the cycle and break it with a global order, a single coordinator, or timeouts with back-off.

Diagnosing a hung pipeline

When a producer-consumer system stops, take a thread dump (jstack, py-spy dump, Go's SIGQUIT stack dump) and classify each thread: waiting on not-full, waiting on not-empty, waiting on a lock, or running. "Everyone waiting on conditions and nobody running" is a lost or misdirected signal (the single-condition-variable bug, or a notify outside the lock); "consumers all blocked on something downstream" is a dependency stall; "producers blocked on a full queue while consumers are blocked on a lock the producer holds" is the wrong-order deadlock from section 2.
myths: The order of the wait calls in the semaphore bounded buffer does not matter, as long as all of them are there.

It matters completely. If the producer takes the mutex before waiting for an empty slot, then with the buffer full it sleeps while holding the mutex, and the consumer, which needs the mutex to remove an item, can never make a slot free. Waits on counting semaphores must come before the mutex; posts can be in either order.
A reader-writer lock always makes read-heavy code faster than a mutex.

Readers still update a shared counter on every lock and unlock, so with short critical sections on many cores the counter's cache line becomes the bottleneck and a reader-writer lock can be slower than a plain mutex. It wins when read sections are long relative to the locking cost. For very short, read-mostly access, sharded locks, seqlocks or RCU-style copy-on-update do better.
Dining philosophers is a puzzle about forks with no practical relevance.

It is the smallest model of a system where each task needs several shared resources at once: transactions locking two rows, a transfer locking two accounts, a thread taking two mutexes. The naive solution's circular wait is exactly the deadlock those systems hit, and the standard fixes (global lock ordering, limiting concurrency, all-or-nothing acquisition) are the ones databases and kernels use.
Using notify_all (broadcast) everywhere is the safe choice.

Broadcast is always correct when waiters recheck their condition, but it wakes every waiter for every change. With 100 consumers waiting and one item added, 99 wake, contend for the mutex, find nothing and go back to sleep: a thundering herd that burns CPU and adds latency. Use separate condition variables per condition so that a single signal reliably wakes a thread that can proceed.
An unbounded queue between producers and consumers avoids blocking, so it is the safer design.

An unbounded queue only moves the problem. If producers are faster than consumers for long enough, the queue grows until memory runs out or latency becomes minutes. A bounded buffer makes producers wait, which is backpressure: it propagates the slowdown to the source, where it can be handled by shedding load or slowing intake.
