FIFO's worst moment is at the fifth access: it evicts page 1, the most heavily used page, because 1 arrived first, and pays for it immediately. LRU keeps 1 because it was just used. OPT does better still by knowing page 3 is never needed again. On the textbook string 7 0 1 2 0 3 0 4 2 3 0 3 2 1 2 0 1 7 0 1 with 3 frames, the counts are FIFO 15, LRU 12, OPT 9, the same ordering.

6. Belady's anomaly

Intuition says more frames means fewer faults. For FIFO, not always. On 1 2 3 4 1 2 5 1 2 3 4 5, FIFO has 9 faults with 3 frames and 10 with 4. With four frames, FIFO's queue happens to line up so that it evicts each page just before it is needed again. LRU and OPT cannot show this anomaly, because they are stack algorithms: the set of pages they would hold with n frames is always a subset of the set with n + 1 frames, so an extra frame can only turn a miss into a hit. That property is one more reason real systems approximate LRU rather than use FIFO.

7. Approximating LRU: the Clock algorithm

Exact LRU would require recording a timestamp or moving a page to the front of a list on every memory access. Hardware does not do that, and software could not keep up. What hardware does provide is the accessed bit in each page-table entry, set automatically on any access (os7). The Clock (second-chance) algorithm uses just that bit. Arrange the frames in a circle with a "hand". To pick a victim:

  1. Look at the page under the hand.
  2. If its accessed bit is 1, it was used recently: clear the bit (give it a second chance) and move the hand on.
  3. If its accessed bit is 0, it has not been used since the hand last passed: evict it, put the new page in that frame, and advance the hand.

The enhanced Clock also looks at the dirty bit and prefers, in order: not accessed and clean (free to evict), not accessed and dirty (schedule a write-back, evict later), accessed and clean, accessed and dirty. Evicting clean pages first avoids I/O on the critical path. On the textbook string from section 5, simple Clock gets 14 faults, between FIFO's 15 and LRU's 12, about what you would expect from a one-bit approximation.

8. Locality, working sets and thrashing

Programs do not touch memory uniformly. In any short window they concentrate on a small set of pages: the current function's code, the stack, the data structures being worked on. Peter Denning formalised this in 1968 as the working set: the set of distinct pages a process referenced in the last Δ time (or Δ references). As long as each process's working set fits in its frames, faults are rare, occurring mainly when the program moves to a new phase.

Thrashing is what happens when the working sets of all running processes add up to more than physical memory. Each process faults, evicting a page another process needs right away, which then faults, and so on. Processes spend their time blocked on disk; CPU utilisation falls. A historic disaster made it worse: schedulers of the 1960s saw low CPU utilisation and admitted more processes to raise it, which shrank everyone's frames further and deepened the collapse.

The cures all reduce demand relative to memory. The working-set model only runs a process if its working set fits; otherwise it is suspended (swapped out entirely) until there is room. The page-fault-frequency approach watches each process's fault rate: above an upper threshold it gets more frames (or, if none are available, a process is suspended); below a lower threshold it gives frames back. Modern systems add memory limits per group of processes (cgroups, os13), and, as a last resort, kill a process (os9's OOM killer).

9. How Linux reclaims memory

Linux does not use textbook Clock directly. For each NUMA node and memory cgroup, it tracks file pages and anonymous pages separately. The classic design keeps two lists for each: an inactive list of candidates for eviction and an active list of pages that have proved themselves by being accessed again. New pages start on the inactive list; a second access promotes them; reclaim scans from the old end of the inactive list, evicting pages whose accessed bit is clear and giving referenced pages another chance; and pages are demoted from active to inactive to keep the lists balanced. Since Linux 6.1, the multi-generational LRU (MGLRU) replaces the two lists with several age generations and finds accessed bits by scanning page tables in bulk, which cut reclaim CPU cost and improved decisions on many workloads.

When reclaim happens is governed by watermarks on free memory per zone. Below the low watermark, the background thread kswapd wakes and reclaims until free memory reaches the high watermark. If allocations outpace it and free memory falls to the min watermark, the allocating process must reclaim itself before it can continue, direct reclaim, which shows up as latency. How the kernel balances evicting file pages versus swapping anonymous ones is biased by vm.swappiness (default 60; 0 strongly prefers file pages, up to 200 for fast swap like zram) and adjusted by feedback about refaults, pages that were evicted and then needed again soon, a sign that list was being cut too deeply.
deep:
Why LRU is not always right: scans and frequency

LRU's weakness is a large one-time scan. A backup reading a 100 GB file once, or a query scanning a big table, touches every page exactly once; under pure LRU each newly read page is "most recent", so the scan flushes the genuinely hot data out of memory, and then the scan's pages are never used again. Solutions separate pages that have been used once from those used repeatedly. Linux's inactive list does this: a page needs a second access to be promoted to active, so a single scan cycles through the inactive list without disturbing the active set. Database buffer pools use similar tricks: PostgreSQL uses small ring buffers for large sequential scans so they do not evict shared buffers; MySQL's InnoDB inserts new pages at the midpoint of its LRU list. Research algorithms such as 2Q, ARC (adaptive replacement cache, which balances recency and frequency and was used in ZFS) and CLOCK-Pro formalise the same idea.

Stack algorithms and why Belady's anomaly cannot hit LRU

An algorithm has the inclusion property if, for every reference string, the pages it keeps with n frames are always a subset of those it keeps with n + 1 frames. LRU has it: with n frames it holds the n most recently used pages, which are among the n + 1 most recently used. OPT has it too. Any algorithm with the property, called a stack algorithm, can never fault more with more frames, because every hit with n frames is also a hit with n + 1. FIFO lacks it because its contents depend on arrival order, which changes with the number of frames. This analysis (Mattson et al., 1970) also gives a practical tool: from one pass over a trace, a stack algorithm's fault count for every memory size can be computed at once, which is how cache-sizing tools build miss-ratio curves.

Major faults are I/O, so I/O scheduling matters

A major fault is a small random read, and under memory pressure many processes issue them at once. On spinning disks each costs a seek; random 4 KiB reads at 100-200 per second can make a thrashing machine take minutes to respond to a keypress. On SSDs and NVMe the raw cost is much lower, so modern systems degrade more gracefully, but writing dirty anonymous pages to swap adds write traffic, and swap readahead (reading neighbouring swap slots) helps only when swapped pages are related. Compressed in-memory swap changes the economics: zram stores swapped pages compressed in RAM (often 2-3:1), so a "swap-in" costs a decompression of a few microseconds instead of I/O; Android, ChromeOS and Fedora use it by default. zswap is a compressed cache in front of a real swap device.

User-space fault handling: userfaultfd

Linux lets a process handle page faults for a region itself. With userfaultfd, faults on registered pages are reported to a user-space thread through a file descriptor; that thread fetches the data from anywhere (another machine's memory, a snapshot, a compressed store) and installs the page. This powers post-copy live migration of virtual machines (the VM starts running on the new host before its memory arrives; pages are pulled over the network on first touch), fast VM and container snapshot restore (Firecracker), and some garbage collectors. It is demand paging with the backing store replaced by your own code.

Telling the kernel what you know: madvise

Replacement and readahead are guesses; applications can improve them. madvise(MADV_SEQUENTIAL) on a mapping says "I will read this once, in order", so the kernel reads ahead aggressively and drops pages soon after use; MADV_RANDOM disables readahead, which wastes I/O for random lookups into a big mapped index; MADV_WILLNEED starts reading pages in before they are touched; MADV_DONTNEED and MADV_FREE tell the kernel that anonymous pages can be discarded (memory allocators use these to return freed memory, os9). Databases and search engines that memory-map large files tune these hints, and choosing wrongly shows up as either wasted disk bandwidth or extra major faults.

Memory cgroups change the unit of reclaim

On a shared host, global LRU would let one container's scan evict another container's hot pages. Memory cgroups (os13) keep separate LRU lists per group, so a group that exceeds its memory.high is throttled and reclaimed first, and one that hits memory.max reclaims from itself and, failing that, has a process OOM-killed inside the group. memory.low and memory.min protect a group's working set from reclaim caused by others. This turns thrashing from a machine-wide collapse into a per-workload problem, which is what made dense container packing workable.
prod:
Recognising memory pressure

"Free" memory near zero is normal on Linux, because the kernel fills spare RAM with page cache; look at MemAvailable in /proc/meminfo (an estimate of how much could be freed without swapping) instead. Signs of real pressure: vmstat 1 showing non-zero si/so (swap in and out per second) persistently; a rising major-fault rate (sar -B shows majflt/s, and per process ps -o maj_flt or pidstat -r); pgscan and pgsteal counters climbing in /proc/vmstat, especially allocstall and pgscan_direct (direct reclaim); kswapd using significant CPU; and PSI. Pressure stall information (/proc/pressure/memory, and memory.pressure per cgroup) reports the share of time in which some tasks (some) or all non-idle tasks (full) were stalled waiting for memory. A sustained full avg10 above a few percent means the workload is losing real time to reclaim.

The thrashing node

A classic Kubernetes incident: a node with swap off gets close to full because pods have generous or missing limits. The kernel cannot swap anonymous memory, so it evicts page cache, including the executable code of every process, which then refaults from disk. The node's disk read rate soars, load average climbs into the hundreds (tasks in D state waiting on I/O count, os2), SSH takes minutes, the kubelet itself stalls and the node goes NotReady. The kernel OOM killer does not fire because reclaim is technically still making progress. Fixes: accurate memory requests and limits so pods hit their own cgroup limit early; kubelet eviction thresholds (memory.available) and system-reserved/kube-reserved so the node keeps headroom; and PSI-based user-space OOM handling (systemd-oomd, Meta's oomd) that kills on sustained pressure rather than on total failure. Kubernetes long required swap to be off; newer versions support it as an opt-in, which with limits can absorb cold memory more gracefully.

Swap: tune it, don't fear it

On servers, a modest amount of swap (or zram) lets the kernel move genuinely cold anonymous memory (startup data, leaked-but-never-touched allocations) out of the way and keep more page cache, and gives a gradual warning slope instead of a cliff. What you must avoid is the hot working set being swapped. Use vm.swappiness to bias reclaim (lower values protect anonymous memory; for latency-critical services, 1-10 is common), and protect critical processes: mlockall() or cgroup memory.min/memory.low so their memory is not reclaimed. Garbage-collected runtimes need special care because a collection touches the whole heap: Elasticsearch documents bootstrap.memory_lock and recommends disabling swap for its JVM, and the general advice is to size heaps well below physical memory.

Latency from the page cache

Even without swap, page-cache eviction causes latency surprises: a service whose data files are memory-mapped or read through the page cache is fast while its working set is cached and suddenly slow after a big batch job, backup or log rotation evicts it. Symptoms are a burst of major faults or disk reads at the start of the day or after a deploy. Remedies include warming caches on startup, isolating batch jobs in cgroups with memory limits (so their page cache is reclaimed within their own group), using O_DIRECT or posix_fadvise(POSIX_FADV_DONTNEED) for one-pass streams, and reserving memory for the hot set with memory.low.

Direct reclaim and compaction stalls

When kswapd cannot keep up with allocation bursts, processes enter direct reclaim and stall, sometimes for tens to hundreds of milliseconds; a request that needs a high-order (multi-page) allocation may also trigger synchronous compaction. Tail latency spikes with no CPU explanation and rising allocstall or compact_stall counters are the signature. Raising vm.watermark_scale_factor (and, carefully, vm.min_free_kbytes) makes kswapd start earlier and keep more headroom; reducing large allocations and THP's synchronous defragmentation (os7) removes compaction stalls.
myths: A page fault is an error.

Most page faults are normal and expected. Touching freshly allocated memory, reading a part of a memory-mapped file for the first time, or writing to a copy-on-write page all fault, and the kernel quietly fixes things up and resumes the instruction. Only a fault on an address with no valid mapping, or one that violates permissions, becomes a crash (SIGSEGV).
Giving a process more frames always reduces its page faults.

For LRU and the optimal algorithm it does, but FIFO can fault more with more frames. On the reference string 1 2 3 4 1 2 5 1 2 3 4 5, FIFO takes 9 faults with three frames and 10 with four. This is Belady's anomaly, and it happens because FIFO's choice of victim ignores how pages are used.
Swap is only used when RAM is completely full.

Linux balances reclaim between the page cache and anonymous memory long before RAM is exhausted, guided by vm.swappiness. It may swap out anonymous pages that have not been touched in hours to keep more file data cached, which can improve overall performance. Free memory near zero is normal on Linux; what matters is whether reclaim keeps up and whether processes stall.
Disabling swap prevents memory problems.

Without swap, anonymous memory can never be reclaimed, so under pressure the kernel can only evict page-cache pages, including the code of running programs, which then must be re-read from disk constantly. The machine can thrash on file pages and become unresponsive before the OOM killer acts. Swap (or zram) gives the kernel somewhere to put truly cold data; what to avoid is relying on it for the hot working set.
LRU is what operating systems actually implement.

Exact LRU would require updating a timestamp or reordering a list on every memory access, billions per second, which no hardware does. Kernels approximate it with the hardware-set accessed bit: the Clock algorithm, Linux's active and inactive lists, and since 6.1 the multi-generational LRU all estimate recency by periodically checking and clearing that bit.
lab:
Simulate the replacement algorithms, reproduce Belady's anomaly, then count real page faults. Python 3; the last step needs Linux or WSL.

  1. Save as replace.py: 
    def fifo(refs, n):
    frames, faults = [], 0
    for p in refs:
        if p not in frames:
            faults += 1
            if len(frames) == n: frames.pop(0)
            frames.append(p)
    return faults

def lru(refs, n):
    frames, faults = [], 0            # least recently used at the front
    for p in refs:
        if p in frames: frames.remove(p)
        else:
            faults += 1
            if len(frames) == n: frames.pop(0)
        frames.append(p)
    return faults

def opt(refs, n):
    frames, faults = [], 0
    for i, p in enumerate(refs):
        if p in frames: continue
        faults += 1
        if len(frames) < n: frames.append(p); continue
        future = refs[i + 1:]
        victim = max(frames, key=lambda q: future.index(q) if q in future else 10**9)
        frames[frames.index(victim)] = p
    return faults

textbook = [7,0,1,2,0,3,0,4,2,3,0,3,2,1,2,0,1,7,0,1]
for f in (fifo, lru, opt):
    print(f.__name__, [f(textbook, n) for n in (1, 2, 3, 4, 5)])
belady = [1,2,3,4,1,2,5,1,2,3,4,5]
print("FIFO 3 vs 4 frames:", fifo(belady, 3), fifo(belady, 4))
print("LRU  3 vs 4 frames:", lru(belady, 3), lru(belady, 4))
  2. Run python replace.py.
  3. Count real faults (Linux/WSL): /usr/bin/time -v python3 -c "b = bytearray(500_000_000)" 2>&1 | grep -E "Maximum resident|page faults".

What to look for. With 3 frames the textbook string gives FIFO 15, LRU 12 and OPT 9, matching the lesson; the lists show LRU's and OPT's faults never rising as frames increase, with OPT always lowest. The Belady line shows FIFO going from 9 faults to 10 when given a fourth frame, while LRU goes from 10 to 8. In step 3, allocating a 500 MB zeroed bytearray causes roughly 120,000 minor faults (500 MB / 4 KiB, fewer if transparent huge pages back part of it) and zero major faults: demand-zero paging, with every page faulted in on first touch and no disk involved. Maximum resident size is about 500 MB plus the interpreter.
recap: With demand paging, a page is brought into memory only when it is first touched; until then its page-table entry is not present and costs no RAM.

A page fault traps to the kernel, which finds the region the address belongs to, checks permissions, gets a free frame (evicting a page if needed), fills it from zeros, a file or swap, updates the page table and restarts the instruction.

Minor faults are satisfied from memory in about a microsecond; major faults need disk I/O, roughly 100 microseconds on an SSD and 10 milliseconds on a spinning disk, so even rare major faults dominate access time.
When memory is full, a replacement algorithm chooses a victim: clean file pages are dropped, dirty ones written back, and anonymous pages written to swap.

The optimal algorithm evicts the page used furthest in the future and is a benchmark only; FIFO is simple but can suffer Belady's anomaly; LRU approximates optimal using the past; Clock approximates LRU with one accessed bit per page.
Programs have locality, so at any time they use a working set of pages; if the sum of working sets exceeds RAM, processes fault constantly and the system thrashes, doing I/O instead of work.
Fixing thrashing means reducing the load (fewer or smaller processes) or adding memory; faster eviction cannot help.
Linux keeps active and inactive lists (or multi-generational LRU) for file and anonymous pages, reclaims in the background with kswapd, and falls back to direct reclaim and finally the OOM killer.
glossary: Accessed (reference) bit
A page-table bit the hardware sets whenever a page is used; replacement algorithms clear and recheck it to estimate recency.
Anonymous memory
Memory not backed by a file, such as the heap and stack; it can only be evicted to swap.
Belady's anomaly
The counterintuitive case where adding frames increases page faults, which can happen with FIFO.
Clock (second chance)
A replacement algorithm that sweeps a circular list of frames, evicting the first page whose accessed bit is clear and clearing set bits as it passes.
Demand paging
Loading a page into memory only when a program first accesses it.
Direct reclaim
A process that needs memory freeing pages itself, synchronously, because background reclaim fell behind; a common cause of latency spikes.
Dirty page
A page modified since it was loaded, which must be written back before its frame can be reused.
Effective access time
The average time per memory access once the probability and cost of faults are included.
FIFO replacement
Evicting the page that has been in memory longest, regardless of how recently it was used.
Frame
A page-sized block of physical memory.
kswapd
Linux's per-node kernel thread that reclaims memory in the background when free memory drops below a watermark.
Locality
The tendency of programs to reuse recently accessed data (temporal) and data near it (spatial).
LRU replacement
Evicting the page that has gone unused for the longest time.
Major fault
A page fault that requires reading from disk (a file or swap).
MGLRU
Multi-generational LRU: Linux's page-aging scheme since 6.1, which sorts pages into several age generations instead of two lists.
Minor fault
A page fault resolved without disk I/O, for example by allocating a zeroed page or mapping a page already in the page cache.
OOM killer
The kernel mechanism that kills a process to free memory when reclaim cannot make progress (os9).
OPT (Belady's MIN)
The optimal replacement algorithm: evict the page whose next use is furthest in the future; requires knowing the future.
Page cache
Kernel memory holding the contents of recently read or written files, which doubles as the backing for memory-mapped files.
Page fault
The exception raised when a page-table entry is not present or forbids the access, handled by the kernel.
PSI
Pressure stall information: Linux statistics of the share of time tasks were stalled waiting for memory, CPU or I/O.
Reference string
The sequence of page numbers a program accesses, used to compare replacement algorithms.
Swap
Disk space (a partition or file) where the kernel stores evicted anonymous pages.
Swappiness
A Linux setting (vm.swappiness, 0-200, default 60) that biases reclaim between anonymous pages and file pages.
Thrashing
A state where the system spends most of its time moving pages in and out instead of doing useful work, because working sets do not fit in memory.
VMA
Virtual memory area: Linux's record of one region of a process's address space, with its range, permissions and backing file.
Working set
The set of pages a process has used in a recent window of time; roughly what it needs resident to run without frequent faults.
zram / zswap
Linux features that compress swapped pages in RAM, as a swap device (zram) or a cache in front of disk swap (zswap).
drill:
Diagnose: the nightly slowdown

A search service runs on 64 GB machines. Its index files (40 GB) are memory-mapped, and its JVM heap is 12 GB. Swap is 8 GB with default swappiness. Every night at 02:00 a backup job reads 200 GB of data files sequentially and sends them to object storage. From about 02:10 until mid-morning, p99 latency is three times higher than usual; CPU is normal. Overnight graphs show disk reads on the index volume jumping from near zero to thousands per second after 02:00, and a few hundred MB of swap in use by morning. Explain the mechanism and propose fixes.

Answer

Mechanism. The index is served from the page cache through memory mapping: queries are fast only while the hot parts of those 40 GB stay resident. The backup reads 200 GB of other files once, and every page it reads enters the page cache, which is shared machine-wide. Memory is full, so reclaim must evict something for each new backup page. The backup's pages are new and recently used, while some index pages have not been touched in the last few minutes, so index pages get evicted (a second access promotes pages to the active list, but less frequently used index pages sit on the inactive list and go first). After the backup, queries touch evicted index pages and take major faults: random reads on the index volume, the disk-read spike in the graphs, and latency triples. The cache only refills as queries happen to touch each page, which takes hours for the colder parts of the index, hence the slow recovery into the morning. The few hundred MB of swap are cold JVM heap or other anonymous pages swapped out as part of the same pressure; harmless unless the GC touches them, in which case they add GC pauses.

Confirm. sar -B or pidstat -r for major faults on the search process after 02:00; vmtouch or fincore on the index files before and after the backup to see how much is resident; /proc/pressure/memory during the backup.

Fixes. Stop the backup from polluting the cache: run it in its own cgroup with a memory.max or memory.high of a few GB, so its page cache is reclaimed within its own group; or have it read with O_DIRECT or call posix_fadvise(..., POSIX_FADV_DONTNEED) after each chunk. Protect the service: put it in a cgroup with memory.low set to cover the hot index plus heap, so reclaim prefers other memory. Lower swappiness for this host and lock the JVM heap (or disable swap for that cgroup) so GC never touches swapped pages. Optionally warm critical index files after the backup (vmtouch -t). Measure p99 and major faults the next night to confirm.
qa: E
What is demand paging?

Demand paging means a page is loaded into physical memory only when the program first touches it. When a program starts, the kernel sets up its address space with page-table entries marked not present; the first access to each page causes a page fault, and the kernel then loads that page from the executable, a file, swap or a zero-filled frame. Programs start faster, use only the memory they actually touch, and can have address spaces larger than RAM.
E
What happens on a page fault?

The CPU traps to the kernel with the faulting address and the type of access. The kernel looks up which region of the address space contains the address; if none, or the access is not allowed, it sends SIGSEGV. Otherwise it obtains a free frame, evicting a page if necessary, fills it (zeros for new anonymous memory, data from the page cache or disk for a file, data from swap for a swapped page), updates the page-table entry to present, and returns, so the faulting instruction runs again and succeeds. If disk I/O is needed the process blocks and another runs meanwhile.
E
What is the difference between a minor and a major page fault?

A minor fault is resolved without disk I/O: the page is newly allocated and zero-filled, already in the page cache, or needs a copy-on-write copy. It costs on the order of a microsecond. A major fault must read from disk, from a file or from swap, and costs about 100 microseconds on an SSD or around 10 milliseconds on a spinning disk. ps -o min_flt,maj_flt and /usr/bin/time -v report both counts.
M
Run FIFO, LRU and OPT on the reference string 1 2 3 1 4 1 5 2 1 4 with three frames.

FIFO: misses on 1, 2, 3; hit on 1; 4 evicts 1; 1 evicts 2; 5 evicts 3; 2 evicts 4; hit on 1; 4 evicts 5: 8 faults. LRU: misses on 1, 2, 3; hit on 1; 4 evicts 2, the least recently used; hit on 1; 5 evicts 3; 2 evicts 4; hit on 1; 4 evicts 5: 7 faults. OPT: misses on 1, 2, 3; hit on 1; 4 evicts 3, never used again; hit on 1; 5 evicts 4, used furthest away; hits on 2 and 1; 4 evicts any: 6 faults. LRU lands between FIFO and the optimum, as usual.
M
Explain the Clock algorithm and why it is used instead of LRU.

Frames are arranged in a circle with a hand pointing at one. Each page has an accessed bit that the hardware sets when it is used. To evict, look at the page under the hand: if its bit is 1, clear it and advance (the page gets a second chance); if 0, evict it. Pages used since the hand last passed survive, so Clock approximates LRU. True LRU would need to update ordering on every memory access, which is impossible in hardware at full speed, while Clock only needs the accessed bit that the MMU already sets.

Follow-up: How does the enhanced version use the dirty bit? — It prefers clean, unreferenced pages first, then dirty unreferenced ones (scheduling their write-back), because evicting a clean page needs no I/O.
M
What is Belady's anomaly?

It is the situation where giving an algorithm more frames causes more page faults. FIFO on 1 2 3 4 1 2 5 1 2 3 4 5 has 9 faults with three frames and 10 with four. It cannot happen with LRU or OPT, which are stack algorithms: the set of pages they hold with n frames is always a subset of what they would hold with n + 1, so more frames can only turn misses into hits.
M
What is thrashing and how can an OS detect and handle it?

Thrashing happens when the combined working sets of running processes exceed physical memory, so processes constantly fault, evicting pages others will need immediately. CPU utilisation drops because everyone waits on disk, and old schedulers that admitted more processes to raise utilisation made it worse. Detect it through high page-fault and swap rates and low progress (on Linux, vmstat si/so, major faults and memory pressure stall information). Handle it by reducing the load: suspend or kill processes, refuse new work, or add memory; the page-fault-frequency approach gives a process more frames when its fault rate is high and takes frames away when it is low.
M
Compute the effective access time with a page-fault rate p, 100 ns memory access and 8 ms to service a fault. What fault rate keeps slowdown under 10%?

EAT = (1 − p) × 100 ns + p × 8,000,000 ns, which is about 100 + 7,999,900p ns. For a 10% slowdown, EAT must be at most 110 ns, so 7,999,900p ≤ 10 and p ≤ about 1.25 × 10⁻⁶: no more than one major fault per 800,000 accesses. That shows why major faults must be extremely rare for performance to be acceptable.
M
Which pages does the kernel prefer to evict and why?

Clean file-backed pages are cheapest: they can be dropped immediately and re-read from the file if needed. Dirty file pages must first be written back. Anonymous pages (heap, stack) have no file behind them, so they can only be written to swap, and without swap they cannot be evicted at all. Among those, the kernel prefers pages that have not been referenced recently, using accessed bits. Linux balances file and anonymous reclaim with vm.swappiness and with feedback about which kind is being refaulted.
H
Why does Linux sometimes stall a process for hundreds of milliseconds even when there is no swap?

When free memory falls below the low watermark, kswapd reclaims in the background; if allocations outpace it and free memory reaches the minimum watermark, the allocating process must do direct reclaim itself, scanning lists and possibly waiting for dirty pages to be written back or compacting memory for a large allocation. Without swap, anonymous memory cannot be reclaimed, so the kernel evicts file pages, including executable code of running programs, which are then refaulted from disk. The process sees stalls; PSI memory 'some' and 'full' values and allocstall counters in /proc/vmstat reveal it. Remedies are more memory, raising min_free_kbytes or watermark_scale_factor so kswapd starts earlier, memory limits on the offending workload, and earlier user-space OOM handling.
H
How does Linux approximate LRU in practice?

Traditionally it kept two lists per memory cgroup and node for each kind of page (file and anonymous): an active list of pages considered hot and an inactive list of candidates. New pages enter the inactive list; a second access promotes them to active; reclaim scans the tail of the inactive list, evicting unreferenced pages, and refills it by demoting pages from the active list. It also tracks refaults, pages evicted and then needed again soon, to rebalance list sizes. Since 6.1, the multi-generational LRU replaces the two lists with several age generations and scans page tables for accessed bits in bulk, which reduced CPU overhead and improved choices on many workloads; distributions such as Fedora and ChromeOS enable it by default.
H
Design question: a Kubernetes node runs many pods and occasionally becomes unresponsive for minutes before pods are OOM-killed. What is happening and what would you change?

Pods without accurate memory limits push the node close to full. With swap off, the kernel can only reclaim file pages, so it evicts the code and data pages of every running process and refaults them constantly: the node thrashes on the page cache while technically having no swap. The kernel OOM killer only acts when reclaim makes no progress at all, which can take minutes. Fixes: set memory requests and limits so pods are OOM-killed inside their own cgroup, configure kubelet eviction thresholds so it evicts pods before the node is in trouble, reserve memory for the system (system-reserved and kube-reserved), and consider a PSI-based user-space killer such as systemd-oomd that acts on sustained memory pressure rather than waiting for total failure.
H
Why is it bad for a garbage-collected heap to be partly swapped out?

A tracing garbage collector visits every live object, and compacting or copying collectors touch large parts of the heap. If some of the heap has been swapped out, every collection triggers major faults across it, turning a GC pause of milliseconds into seconds or more, during which the application is stopped. That is why JVM and Elasticsearch guidance is to size the heap well within physical memory, lock it in memory or disable swap for the process, and leave the rest of RAM to the page cache.

t: Memory allocation: malloc, mmap, copy-on-write, fragmentation and the OOM killer
sum: How a process gets memory from the kernel (brk, mmap, overcommit), how malloc carves it into objects (free lists, size classes, arenas), why freed memory often does not return, how the kernel allocates its own memory (buddy and slab), how copy-on-write works, and what the OOM killer does when memory runs out.
prereq: os7
Memory is mapped page by page through page tables with present and writable bits; huge pages and TLB reach affect performance.
os8
Pages are faulted in on first touch; under pressure the kernel reclaims file pages or swaps anonymous ones, and thrashing sets in when working sets do not fit.
py8
CPython layers its own small-object allocator (pymalloc) on top of malloc, which is one reason Python processes rarely shrink.
why:
A service's memory graph climbs during the day, as expected, and then stays at the peak all night although traffic has dropped to almost nothing. A Python worker processes a large file, deletes every reference to the data, calls the garbage collector, and still reports 3 GB resident. A Java container with a 2.5 GB heap keeps getting killed for exceeding its 4 GB limit although the heap never fills. A machine with plenty of "free" memory refuses to start a process; another, with none, happily lets a program allocate 100 GB. And sometimes, in the middle of the night, the kernel picks a perfectly healthy database and kills it.

All of these are consequences of how memory is allocated, which happens at two levels. The kernel hands out memory to processes in page-sized pieces, lazily and often optimistically. Inside each process, an allocator (malloc in C, and the runtimes of Python, Java and Go built on similar ideas) carves those pages into objects of every size and decides when, if ever, to give pages back. Between them sit copy-on-write, which makes fork cheap and memory accounting confusing, and the OOM killer, the last resort when promises cannot be kept.

Interviews probe this from both ends. Classic questions: "what happens when you call malloc?", "what is fragmentation?", "explain copy-on-write", "how does the buddy system work?". Senior questions: "why does this service's memory never come down?", "why was this container OOMKilled?", "what is overcommit and should we disable it?", "design an allocator for this workload".

This lesson follows memory from the kernel to your objects and back: brk and mmap, overcommit, how malloc works inside (free lists, size classes, arenas), fragmentation and why freed memory stays, the kernel's own buddy and slab allocators, copy-on-write in detail, and the OOM killer, then how to diagnose memory growth in production.
primer:
Wholesale and retail

Think of memory allocation as two shops. The kernel is a wholesaler: it sells memory only in large, page-aligned lots (4 KiB at the smallest, usually much more), and each purchase is a system call, which is relatively slow. The allocator inside your process is a retailer: it buys wholesale lots and sells them to your code in any size you like, 24 bytes here, 3 KiB there, quickly, with no system call. When you return an item (free), the retailer puts it back on its own shelves for the next customer; it rarely sends anything back to the wholesaler. That one fact explains most "my memory never goes down" mysteries.

The analogy breaks in a helpful way. The wholesaler does not even deliver the goods when you buy them. Buying a lot only reserves addresses; the kernel puts real memory behind each page the first time you touch it (os8's demand paging). So a process can "own" 10 GB of address space while using 100 MB of RAM.

Three ideas to hold on to

Lazy, optimistic allocation. The kernel reserves address space instantly and backs it with frames only when touched. By default Linux even promises more than it has (overcommit), which works because most programs never touch everything they allocate: a thread reserves an 8 MB stack and uses 40 KB of it; a runtime reserves a large range to keep its heap contiguous. The catch is that a promise is not a guarantee, and the bill can arrive at an awkward moment, during an ordinary memory write rather than during the allocation call.

Copy-on-write. When memory is duplicated, by fork or by mapping a file privately, the kernel shares the pages read-only and copies a page only when someone writes to it. It makes process creation cheap and lets many processes share one copy of a program's code and unchanged data. It also makes the question "how much memory does this process use?" surprisingly hard to answer, because a page may belong to several processes at once.

The OOM killer. If the promises come due and reclaim (os8) cannot free enough, the kernel has no failed system call to report the problem through, so it kills a process instead. Which process dies is a policy decision you can influence, and in containers the decision is made per group of processes against the group's own limit.

What each layer costs

The layers differ hugely in speed. A small malloc served from a per-thread cache costs around 10-20 nanoseconds. One that has to take a lock and search the allocator's free lists costs more. One that needs fresh memory from the kernel costs a system call (os1) plus, later, one page fault per 4 KiB page touched, each with the kernel zeroing a page. That is why allocators buy from the kernel in big pieces and hoard what they get, and why the patterns in this lesson, keeping memory rather than returning it, are deliberate trade-offs of memory for speed rather than bugs.
body:
1. Getting memory from the kernel: brk and mmap

A process's classic heap sits just above its data segment, and its top is called the program break. brk (or the older sbrk(increment)) moves the break up to grow the heap or down to shrink it. Simple, but the heap must be contiguous, so it can only shrink from the top.

mmap is the general tool: map a region of a given length anywhere in the address space, either anonymous (zero-filled memory with no file) or backed by a file, and either private or shared. munmap removes it. Allocators use anonymous mmap for large blocks and for whole arenas, because each mapping can be released independently.

Neither call allocates physical memory. Both create or extend a virtual region (a VMA, os8) and return. The first read of an untouched anonymous page maps the shared zero page, a single read-only page of zeros; the first write faults again and gets a private zeroed frame. You can watch this: malloc(1 GB) returns in microseconds, and the process's RSS (resident set size) only grows as you write to the memory, about 262,144 minor faults for the whole gigabyte.

2. Overcommit: promising more than you have

If the kernel only reserves address space, how much should it let processes reserve? Linux's answer is set by vm.overcommit_memory:

ModeBehaviourConsequence
0 (default, heuristic)Refuse only requests obviously larger than RAM plus swapMost allocations succeed; shortage shows up later as OOM kills
1 (always)Never refuseUseful for sparse workloads; maximum OOM risk
2 (strict)Refuse once committed memory would exceed CommitLimit = swap + RAM × overcommit_ratio/100 (ratio defaults to 50)malloc can fail with NULL; OOM kills become rare

Why overcommit at all? Because programs reserve far more than they use: thread stacks reserve 8 MB each but touch kilobytes; runtimes reserve large address ranges; and fork of a 20 GB process would need another 20 GB of commitment under strict accounting, even if the child immediately calls exec. /proc/meminfo shows Committed_AS (total promised) and CommitLimit; on a typical desktop, Committed_AS exceeds physical RAM comfortably.

3. Inside malloc: blocks, headers and free lists

An allocator must answer two questions fast: where is a free block of at least n bytes, and how big was the block being freed? The basic design: every block (glibc calls them chunks) carries a small header with its size, and free chunks are linked into free lists. In glibc on 64-bit systems the size field takes 8 bytes and chunks are multiples of 16 bytes, so malloc(24) gets a 32-byte chunk; malloc(1) also gets 32, the minimum. That rounding is internal fragmentation.

Two operations keep the heap usable:

  • Splitting: to serve a 100-byte request from a free 1,000-byte chunk, cut off what is needed and put the remainder back on a free list.
  • Coalescing: when a chunk is freed and its neighbour is also free, merge them into one larger free chunk, so the heap does not degrade into tiny pieces. The header (and, for free chunks, a footer) lets the allocator find neighbours' sizes in constant time.

Which free block to pick? First fit takes the first big-enough block (fast, but small fragments pile up at the front); best fit takes the smallest big-enough block (less waste per request, but leaves tiny unusable slivers and needs searching); next fit continues from where the last search ended. Real allocators avoid searching altogether by keeping separate lists per size range, called bins or size classes, so a request goes straight to the list that can serve it.

4. glibc malloc in practice

glibc's allocator (ptmalloc) layers several mechanisms:

  1. tcache: a small per-thread cache of recently freed chunks per size (up to 7 per size, for chunks up to about 1 KiB), checked first with no locking at all.
  2. Bins: per-arena free lists for small sizes (exact sizes), large sizes (ranges, sorted), plus an "unsorted" list where freed chunks wait briefly so they can be reused immediately or coalesced.
  3. The top chunk: the free space at the end of the heap, split to serve requests no bin can; when it is exhausted the heap grows with brk, and when it grows large enough after frees (128 KiB by default, M_TRIM_THRESHOLD) the heap is trimmed back.
  4. Direct mmap for big requests: at or above the mmap threshold (128 KiB by default, raised dynamically up to 32 MiB as the program frees large blocks), the chunk gets its own mapping, and free unmaps it at once.
  5. Arenas: to reduce lock contention, threads are spread over multiple arenas, each with its own lock and heap; on 64-bit systems glibc allows up to 8 × (number of cores) arenas by default. MALLOC_ARENA_MAX caps this.

Here is a short trace on a fresh 64-bit process:

p = malloc(24)       # tcache/bins empty → split 32 bytes from the top chunk
q = malloc(5000)     # split 5,008 bytes from the top chunk
r = malloc(200000)   # ≥ 128 KiB → separate mmap of ~200 KiB (page-rounded)
free(p)              # 32-byte chunk → this thread's tcache
s = malloc(20)       # also a 32-byte chunk → served straight from tcache (s == p)
free(r)              # munmap: those pages go back to the kernel immediately
free(q)              # 5,008-byte chunk → unsorted bin; may coalesce with top

5. Fragmentation, and why memory does not come back

Suppose a program allocates 10,000 objects of 1 KiB (about 10 MB of heap) and then frees every other one. Now about 5 MB of the heap is free, in 5,000 holes of 1 KiB each, each sandwiched between live objects. A 2 KiB request cannot use any of them, so the heap grows. And the heap cannot be trimmed, because trimming only works from the top, where a live object sits. This is external fragmentation within the heap, and it is the main reason a long-running process's RSS stays near its historical peak.

Allocators fight this in several ways. Size classes keep like-sized objects together so holes are reusable by the next object of that size. Allocators can release whole free pages in the middle of the heap with madvise(MADV_DONTNEED) or MADV_FREE, which keeps the address range but drops the frames (glibc does this in malloc_trim(); jemalloc and tcmalloc do it routinely with decay timers). And programs can avoid the pattern by allocating long-lived and short-lived objects from different pools or arenas, so short-lived ones can be released wholesale.

6. Multithreaded allocators

A single heap with one lock would serialise every allocation in a 64-thread server (os4's contention problem). Modern allocators are designed around thread caches: each thread keeps free objects per size class and serves most requests from them without any locks, exchanging batches with a central pool only when its cache runs empty or overflows. jemalloc (FreeBSD's allocator, used by Redis and many large services), tcmalloc (Google's, with per-CPU caches using restartable sequences) and mimalloc (Microsoft's, with per-page free lists) all follow this pattern, and also organise memory into page-sized runs dedicated to one size class, which bounds fragmentation. The trade-off is memory held idle in caches per thread, and glibc's per-thread arenas, in particular, can multiply fragmentation in programs with hundreds of threads. Swapping allocators usually needs no code change: LD_PRELOAD=libjemalloc.so.

7. How the kernel allocates its own memory: buddy and slab

The kernel manages physical frames with the buddy allocator. Free memory is kept in blocks of 2order contiguous pages, from order 0 (4 KiB) to order 10 (4 MiB), with a free list per order. Worked example: a request for order 1 (8 KiB) when only an order-3 block (32 KiB, pages 0-7) is free:

  1. Split the order-3 block into two order-2 buddies: pages 0-3 and 4-7. Put 4-7 on the order-2 list.
  2. Split pages 0-3 into order-1 buddies: 0-1 and 2-3. Put 2-3 on the order-1 list.
  3. Return pages 0-1.

When pages 0-1 are freed, the allocator checks their buddy (2-3, found by flipping one bit of the block's page number). If it is free, they merge into 0-3, whose buddy 4-7 is also free, so they merge back into 0-7. Merging only equal-size buddies keeps it fast and limits fragmentation, though a long-running system still ends up with few high-order blocks free; /proc/buddyinfo shows the count per order, and compaction migrates pages to rebuild large blocks (needed for huge pages, os7).

On top of the buddy allocator sits the slab layer (SLUB on modern Linux). The kernel allocates millions of identical small objects (inodes, directory entries, socket buffers, task structures). A slab cache takes pages from the buddy allocator and divides them into slots of one object type, with per-CPU free lists for lock-free fast paths. kmalloc uses general caches of common sizes. slabtop shows which caches hold the most memory, the place to look when "used" memory is high but no process owns it (the dentry and inode caches after scanning millions of files are a common, reclaimable example).

8. Copy-on-write in detail

os2 introduced copy-on-write for fork. Here is the mechanism page by page:

  1. At fork, the kernel copies the parent's page tables for the child. For every private writable page, it clears the writable bit in both page tables and increments the frame's share count. Both processes now map the same frames, read-only.
  2. Reads by either process proceed normally: no fault, no copy.
  3. A write by, say, the child faults (writable bit clear). The kernel checks the region: it is supposed to be writable, so this is copy-on-write, not an error. If the frame is still shared, it allocates a new frame, copies the 4 KiB, maps the copy writable in the child, and decrements the original's share count. If the frame is no longer shared (the other process already copied or exited), it simply sets the writable bit again, no copy needed.
  4. The faulting instruction restarts and succeeds.

The same mechanism serves private file mappings (MAP_PRIVATE): a program's data segment is mapped from the executable copy-on-write, so every running instance shares the file's pages until it modifies a global variable. Copy-on-write is also why memory accounting after fork is confusing: both processes report the shared pages in their RSS, which is why PSS (os2, os7) exists.

9. When memory runs out: the OOM killer

When an allocation needs a frame and reclaim (os8) cannot free one after repeated attempts, the kernel invokes the OOM killer (out of memory). It cannot fail the allocation, because the "allocation" is often a page fault in the middle of some instruction, with no system call to return an error from. So it frees memory the only way left: by killing a process.

Choosing the victim. For each eligible process, the kernel computes a badness score: roughly the process's memory footprint (resident memory plus swap entries plus page-table pages) as a share of the memory available, scaled to 0-1000, plus the process's oom_score_adj (-1000 to +1000). The highest score dies with SIGKILL. -1000 means never kill (sshd and critical daemons often set it); /proc/<pid>/oom_score shows the current score. The kernel log records the event: "Out of memory: Killed process 4321 (java) total-vm:..., anon-rss:..., oom_score_adj:0".

In cgroups. Containers usually die from a cgroup limit rather than global exhaustion. When a cgroup reaches memory.max, the kernel first reclaims within the group (including its page cache); if that fails, it OOM-kills a process inside the group only. Kubernetes reports this as OOMKilled with exit code 137 (128 + signal 9). memory.high, set below max, throttles and reclaims a group before it reaches the hard limit, and memory.oom.group kills all processes in the group together, which suits services where a partial kill leaves a broken half.
deep:
How tcache and freed chunks become security bugs

Allocators keep their bookkeeping inside the freed memory itself: a free chunk's first bytes hold the pointer to the next free chunk. A use-after-free bug writes into such a chunk after free, overwriting that pointer, and a later malloc can be tricked into returning an attacker-chosen address, the root of many heap exploits. A double free puts the same chunk on a free list twice, so two later allocations overlap. glibc has added hardening over the years: checks for obvious double frees in tcache, "safe-linking" (since 2.32) that mangles free-list pointers with address bits so forged pointers fail alignment checks, and integrity checks on chunk sizes. Tools find these bugs before attackers do: AddressSanitizer replaces the allocator with one that keeps freed memory poisoned in quarantine and checks every access; production allocators such as Scudo (Android) and hardened_malloc trade some speed for randomisation and isolation.

Per-CPU caches and restartable sequences

Per-thread caches waste memory in programs with thousands of threads, most of them idle, each holding its own stash. tcmalloc's newer design uses per-CPU caches instead: a thread allocates from the cache of whichever CPU it is running on. The danger is being preempted or migrated halfway through updating that cache. Linux's restartable sequences (rseq) solve this: the thread registers a critical region, and if the kernel preempts or migrates it inside the region, it restarts the thread at an abort handler instead of resuming mid-update. The result is lock-free, atomic-free per-CPU operations with memory bounded by core count rather than thread count.

Arena allocation and region-based memory

When many objects share a lifetime, such as everything allocated while handling one request or compiling one function, freeing them individually is wasted work. An arena (region, bump allocator) allocates by bumping a pointer through a large block and frees everything at once by resetting the pointer. It is extremely fast and has zero fragmentation within its lifetime. Compilers, game engines (per-frame arenas), protobuf's arena option, and Postgres's memory contexts use it; Go and Java's young generation achieve a similar effect with bump allocation plus a copying collector.

Kernel same-page merging and memory deduplication

KSM (kernel same-page merging) scans memory regions that applications mark with madvise(MADV_MERGEABLE), finds pages with identical contents, and merges them into one copy-on-write page. It is useful for hosts running many similar VMs, where guest kernels and libraries are identical, saving substantial memory at the cost of scanning CPU. It has a security side effect: writing to a merged page takes longer (the copy), which leaks whether another process had an identical page, a timing side channel that led cloud providers to disable cross-tenant merging.

Garbage-collected runtimes sit on the same layers

Java, Go, .NET and JavaScript engines do not call malloc for each object. They reserve large regions with mmap and allocate objects inside them by bumping a pointer in a thread-local buffer, which is even faster than a thread-cached malloc. Freeing is done by the garbage collector in bulk. The kernel-facing behaviour is the same, though: the runtime decides when to hand memory back (the JVM's -XX:SoftMaxHeapSize and periodic uncommit in G1 and ZGC, Go's background scavenger returning pages with MADV_DONTNEED or MADV_FREE), and until it does, the pages count as resident. With MADV_FREE, freed pages stay counted in RSS until the kernel actually needs them, which is why Go programs once appeared to "leak" on Linux: RSS stayed high although the memory was reclaimable. Go 1.16 switched its default back to MADV_DONTNEED for clearer accounting.

NUMA placement: first touch

On multi-socket machines (os3), the kernel's default policy places a page on the NUMA node of the CPU that first touches it, not the one that allocated it. A program that initialises a big array from one thread puts all of it on one node, and then threads on the other socket access it remotely at higher latency and lower bandwidth. Solutions: initialise data in parallel from the threads that will use it, set policies with numactl --interleave=all or mbind, or let automatic NUMA balancing migrate pages towards their users (it samples accesses by temporarily unmapping pages, at some CPU cost). Databases often recommend interleaving their buffer pools.
prod:
Leak, fragmentation or cache?

"Memory keeps growing" has three common explanations, and the fix depends on which. A leak: live objects accumulate (unbounded caches, lists that are appended to forever, listeners never removed); heap profilers (heaptrack, jemalloc's profiling, tracemalloc in Python (py8), heap dumps in Java) show the growing call site. Fragmentation or allocator retention: live data is stable but RSS is not; compare the allocator's own statistics (malloc_info/malloc_stats in glibc, stats.allocated versus stats.resident in jemalloc) with RSS, and if "allocated" is flat while "resident" climbs, it is the allocator holding free memory. Cache: page cache or slab growth that is reclaimable under pressure; it appears in buff/cache or in a container's memory.stat as file, not in the process's anonymous RSS. /proc/<pid>/smaps_rollup breaks a process's memory into anonymous, file-backed, shared and swapped.

The glibc arena problem

Multithreaded programs on glibc, especially JVMs with many native threads and Python or Ruby servers with threads, can see native memory balloon because each of up to 8 × cores arenas fragments independently, and freed memory in one arena cannot serve another thread's requests. Two widely used mitigations: set MALLOC_ARENA_MAX=2 (or 4) in the environment, trading some contention for much lower fragmentation, or switch to jemalloc or tcmalloc with LD_PRELOAD. Many teams report RSS drops of tens of percent from either change; measure throughput too, since fewer arenas can increase lock contention.

OOMKilled containers

When a pod shows OOMKilled (exit 137), first establish whether it was the container's own limit or node pressure (the kubelet evicting pods shows up differently, as an eviction event). Then account for everything the cgroup counts: anonymous memory of every process in the container, page cache from files it read or wrote (reclaimable, but counted until reclaimed), kernel memory such as socket buffers, and tmpfs files (an emptyDir with medium: Memory lives in RAM). For JVMs, the heap is only part: metaspace, threads, code cache, direct buffers and native allocations need headroom; modern JVMs size the heap from the container limit (-XX:MaxRAMPercentage), and leaving 25% or more for non-heap use is common practice. Go programs can set GOMEMLIMIT so the GC works harder before the limit. Watch memory.events (high, max, oom, oom_kill counters) to see how close a container runs to its limit before it dies.

Protecting what matters from the OOM killer

On hosts that run a mix of workloads, set oom_score_adj so that the right thing dies: negative for critical daemons (systemd sets OOMScoreAdjust= per unit; Kubernetes assigns -997 to Guaranteed pods and up to 1000 to BestEffort pods), positive for batch work that can be retried. Because the kernel OOM killer acts late, after the system may have thrashed for minutes (os8), production fleets increasingly run user-space killers (systemd-oomd, oomd, earlyoom) that kill based on sustained memory pressure (PSI) or free-memory thresholds, which keeps the machine responsive.

Allocation in hot paths

Allocation is cheap but not free, roughly tens of nanoseconds for a cached small allocation, and much more when it falls through to locking, page faults or system calls. Latency-critical code (trading systems, packet processing, game loops, inference servers) avoids allocating in steady state: preallocate buffers, reuse objects through pools, use arenas per request. Profilers show the cost under names like malloc, _int_malloc, page_fault and clear_page (the kernel zeroing new pages). A burst of first-touch faults after startup or a big allocation also explains why a service is slow for its first few seconds; pre-touching memory (MAP_POPULATE, -XX:+AlwaysPreTouch in the JVM) moves that cost to startup.
myths: If malloc returns a non-NULL pointer, the memory is really available.

With Linux's default overcommit setting, malloc of a large block only reserves address space; physical pages are allocated when first written. If the machine later runs out of memory while you touch those pages, there is no error code to return, because no system call is in progress: the OOM killer kills some process instead, possibly yours. Strict accounting (vm.overcommit_memory=2) makes allocation fail up front instead, at the cost of refusing allocations that would never have been used.
free() gives memory back to the operating system.

free() usually returns the block to the allocator's own free lists for reuse inside the process. Memory goes back to the kernel only when a whole mmap-allocated block is freed, when free space at the top of the heap is trimmed, or when the allocator explicitly releases whole free pages with madvise. A heap fragmented by a few long-lived objects can keep its resident size high for the life of the process.
A process killed by the OOM killer must have been leaking memory.

The OOM killer chooses a victim mostly by how much memory it uses, adjusted by oom_score_adj, not by who caused the shortage. A large, well-behaved database can be killed because a small runaway process pushed the machine over the edge. In containers, a cgroup hitting its own memory.max kills a process inside that cgroup, which may simply mean the limit is too low for a normal peak.
Copy-on-write makes fork() essentially free.

It avoids copying data pages at fork time, but the kernel still copies all page tables and marks every writable page read-only, which takes noticeable time for large processes. Afterwards, every first write to a shared page costs a page fault and a 4 KiB copy, so a write-heavy parent can end up duplicating much of its memory during the child's lifetime.
Memory fragmentation is a problem of the past now that we have virtual memory.

Paging removed external fragmentation of physical memory for ordinary pages, but fragmentation is alive at two other levels: inside each process's heap, where free chunks scattered between live objects cannot be returned or reused for larger requests, and in physical memory for huge pages and multi-page kernel allocations, which need contiguous frames and may require compaction.
lab:
Watch lazy allocation, copy-on-write and memory accounting in a real process. Linux or WSL with Python 3.

  1. Save as mem.py: 
    import mmap, os, time

def rss():
    with open(f"/proc/{os.getpid()}/status") as f:
        return next(l.split()[1] for l in f if l.startswith("VmRSS")) + " kB"

def roll(pid):
    out = {}
    with open(f"/proc/{pid}/smaps_rollup") as f:
        for l in f:
            k = l.split(":")[0]
            if k in ("Rss", "Pss", "Shared_Clean", "Shared_Dirty", "Private_Dirty"):
                out[k] = l.split()[1] + " kB"
    return out

size = 512 * 1024 * 1024
m = mmap.mmap(-1, size, flags=mmap.MAP_PRIVATE)   # private anonymous, untouched
print("after mmap:   ", rss())
for i in range(0, size // 2, 4096): m[i] = 1   # touch the first half
print("touched half: ", rss())

pid = os.fork()
if pid == 0:
    time.sleep(1)                           # shared with parent, copy-on-write
    print("child before:", roll(os.getpid()))
    for i in range(0, size // 4, 4096): m[i] = 2   # write a quarter
    print("child after: ", roll(os.getpid()))
    os._exit(0)
os.waitpid(pid, 0)
  2. Run python3 mem.py.
  3. Look at the system-wide numbers: grep -E "Committed_AS|CommitLimit|AnonPages|PageTables" /proc/meminfo and cat /proc/sys/vm/overcommit_memory.

What to look for. After mmap of 512 MiB, RSS barely moves: only address space was reserved. Touching half adds about 262,144 kB (256 MiB) to RSS, page by page (the extra beyond that is the interpreter). In the child before writing, its touched pages are shared with the parent: Shared_Dirty is around 256 MiB, and Pss is about half of Rss because each shared page is split between two processes. After the child writes a quarter of the mapping (the first 128 MiB, all inside the touched half), about 131,072 kB moves from shared to Private_Dirty: copy-on-write copied exactly the pages written, no more. Committed_AS is usually larger than physical RAM on a desktop, which is overcommit in action.
recap: A process gets memory from the kernel in large pieces, by moving the heap's end with brk or mapping regions with mmap, and the kernel only assigns physical pages when they are first touched.
Linux overcommits by default, promising more memory than exists on the bet that much will never be touched; strict mode (overcommit_memory=2) refuses allocations beyond swap plus a fraction of RAM.

malloc carves those regions into blocks, tracks free blocks in lists by size, splits large free blocks and coalesces neighbours, and uses mmap directly for big requests (128 KiB and up by default in glibc).
Heap fragmentation means free memory is scattered in holes that cannot serve larger requests or be returned to the kernel; long-lived objects pinned among short-lived ones are the usual cause.
Multithreaded allocators use per-thread caches and multiple arenas to avoid lock contention, trading extra memory for speed; jemalloc, tcmalloc and mimalloc are designed around this.
Inside the kernel, the buddy allocator manages physical pages in power-of-two blocks and slab caches carve pages into fixed-size kernel objects.
Copy-on-write shares pages read-only after fork or for private file mappings and copies a page only when someone writes it.

When reclaim cannot free memory, the OOM killer kills the process with the highest badness score, mostly its memory footprint adjusted by oom_score_adj; in a cgroup, the limit triggers an OOM kill inside that group.

Diagnose memory problems by separating leaks (live memory grows), fragmentation (heap free space grows but is not returned) and cache (reclaimable memory), using allocator statistics, smaps and cgroup counters.
glossary: Anonymous mapping
Memory from mmap not backed by any file, zero-filled on first touch; used for heaps, stacks and large allocations.
Arena
An independent heap region with its own lock in glibc malloc, so threads using different arenas do not contend.
brk / sbrk
System calls that move the end of the heap segment to grow or shrink it.
Buddy allocator
The kernel's physical page allocator, which hands out blocks of 2^n pages and splits or merges equal-size 'buddies'.
Coalescing
Merging adjacent free blocks into one larger free block.
CommitLimit / Committed_AS
In /proc/meminfo, the most memory the kernel will promise under strict overcommit, and the total currently promised.
Copy-on-write (COW)
Sharing a page read-only between two users and copying it only when one of them writes.
First fit / best fit
Allocation policies that choose the first free block large enough, or the smallest block large enough.
Fragmentation (heap)
Free memory in a heap divided into small, scattered holes that cannot satisfy larger requests or be returned to the kernel.
jemalloc / tcmalloc / mimalloc
Alternative malloc implementations designed for multithreaded performance and lower fragmentation.
KSM
Kernel same-page merging: a Linux feature that finds identical pages in marked regions and merges them into one copy-on-write page.
MADV_FREE / MADV_DONTNEED
madvise flags that let the kernel drop a range's pages: DONTNEED frees them at once; FREE lets the kernel take them lazily when memory is needed.
madvise
A system call giving the kernel hints about a memory range, such as MADV_DONTNEED or MADV_FREE to release its pages.
malloc
The C library function that allocates a block of memory from the process's heap or a new mapping.
mmap
The system call that maps a file or anonymous memory into the address space.
mmap threshold
The request size above which glibc malloc uses a separate mmap instead of the heap (128 KiB by default, adjusted dynamically).
OOM killer
The Linux mechanism that kills a process to free memory when reclaim cannot satisfy an allocation.
oom_score_adj
A per-process value from -1000 to 1000 added to its OOM badness; -1000 exempts it from the OOM killer.
Overcommit
Promising processes more memory than RAM plus swap, on the assumption they will not touch all of it.
Page cache
Kernel memory caching file contents; reclaimable, and counted against a cgroup's memory usage.
PSS
Proportional set size: resident memory with each shared page divided among the processes sharing it.
RSS
Resident set size: the amount of a process's memory currently in physical RAM.
Size class
A fixed allocation size (16, 32, 48 bytes and so on) that an allocator rounds requests up to, keeping a free list per class.
Slab allocator
A kernel allocator that keeps caches of pre-sized objects carved from pages, such as inodes or socket buffers.
SLUB
The default slab allocator implementation in modern Linux kernels.
tcache
glibc's small per-thread cache of recently freed chunks, checked before any locking.
Thread cache
A per-thread store of free blocks that lets most allocations avoid shared locks.
Zero page
A single shared page of zeros the kernel maps for reads of untouched anonymous memory, until the first write.
drill:
Diagnose: the API whose memory never comes down

A C++ API server (glibc malloc, 96 worker threads on a 24-core machine) handles bursty traffic. Each request builds a response of 50-500 KB in many small allocations, plus a few long-lived entries added to an in-memory cache (bounded at 1 GB). Daily RSS climbs from 2 GB at start to 9 GB at peak and stays at 9 GB overnight. Heap profiling shows live allocations of about 1.8 GB at peak and 1.3 GB at night. The container limit is 10 GB, and twice last month the process was OOMKilled during a traffic spike. Explain the gap between live memory and RSS, why it does not come down, and what you would change.

Answer

The gap. Live data is under 2 GB but RSS is 9 GB, so about 7 GB is memory the allocator holds but the program is not using: allocator retention and fragmentation, not a leak (the profiler would show growing live allocations for a leak). Three mechanisms combine. First, glibc arenas: 96 threads on 24 cores can use up to 8 × 24 = 192 arenas, so threads spread over many independent heaps; each grows to cover its share of the peak, and free memory in one arena cannot serve another. Second, interleaved lifetimes: request objects (short-lived) are allocated next to cache entries (long-lived) in the same heaps; when requests finish, their memory is free but scattered between pinned cache entries, so heaps cannot be trimmed from the top. Third, the dynamic mmap threshold: after the program frees some large blocks, glibc raises the threshold, so later 200-500 KB responses are carved from the heaps instead of using separate mappings that would have been returned on free.

Why it stays. Trimming only releases free memory at the top of each heap, and glibc does not routinely madvise away free pages in the middle. So RSS sits at the historical peak, and each new spike can push it higher if the new peak's allocation pattern does not line up with existing holes, eventually reaching the 10 GB limit: OOMKilled.

Changes. (1) Switch to jemalloc or tcmalloc (via LD_PRELOAD first, to test), which pack objects by size class and return free pages to the kernel with decay timers; or, staying on glibc, set MALLOC_ARENA_MAX=2-4 and call malloc_trim(0) periodically. (2) Separate lifetimes: allocate cache entries from a dedicated pool or arena, and build responses in a per-request arena that is reset when the request ends, so request garbage never fragments the long-lived heap. (3) Make the response buffer a single large allocation (or a reused buffer per thread) rather than many small pieces. (4) Pin the mmap threshold (M_MMAP_THRESHOLD) if large blocks should always be returned. Then measure: allocator stats versus RSS under a replayed day of traffic, peak RSS, latency and throughput, and the cgroup's memory.events.
qa: E
How does a process get memory from the operating system?

Through two system calls. brk (wrapped by sbrk) moves the end of the heap segment up or down. mmap maps a new region anywhere in the address space, either anonymous memory or a file. Both only reserve virtual address space; the kernel assigns physical frames when the pages are first touched. User code rarely calls them directly; malloc and language runtimes request large chunks and divide them up.
E
What does malloc do?

It finds a free block of at least the requested size in the process's heap, marks it as used and returns a pointer to it. It keeps metadata, usually a small header with the block's size, and lists of free blocks grouped by size. If no suitable free block exists it grows the heap with brk or, for large requests, maps a separate region with mmap. free() puts the block back on a free list and merges it with free neighbours.
E
What is copy-on-write?

Copy-on-write lets two processes share the same physical pages until one of them modifies a page. After fork, parent and child page tables point to the same frames, all marked read-only. A write to such a page causes a page fault; the kernel allocates a new frame, copies the 4 KiB page, maps the copy writable for the writer, and lets the write proceed. Pages that are never written are never copied.
M
What is memory overcommit, and what are Linux's modes?

Overcommit means the kernel promises more memory than it can back with RAM and swap, betting that processes will not touch everything they allocate. vm.overcommit_memory=0 (default) uses a heuristic that refuses only obviously impossible requests; 1 always allows; 2 enforces strict accounting, refusing allocations once committed memory would exceed swap plus overcommit_ratio percent of RAM (50% by default). Overcommit makes fork of large processes and sparse allocations possible; the price is that running out shows up later as an OOM kill rather than as a failed malloc.

Follow-up: When would you choose mode 2? — On machines where an OOM kill is worse than an allocation failure the application can handle, such as some database servers, after sizing swap and overcommit_ratio so legitimate workloads still fit.
M
Why does a process's memory usage often not go down after it frees lots of memory?

Because free() returns memory to the allocator, not the kernel. Heap memory can only be returned by shrinking the top of the heap, which is blocked if any live object sits above the free space, or by releasing whole free pages with madvise, which allocators do only in some situations. Objects allocated at different times interleave, so a few long-lived objects pin pages full of free space. Large mmap-allocated blocks are returned immediately. Calling malloc_trim, tuning the allocator, or switching to jemalloc or tcmalloc, which return memory more aggressively, often helps.
M
Explain internal and external fragmentation in a heap allocator.

Internal fragmentation is waste inside allocated blocks: rounding a 33-byte request up to a 48-byte size class wastes 15 bytes, plus header overhead. External fragmentation is free memory split into non-adjacent holes: after allocating ten thousand 1 KiB objects and freeing every other one, 5 MB is free but no single hole can hold a 2 KiB object, and the heap cannot shrink. Size classes and slabs reduce external fragmentation at the cost of some internal fragmentation.
M
How does the Linux buddy allocator work?

Physical memory is managed in blocks of 2^order pages, from order 0 (one 4 KiB page) up to order 10 (4 MiB). To allocate order k, take a free block of that order, or split a larger block in half repeatedly, putting the unused halves on the free lists of their orders. Each block's buddy is the other half it was split from; when a block is freed and its buddy is also free, they merge into a block of the next order, and so on upward. Finding a buddy is a single XOR on the block's address, which makes it fast. /proc/buddyinfo shows free blocks per order.
M
What is the slab allocator and why does the kernel need it?

The kernel allocates huge numbers of small, fixed-size objects: inodes, dentries, socket buffers, task structures. Allocating each from the page allocator would waste most of a page and be slow. A slab cache takes pages from the buddy allocator and divides them into slots for one object type, keeping per-CPU free lists so allocation is fast and lock-free in the common case. kmalloc uses general caches for power-of-two-ish sizes. slabtop and /proc/slabinfo show the caches, which is where kernel memory leaks are found.
M
How does the OOM killer choose a victim?

It computes a badness score for each eligible process, essentially the share of memory it uses (resident memory, swap and page tables) scaled to 0-1000, and adds oom_score_adj (-1000 to 1000). The highest score is killed with SIGKILL; a process with oom_score_adj of -1000 is never chosen. /proc/PID/oom_score shows the current score. If a cgroup hits its memory.max, the kill happens among that cgroup's processes only, and memory.oom.group can make the whole group die together.
H
A Java service in a container with a 4 GiB limit and a 2.5 GiB heap is repeatedly OOMKilled. GC logs show the heap never full. Where is the memory going?

The container limit covers the whole process and its page cache, not just the Java heap. Beyond the heap the JVM uses metaspace, code cache, thread stacks (each thread reserves up to 1 MiB of stack by default, touched as it grows), GC data structures, direct ByteBuffers and memory-mapped files, plus native libraries using malloc. glibc creates up to eight arenas per core for multithreaded programs, which can add hundreds of megabytes of fragmented native heap. Measure with Native Memory Tracking (-XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary) and the cgroup's memory.stat; fixes include capping direct memory and metaspace, setting MALLOC_ARENA_MAX=2 or using jemalloc, reducing thread counts, and leaving headroom of 25-40% above the heap.
Follow-up: Why does exit code 137 mean OOM? — 137 is 128 + 9, a process killed by SIGKILL, which is how both the kernel and cgroup OOM killer terminate processes.
H
How do modern allocators like jemalloc or tcmalloc reduce contention and fragmentation?

They give each thread (or CPU) a cache of free objects per size class, so most malloc and free calls touch only thread-local data with no locks. Behind the caches, memory is organised in runs or spans of pages each dedicated to one size class, which limits external fragmentation because like-sized objects are packed together. They periodically return completely free pages to the kernel with madvise, with decay timers to avoid churning. The trade-off is memory held in caches per thread, and tuning knobs for how aggressively to return memory.
H
What happens, page by page, when a process forks and then the child writes to a 1 GiB array it inherited?

At fork, the kernel copies the parent's page tables (about 2 MiB of last-level entries for 1 GiB of 4 KiB pages) and marks every writable private page read-only in both processes, incrementing each frame's share count. Nothing is copied yet. When the child writes to the array, each first write to a page faults; the kernel sees a copy-on-write page shared by two processes, allocates a new frame, copies 4 KiB, maps it writable in the child and lets the write proceed. If the child writes the whole array, that is 262,144 faults and 1 GiB copied, spread over its execution. If the parent's share count drops to one because the child exited, the parent's next write just makes its existing page writable without copying.
H
Design a memory allocator for a high-throughput server that allocates and frees millions of 64-byte request objects per second.

Use a size-class or object-pool design: request objects of one fixed size come from slabs carved out of large page-aligned chunks, so there is no per-object header and no searching. Keep a free list per thread (or per core) so allocation and free are a pointer pop and push without locks; when a thread's cache grows too large, return a batch to a shared pool, and refill in batches when empty. Allocate per-request memory from an arena that is reset wholesale when the request finishes, if objects do not outlive the request. Return whole empty slabs to the system lazily. This is what tcmalloc, jemalloc and Linux's slab allocator do, specialised to a known size and lifetime.
