t: I/O: interrupts, DMA, blocking vs non-blocking, select/poll/epoll and io_uring
sum: How data moves between devices and programs: device registers, polling versus interrupts, DMA and descriptor rings, the block layer and I/O schedulers, the five I/O models, how select, poll and epoll work inside the kernel and why they scale differently, and how io_uring replaces system calls with shared rings.
prereq: os1
Hardware interrupts enter the kernel through handlers registered at boot; every system call costs a mode switch, so batching them matters.
net13
A socket is a file descriptor with kernel buffers; servers handle many connections with non-blocking sockets and an event loop, using readiness APIs such as epoll.
os10
File reads and writes normally go through the page cache; O_DIRECT bypasses it and fsync waits for stable storage.
why:
A web server answers a request: it receives bytes from a network card, maybe reads a file from an SSD, and sends bytes back. Each of those devices works on its own schedule, millions of times slower or faster than the CPU's view of time. The network card might deliver a packet now, or in three seconds. The SSD takes 80 microseconds, an eternity of 300,000 CPU cycles. The kernel has to coordinate all of this: tell devices what to do, find out when they are done, move the data to the right place, and wake the right thread, without wasting CPU waiting and without drowning in overhead when events arrive millions of times per second.

How a program asks for I/O shapes everything about its architecture. A thread per connection that simply blocks is easy to write but costs memory and context switches at scale. An event loop with non-blocking sockets and epoll handles tens of thousands of connections on one thread, as net13 showed, but stalls if anything blocks. io_uring promises asynchronous everything with almost no system calls, and comes with security concerns. Underneath, interrupts and DMA decide how much CPU a gigabyte of traffic costs.

Interviewers ask about this layer in two ways. Classic OS questions: "polling versus interrupts", "what is DMA", "blocking versus non-blocking versus asynchronous I/O", "how does epoll differ from select". Systems questions: "why is your event loop stalling", "why can't epoll make file reads asynchronous", "what is io_uring and why is it fast", "how would you find where this I/O latency comes from".

This lesson starts at the hardware (registers, polling, interrupts, DMA and descriptor rings), moves through the block layer and I/O schedulers, lays out the five I/O models, opens up select, poll and epoll to show why their costs differ, and finishes with io_uring and how to diagnose I/O problems in production. It builds on the socket-level view in net13 and the page cache from os8 and os10.
primer:
A restaurant kitchen and its waiters

Think of the CPU as a waiter and the devices as kitchen stations. The waiter could stand at the grill asking "is it ready yet?" every few seconds: that is polling, simple and quick to notice when the food is ready, but the waiter serves nobody else while standing there. Or the grill could ring a bell when an order is ready, and the waiter comes when called: that is an interrupt, efficient when orders are occasional, but if the bell rings every two seconds the waiter does nothing but run back and forth. And instead of carrying every plate personally, the waiter can leave a list of orders on a board and let kitchen porters carry dishes directly to tables, checking back only when a batch is finished: that is DMA with a descriptor ring.

Programs face the same choice one level up. A thread can wait at the counter for its one order (blocking I/O). It can keep asking "ready yet?" (non-blocking I/O with retries). It can ask a manager "tell me which of my 10,000 orders are ready" (I/O multiplexing: select, poll, epoll). Or it can hand over the orders and be told when the food has been delivered to the table (asynchronous I/O: io_uring).

The analogy breaks on speed ratios, which are extreme. An SSD read takes around 100 microseconds; a CPU does hundreds of thousands of operations in that time. A 100 Gb/s network card can deliver over 8 million small packets per second; at that rate even a microsecond of overhead per packet consumes eight cores. Every design in this lesson is about keeping that per-event overhead small.

Two numbers that drive every design

Two quantities explain most I/O design decisions. The first is latency per operation: how long one read or one packet takes from request to completion, from tens of nanoseconds for a cached page to roughly 10-100 µs for an NVMe SSD, around 10 ms for a spinning disk, and milliseconds or more across a network. The second is overhead per operation: the CPU time spent on bookkeeping around each I/O, such as a system call (os1), an interrupt, a context switch to wake a thread, a copy between buffers. When devices were slow, overhead hardly mattered; a 10 ms disk read dwarfed a 5 µs system call. Today devices are fast enough that overhead is often the larger cost, so modern interfaces are all about doing more per kernel crossing: batching requests, polling instead of interrupting when busy, and handing completions back through shared memory. Keep asking "what is the overhead per operation here, and how is it amortised?" as you read.
body:
1. Talking to a device: registers

Every device presents a few registers: a status register (busy, ready, error), a command register (what to do), and data or address registers. The CPU reaches them in one of two ways. x86 has special in/out instructions for a separate I/O port space, now used only by legacy devices. Almost everything else uses memory-mapped I/O (MMIO): the device's registers appear at physical addresses, and ordinary load and store instructions to those addresses go to the device instead of RAM. The kernel maps those addresses uncached, so every access really reaches the device. Because only the kernel maps them (os7), user programs cannot touch devices directly, which is what makes drivers part of the kernel's protection boundary (os1).

2. Polling versus interrupts

To read a disk block the simple way, a driver writes the command and block number into the device's registers, then waits for completion. Waiting by polling means looping on the status register until "ready" appears. If the device takes 100 µs, the CPU wastes 100 µs. Waiting by interrupt means the driver puts the requesting thread to sleep and the CPU runs something else; when the device finishes, it raises an interrupt, the handler runs (os1), notes the completion and wakes the thread.

Which is better depends on timing. An interrupt costs a fixed amount, roughly a microsecond or more including the handler, the context disruption and the eventual wake-up. For slow, infrequent events (a keypress, a disk read on a mostly idle machine) interrupts are clearly better. For very fast devices or very frequent events, the fixed cost dominates: an NVMe read that completes in 10 µs might spend a noticeable share of that on interrupt handling, and a network card receiving millions of packets per second would bury the CPU in interrupts. That is why modern drivers are hybrid: interrupt when idle, poll when busy. Two related techniques: interrupt coalescing, where the device waits until several completions accumulate or a few microseconds pass before interrupting (tunable on network cards with ethtool -C), and Linux's NAPI, where the first packet's interrupt switches the driver into polling mode until the receive ring is empty.

3. DMA and descriptor rings

Moving data byte by byte through registers (programmed I/O) would cost the CPU one instruction per word, impossible at gigabytes per second. With direct memory access, the device itself reads or writes main memory. The driver's job becomes bookkeeping: tell the device which memory to use, and find out when it is done.

Fast devices do this with descriptor rings: circular arrays in memory, shared between driver and device, each entry describing one buffer (physical address and length) plus status flags. For a network card receiving packets:

  1. The driver allocates, say, 1,024 packet buffers and writes their addresses into the receive ring, then tells the card (by writing a "tail" register) that those entries are available.
  2. Each arriving packet is DMA'd by the card into the next available buffer; the card writes the packet length into the descriptor and sets its "done" flag.
  3. The card raises an interrupt (or the driver is already polling). The driver walks the ring from where it left off, hands each completed buffer to the network stack, puts fresh buffers in those slots, and advances the tail register.

Storage works the same way. An NVMe SSD uses submission queues and completion queues in host memory: the driver writes a command (read 8 blocks at LBA 1,234,567 into these pages) into a submission queue and rings a doorbell register; the drive executes it, DMAs the data, posts an entry to the completion queue and interrupts. NVMe allows up to 65,535 queue pairs, so Linux gives each CPU its own, and CPUs never contend with each other to issue I/O. Keep this picture in mind: io_uring, later in the lesson, applies exactly this design to the boundary between programs and the kernel.

4. The block layer and I/O schedulers

Between file systems and storage drivers sits the block layer. A file system submits requests ("read these sectors into these pages"); the block layer may merge adjacent requests into one larger one, schedule them, apply cgroup I/O limits (os13) and accounting, and dispatch them to the driver. Since Linux 5.0 the block layer is fully multi-queue (blk-mq): per-CPU software queues map onto however many hardware queues the device has.

On spinning disks, ordering mattered enormously: a seek costs several milliseconds, so serving requests in disk order rather than arrival order (the "elevator" algorithm) multiplied throughput. Modern Linux offers a few schedulers, set per device in /sys/block/<dev>/queue/scheduler:

SchedulerIdeaTypical use
nonePass requests straight throughNVMe and fast SSDs (usual default)
mq-deadlineSort for locality but guarantee each request a deadline; prefer readsSATA SSDs and HDDs (common default)
bfqFair share of bandwidth per process or cgroupDesktops, slow devices, mixed interactive loads
kyberThrottle queue depth to meet latency targetsFast devices where tail latency matters

For NVMe the answer is usually none: there is no seek to optimise, the drive schedules internally across its flash channels, and the most valuable thing the kernel can do is stay out of the way.

5. The five ways a program can wait

Every input operation has two phases: waiting for data to be ready (a packet to arrive, a disk block to be read) and copying it from the kernel into the program's buffer. Richard Stevens' classic Unix Network Programming classifies I/O models by how a program experiences those phases:

ModelWaiting for dataCopyingExample
BlockingThread sleeps in the callInside the same callread() on a blocking socket
Non-blockingCall returns EAGAIN; program retriesInside the successful callO_NONBLOCK + retry loop
MultiplexingThread sleeps in select/poll/epoll for many fdsSeparate read on each ready fdNginx, Redis, asyncio, Node.js
Signal-drivenKernel sends SIGIO when readySeparate readRare today
AsynchronousProgram submits and continuesDone by the kernel; program told on completionio_uring, Windows IOCP

The first four are readiness-based: the kernel tells you when you can do the operation, and you then do it yourself. The last is completion-based: the kernel tells you when it has done it. net13 traced how servers use each; here we look inside the kernel to see why their costs differ.

6. Inside select and poll

select(nfds, readfds, writefds, exceptfds, timeout) takes bitmaps of descriptor numbers. On every call, the kernel copies the bitmaps in, and for each descriptor up to nfds: checks whether it is ready, and if not, adds the calling thread to that descriptor's wait queue (the list the kernel wakes when that socket gets data). If none is ready, the thread sleeps; when any wakes it, the kernel scans all descriptors again, removes the thread from every wait queue, writes back the bitmaps, and returns. The program then scans the bitmaps to find which are set. poll() replaces the fixed-size bitmaps with an array of {fd, events, revents} structures, removing select's limit of descriptor numbers below FD_SETSIZE (1,024), but does the same work.

So every call costs O(n) in the number of watched descriptors, regardless of how many are active. A server with 10,000 connections, of which 10 are active at any moment, does 10,000 checks to find 10. That was the heart of the C10K problem (net13).

7. Inside epoll

epoll separates the two jobs that select repeats on every call. epoll_create1() makes an epoll instance, itself a file descriptor, holding an interest list (a red-black tree of registered descriptors) and a ready list. epoll_ctl(ADD, fd, events) registers a descriptor once: the kernel inserts it into the tree and attaches a small callback to the descriptor's wait queue. From then on:

  1. When data arrives on the socket, the network stack wakes the socket's wait queue as usual, which runs epoll's callback.
  2. The callback appends that descriptor to the epoll instance's ready list (if not already there) and wakes any thread sleeping in epoll_wait.
  3. epoll_wait() copies up to maxevents entries from the ready list to the program and returns. If the list is empty, it sleeps.

Level- versus edge-triggered. In the default level-triggered mode, a descriptor that remains readable stays on the ready list and is reported on every epoll_wait. With EPOLLET (edge-triggered), it is reported only when new data arrives; if the program reads half the data and waits again, it will not hear about this descriptor until more data comes, and the remaining bytes sit unread. Edge-triggered code must therefore use non-blocking descriptors and read (or write) until EAGAIN. net13 discusses when each fits; two more flags matter for multithreaded servers. EPOLLONESHOT disables a descriptor after one event until it is re-armed, so two threads never handle the same connection at once. EPOLLEXCLUSIVE (Linux 4.5) wakes only one of several epoll instances waiting on the same descriptor, avoiding the thundering herd (os5) on a shared listening socket.

macOS and the BSDs have kqueue, which plays the same role as epoll and also covers timers, signals, process exits and file changes in one interface. Windows takes the completion route with I/O completion ports.

8. The hole in readiness: regular files

Readiness APIs work for sockets, pipes and terminals, whose "not ready" state can last forever. Regular files are different: the kernel considers them always ready, because a disk read completes in bounded time. So epoll reports a file descriptor as readable immediately, and the following read() still blocks the thread while the disk fetches uncached data, freezing the entire event loop for 100 µs to tens of milliseconds. This is why libuv (Node.js) uses a thread pool for file system calls, why Python's asyncio offers run_in_executor and asyncio.to_thread for file work, and why nginx has thread pools for file reads. The older Linux AIO interface (io_submit) offered asynchronous file I/O, but only reliably with O_DIRECT, and it could still block in surprising places, so it saw little use outside databases. That gap is a major reason io_uring was created.

9. io_uring: I/O through shared rings

io_uring, added in Linux 5.1 (2019) by Jens Axboe, gives programs the same structure NVMe gives drivers. Setting up an instance with io_uring_setup() creates two ring buffers in memory shared between the program and the kernel:

  • A submission queue (SQ): the program writes submission queue entries (SQEs), each describing one operation: opcode (read, write, accept, connect, send, recv, openat, fsync, timeout, and dozens more), file descriptor, buffer address, length, offset, and a 64-bit user_data tag to match results.
  • A completion queue (CQ): the kernel writes completion queue entries (CQEs), each with the user_data tag and a result (bytes transferred or a negative error).

The flow: the program fills several SQEs, advances the SQ tail, and calls io_uring_enter() once to submit them all (optionally also waiting for some number of completions). The kernel executes each operation, completing it inline if it can (data already in the page cache, a socket with data waiting) or handing it to internal async workers or poll-based retry if it would block, and posts CQEs. The program reads CQEs straight from shared memory and advances the CQ head; no system call is needed to collect results.

Where the speed comes from: batching (one kernel entry for many operations, which matters more since Meltdown mitigations made each entry dearer, os1); completion semantics (one step does the wait and the copy, instead of epoll_wait followed by read); uniformity (files, sockets, timers and file-system operations all asynchronous through one interface); and optional modes that remove more overhead. SQPOLL runs a kernel thread that polls the submission ring, so a busy program submits work just by writing to memory. Registered files and buffers pre-register descriptors and pin memory once, avoiding per-operation lookups and page pinning. Linked SQEs chain operations (read then write, with a timeout) so they run in order without returning to user space. Most programs use it through liburing or runtime support (Rust's tokio-uring and glommio, Java's Netty incubator transport, databases such as ScyllaDB and TigerBeetle, and io_uring use for some file operations in libuv, and an optional io_uring method in PostgreSQL 18's new asynchronous I/O).

The caveat is security. io_uring exposes a large, fast-moving kernel surface that bypasses some of the usual syscall-filtering points. In 2023 Google reported that most of the kernel exploits submitted to its kernel bug bounty in the previous year targeted io_uring, and it disabled or restricted io_uring on ChromeOS, Android apps and its production servers; Docker's default seccomp profile blocks the io_uring system calls too. A sysctl (kernel.io_uring_disabled, Linux 6.6) lets administrators turn it off or limit it to a group.
deep:
Receive livelock and why polling came back

In 1996, Mogul and Ramakrishnan showed that interrupt-driven kernels collapse under packet floods: each packet's interrupt preempts whatever is processing earlier packets, so at high enough rates the CPU spends all its time acknowledging packets it never finishes processing, and useful throughput falls to zero while the CPU is 100% busy. The fix is to bound the work done in interrupt context and switch to polling under load, processing a budget of packets per poll and dropping excess input early. Linux's NAPI (2001) implements exactly this: the first packet's interrupt disables further receive interrupts on that queue and schedules a poll in softirq context; the poll processes up to a budget (64 packets per device by default) per round and only re-enables interrupts when the ring is empty. Busy polling (SO_BUSY_POLL) lets a latency-sensitive socket reader spin on the device queue directly for a few microseconds, trading CPU for lower latency.

Spreading interrupts and packet processing across CPUs

A single queue and a single interrupt would serialise all network processing on one CPU. Modern cards have many receive queues and use receive-side scaling (RSS): a hash of each packet's addresses and ports picks the queue, so all packets of one connection land on the same queue and CPU (preserving order and cache locality) while different connections spread out. Each queue has its own interrupt (MSI-X), which can be pinned to a CPU via /proc/irq/<n>/smp_affinity, usually managed by irqbalance. Software equivalents (RPS, RFS) do the spreading in the kernel for cards with fewer queues, and RFS steers packets to the CPU where the consuming thread runs. Getting this wrong shows up as one CPU at 100% in softirq (si in top) while others idle.

Avoiding copies: zero-copy paths

A classic file-serving path copies data twice: disk to page cache by DMA, page cache to a user buffer by read(), user buffer to socket buffer by write(), then DMA to the card. sendfile() lets the kernel send page-cache pages to a socket directly, skipping the user-space copies, which is how nginx and Kafka serve static data efficiently. splice() moves data between a pipe and another descriptor by passing page references. MSG_ZEROCOPY lets send() transmit from user pages without copying, notifying the program via the error queue when the pages can be reused; it pays off only for large sends because of the bookkeeping. kTLS moves TLS encryption into the kernel (or the card) so even encrypted traffic can use sendfile. io_uring adds registered buffers and zero-copy send and receive paths for the same reasons.

Polled storage I/O

NVMe devices can complete reads in under 10 µs, comparable to the cost of an interrupt plus a context switch to wake the waiting thread. For such devices Linux supports polled I/O: the submitting thread (or an io_uring instance created with IORING_SETUP_IOPOLL) spins on the completion queue instead of sleeping, so completions are noticed within nanoseconds. It burns a core per polling context, so it is used where latency or IOPS per core matter more than CPU efficiency, such as storage engines and benchmarks; SPDK takes the extreme route of a user-space NVMe driver that polls with no kernel involvement at all.

Who wakes whom: the cost of a wake-up

Even with perfect devices, a blocking read on an idle thread involves a chain of hand-offs: the interrupt handler records completion, the kernel marks the sleeping thread runnable, the scheduler eventually runs it on some CPU (maybe a different one, with cold caches), and only then does the program see its data. Each step adds microseconds of latency and jitter, and at high rates the wake-ups themselves become a large share of CPU. That is the deeper reason event loops and io_uring batch completions, why NAPI and polled I/O spin while busy, and why latency-critical systems pin the consuming thread to the CPU that handles the device's interrupts.

Why asynchronous file I/O took so long on Linux

File I/O can block in many places beyond the device: page-cache misses, metadata reads to find the blocks, journal waits, memory allocation, locks inside the file system. Making all of those asynchronous inside the kernel is a huge change, which is why Linux AIO only worked for O_DIRECT on some file systems and quietly blocked otherwise. io_uring took a pragmatic approach: try the operation non-blockingly inline, and if it would block, hand it to a pool of kernel worker threads (io-wq) that perform it synchronously, so the program never blocks. Later versions reduced the use of workers by adding non-blocking paths in file systems and block layers. The design shows a recurring systems pattern: when you cannot make an operation asynchronous at the bottom, move the blocking onto threads you control.
prod:
Looking at interrupts

/proc/interrupts shows, per CPU, how many interrupts each device line has raised; watching it with watch -d reveals which CPUs handle network and storage interrupts. mpstat -P ALL 1 and top (press 1) show per-CPU %irq and %soft. A single CPU saturated with softirq work while others idle means interrupts and packet processing are not spread: check that the card has multiple queues (ethtool -l), that RSS is enabled, and that irqbalance or manual affinity distributes queue interrupts. ksoftirqd/N running hot means softirq work has overflowed into its fallback thread on CPU N. For latency-critical applications, a common pattern is to keep interrupts off the cores running the application's threads (or deliberately on the same core, to keep data cache-hot); measure both.

Storage latency, queue depth and utilisation

iostat -x 1 is the first tool: per device, r/s and w/s (IOPS), rkB/s and wkB/s (throughput), r_await and w_await (average latency including time queued), aqu-sz (average number of requests in flight) and %util. %util is misleading for SSDs and NVMe: it measures the share of time at least one request was in flight, so a device that can serve 64 requests in parallel can show 100% while far from saturated; use latency and IOPS against the device's specification instead. For distributions, the eBPF tools biolatency (histogram of block I/O latency) and biosnoop (each I/O with process, size and latency) show tail behaviour and who causes it. Cloud block volumes add their own limits: provisioned IOPS and throughput caps and burst credits, which produce sudden latency cliffs when exhausted.

Event-loop stalls

In epoll-based servers (Node.js, Python asyncio, Netty, Redis), the canonical I/O incident is a blocked loop: one handler does a synchronous file read, a DNS lookup, a CPU-heavy parse or a blocking database call, and every other connection on that loop waits. Measure event-loop lag (schedule a timer and measure how late it fires; Node's monitorEventLoopDelay, asyncio's debug mode which logs callbacks slower than 100 ms). Fixes: move blocking work to thread pools or io_uring, split CPU work into worker processes, and make sure file access in the request path is either cached in memory or asynchronous. Redis, single-threaded by design, documents its own version: avoid slow commands (KEYS, large SMEMBERS) that block all clients.

Choosing an I/O model

For most services the choice is about developer time, not microseconds. A thread or virtual thread per request with blocking calls is simplest and fine up to thousands of concurrent requests. An event loop (epoll via your runtime) is the standard for tens of thousands of mostly idle connections. io_uring pays off for storage-heavy engines, very high request rates per core, or when file I/O must be asynchronous; check that your kernel, container runtime's seccomp profile and security policy allow it before depending on it. Whatever the model, bound concurrency to what the devices can usefully absorb: more in-flight I/O than the device's internal parallelism only adds queueing latency.

Writes that look like reads

A frequent surprise: read latency spikes on a database volume every few seconds, and the cause is writes. Large write-back bursts from the page cache (os10), journal commits or an SSD's internal garbage collection occupy the device and reads queue behind them. Signs are periodic w/s bursts aligned with r_await spikes. Remedies: smoother write-back (lower dirty thresholds), separating write-heavy data (logs, WAL) onto another device, I/O cgroup limits on bulk writers, and leaving free space on SSDs so garbage collection has room.
myths: epoll makes disk file I/O asynchronous.

epoll reports readiness, and regular files are always considered ready, so epoll returns them immediately and the following read() still blocks if the data is not in the page cache. That is why Node.js (libuv) runs file operations on a thread pool. Truly asynchronous file I/O on Linux needs io_uring (or the older, limited Linux AIO with O_DIRECT).
Interrupts are always better than polling.

Interrupts are efficient when events are rare, because the CPU does nothing until a device needs it. At very high event rates, the fixed cost of each interrupt (entering the kernel, saving state, cache disruption) dominates and can starve real work, a condition called receive livelock. High-speed network and storage drivers switch to polling under load (Linux NAPI, NVMe polled queues, io_uring SQPOLL, DPDK).
Non-blocking I/O and asynchronous I/O are the same thing.

Non-blocking I/O means a call returns immediately with EAGAIN if it cannot make progress, and the program must ask again later, usually after a readiness notification from epoll. Asynchronous I/O means the program submits an operation and is told later that it has completed, with the data already copied. epoll-based servers use the first model; io_uring and Windows IOCP provide the second.
select is fine as long as you have fewer than 1,024 descriptors.

The FD_SETSIZE limit is about descriptor numbers, not counts: a program with only 10 sockets will corrupt memory if one of them happens to be fd 1,500 and it uses select. And select and poll still copy and scan the entire set on every call, so their cost grows with the number of watched descriptors even when only one is active. epoll costs are proportional to the number of ready descriptors.
DMA means the CPU is not involved in I/O.

DMA removes the CPU from copying the bytes, but the CPU still sets up descriptors, programs the device, handles completion interrupts, and often copies data again between kernel and user buffers. At high rates those per-operation costs, not the byte copying, become the bottleneck, which is what interrupt coalescing, batching and zero-copy APIs attack.
lab:
Measure why epoll scales and select/poll do not. Linux or WSL, Python 3.

  1. Save as mux.py: 
    import os, select, time, resource
soft, hard = resource.getrlimit(resource.RLIMIT_NOFILE)
resource.setrlimit(resource.RLIMIT_NOFILE, (min(hard, 20000), hard))

def bench(n, rounds=200):
    pipes = [os.pipe() for _ in range(n)]
    reads = [r for r, w in pipes]
    os.write(pipes[-1][1], b"x")              # exactly one ready fd
    p = select.poll()
    for r in reads: p.register(r, select.POLLIN)
    ep = select.epoll()
    for r in reads: ep.register(r, select.EPOLLIN)
    t = time.perf_counter()
    for _ in range(rounds): assert len(p.poll(0)) == 1
    t_poll = (time.perf_counter() - t) / rounds * 1e6
    t = time.perf_counter()
    for _ in range(rounds): assert len(ep.poll(0)) == 1
    t_ep = (time.perf_counter() - t) / rounds * 1e6
    print(f"{n:6} fds: poll {t_poll:8.1f} µs/call   epoll {t_ep:6.1f} µs/call")
    ep.close()
    for r, w in pipes: os.close(r); os.close(w)

for n in (10, 100, 1000, 5000):
    bench(n)
  2. Run python3 mux.py. If it fails with "Too many open files", run ulimit -n 20000 first (each pipe uses two descriptors).
  3. Edge versus level: in a Python shell, create a pipe, register its read end with select.EPOLLIN | select.EPOLLET, write 10 bytes, call ep.poll(0) twice; then read 5 bytes and poll again; then write 1 more byte and poll.

What to look for. With one ready descriptor in every case, poll's time per call grows roughly in proportion to the number of descriptors (the kernel checks every one and Python builds the full list), from a few microseconds at 10 to hundreds at 5,000, while epoll stays nearly flat, since it only returns the ready list. That flat line is why event-driven servers can hold tens of thousands of idle connections. In step 3, edge-triggered epoll reports the pipe on the first poll after the write but not on the second, and not after the partial read, even though 5 bytes are still waiting; only the new write produces another event. That is the "must drain until EAGAIN" rule in action.
recap: The CPU controls devices by reading and writing their registers, through special I/O instructions or, more commonly, memory-mapped addresses.

With polling, the CPU repeatedly checks a device's status; with interrupts, the device signals the CPU when it needs attention; polling wins at very high event rates and interrupts win when events are sparse.
DMA lets a device transfer data directly to or from memory; drivers describe transfers in descriptor rings shared with the device and the device interrupts when entries complete.
The block layer turns file-system requests into device requests, merging and scheduling them; modern NVMe devices have many hardware queues and usually run with no I/O scheduler at all.
Programs can do I/O in five ways: blocking, non-blocking with retries, multiplexed readiness (select, poll, epoll), signal-driven, and asynchronous completion.

select and poll pass and scan the whole set of descriptors on every call, so cost grows with the number watched; epoll registers interest once and keeps a ready list filled by callbacks, so each wait costs roughly the number of ready descriptors.
epoll can be level-triggered (reports while ready) or edge-triggered (reports on changes, so the program must drain until EAGAIN); EPOLLONESHOT and EPOLLEXCLUSIVE help multithreaded servers.
Readiness APIs do not help regular files, which are always 'ready'; that is why event loops use thread pools for disk I/O.

io_uring lets programs place requests in a submission ring and collect results from a completion ring in shared memory, batching or even eliminating system calls and supporting files, sockets and many other operations asynchronously.

In production, watch interrupt distribution, device latency and queue depth, and choose the I/O model by workload: threads for simplicity, epoll for many idle connections, io_uring for maximum throughput.
glossary: Asynchronous I/O
An I/O model in which the program submits an operation and is notified when it has completed, with no blocking and no retrying.
Block layer
The part of the kernel that sits between file systems and block-device drivers, queueing, merging and dispatching requests.
Completion queue (CQ)
In io_uring, the ring where the kernel places results of finished operations for the program to read.
Descriptor ring
A circular array in memory shared by a driver and a device, each entry describing a buffer to send or fill.
Device register
A small storage location on a device that the CPU reads or writes to control it or check its status.
DMA
Direct memory access: a device reading or writing main memory itself, without the CPU copying each byte.
EAGAIN / EWOULDBLOCK
The error a non-blocking call returns when it cannot proceed right now.
Edge-triggered
An epoll mode that reports a descriptor only when its state changes, so the program must read or write until EAGAIN.
epoll
Linux's scalable readiness interface: register descriptors once, then wait for a list of those that are ready.
Interrupt
A hardware signal from a device that makes the CPU run a kernel handler.
Interrupt coalescing
A device delaying its interrupt until several events have accumulated or a short timer expires, trading latency for lower CPU cost.
I/O scheduler
A block-layer policy (none, mq-deadline, bfq, kyber) that orders and merges requests before they reach the device.
IOCP
Windows I/O completion ports: a completion-based asynchronous I/O interface.
IOPS
I/O operations per second, the usual throughput measure for storage devices.
io_uring
A Linux interface (since 5.1) for asynchronous I/O through submission and completion rings shared between the program and the kernel.
kqueue
The BSD and macOS equivalent of epoll, also covering timers, signals and file changes.
Level-triggered
An epoll mode (the default) that reports a descriptor on every wait as long as it remains ready.
Linux AIO
The older asynchronous I/O interface (io_submit), useful mainly with O_DIRECT and largely superseded by io_uring.
Memory-mapped I/O (MMIO)
Controlling a device by reading and writing addresses that map to its registers rather than to RAM.
NAPI
Linux's network receive design that switches from interrupts to polling while packets keep arriving.
Non-blocking I/O
Calls that return immediately with EAGAIN instead of waiting when no progress is possible.
NVMe
A storage protocol for SSDs on PCIe with many parallel submission and completion queues in host memory.
poll / select
Older readiness calls that take the full set of descriptors on each call and scan it.
Polling
The CPU repeatedly checking a device or queue for work instead of waiting for an interrupt.
Queue depth
The number of I/O requests outstanding at a device at once.
Readiness notification
Being told that an operation on a descriptor can now proceed without blocking, as select, poll and epoll do.
RSS (receive-side scaling)
A network-card feature that hashes each packet's addresses and ports to choose one of several receive queues, spreading work across CPUs.
SPDK
Storage Performance Development Kit: user-space NVMe drivers that poll devices directly, bypassing the kernel.
SQPOLL
An io_uring mode in which a kernel thread polls the submission ring, so the program can submit without any system call.
Submission queue (SQ)
In io_uring, the ring where the program places request entries for the kernel to execute.
Wait queue
A kernel list of tasks or callbacks waiting for an event on an object such as a socket.
drill:
Diagnose: the API that freezes when the log disk is slow

A Python asyncio API service handles about 3,000 requests per second on one event loop per process. Every request appends an audit line to a local file with a plain open(...).write() call inside the coroutine. Normally p99 latency is 15 ms. Several times a day, p99 jumps to 2-3 seconds for a minute, across all endpoints, including health checks; CPU drops during these periods. The incidents coincide with a nightly-style log compression job that runs at random times on the same disk, and iostat then shows w_await on that disk above 500 ms. Explain the mechanism, why epoll does not prevent it, and fix it.

Answer

Mechanism. The audit write is a synchronous file operation executed on the event-loop thread. Usually it is fast: write() copies into the page cache and returns in microseconds (os10). But when the compression job floods the disk with writes, dirty memory rises past the dirty limits and the kernel throttles writers: write() calls block until write-back catches up, and with w_await above 500 ms that can mean hundreds of milliseconds per call. Opening the file each time can also block on metadata and journal waits. While the loop thread is blocked, no other coroutine runs: health checks, other endpoints and already-arrived responses all wait. CPU drops because the only thread is asleep in the kernel.

Why epoll does not help. asyncio's event loop uses epoll to know when sockets are ready. File descriptors for regular files are always reported ready, and asyncio does not route ordinary file writes through the selector at all; a write() to a file is just a blocking system call made directly by the coroutine. Readiness-based multiplexing has no way to make it non-blocking.

Fix. Take file I/O off the loop. Simplest: push audit lines onto an asyncio.Queue (bounded) and have one background writer thread (or asyncio.to_thread worker) drain it, keeping the file open and writing in batches; if the queue fills because the disk is slow, decide explicitly whether to drop lines (count them) or apply backpressure. Alternatively log to stdout and let the platform's agent handle files, or use an io_uring-based async file library. Separately, isolate the compression job: run it under an I/O cgroup limit (io.max) or with ionice -c3, and consider lower dirty-memory thresholds so writers are not throttled in large bursts. Add an event-loop-lag metric and alert so the next blocking call is caught before users notice.
qa: E
What is the difference between polling and interrupt-driven I/O?

With polling, the CPU repeatedly reads a device's status register to see if it is ready, which wastes CPU when the device is slow but has no per-event overhead. With interrupts, the CPU does other work and the device raises an interrupt when it needs attention, which is efficient for infrequent events. Each interrupt has a fixed cost, so at very high event rates systems switch to polling or coalesce interrupts.
E
What is DMA and why is it needed?

Direct memory access lets a device transfer data to or from main memory itself. Without it, the CPU would copy every byte through device registers (programmed I/O), which at gigabytes per second would consume whole cores. With DMA the driver gives the device the address and length of a buffer, the device performs the transfer, and it interrupts the CPU when done.
E
What is the difference between blocking and non-blocking I/O?

A blocking call waits until it can complete: read on a socket with no data puts the thread to sleep until data arrives. A non-blocking call returns immediately; if it cannot make progress it fails with EAGAIN and the program must try again later, typically after a readiness notification. Non-blocking I/O lets one thread manage many descriptors.
M
Describe the five I/O models from Stevens' Unix Network Programming.

Blocking I/O: the call waits for data and for the copy into the user buffer. Non-blocking I/O: the call returns EAGAIN until data is there, so the program polls. I/O multiplexing: the program blocks in select, poll or epoll on many descriptors and then does non-blocking reads on the ready ones. Signal-driven I/O: the kernel sends SIGIO when a descriptor becomes ready. Asynchronous I/O: the program starts the operation and is notified when the data has already been copied. Only the last avoids blocking in the copy step; the first four are synchronous in that sense.
M
Why does epoll scale better than select and poll?

select and poll take the whole set of descriptors on every call; the kernel copies it in, checks each descriptor's state and registers the caller on each one's wait queue, then the program scans the result, so every call costs O(n) in the number watched. epoll splits registration from waiting: epoll_ctl adds a descriptor once, attaching a callback to its wait queue; when the descriptor becomes ready the callback adds it to the epoll instance's ready list; epoll_wait just returns entries from that list. The cost per wait is proportional to the number of ready descriptors, which is what matters with ten thousand mostly idle connections.

Follow-up: Is epoll always faster? — With a handful of descriptors that are all busy, poll can be just as fast, and epoll_ctl calls to change interest add overhead; the advantage is for many descriptors with few active.
M
Explain level-triggered versus edge-triggered epoll and the bug edge-triggered invites.

Level-triggered, the default, reports a descriptor on every epoll_wait while it remains readable or writable. Edge-triggered reports it only when its state changes, for example when new data arrives. With edge-triggered mode, if the program reads only part of the available data and goes back to epoll_wait, no new event will come until more data arrives, so the remaining data sits unread and the connection appears to hang. Edge-triggered code must loop reading until EAGAIN, and use non-blocking descriptors.
M
Why do event-loop runtimes like Node.js use a thread pool for file operations?

Readiness APIs report regular files as always readable and writable, because the kernel's model is that disk reads complete in bounded time. A read of uncached data still blocks the thread while the disk works, which would stall the whole event loop. So libuv runs file operations, DNS lookups and some other blocking calls on a small thread pool and posts completions back to the loop. io_uring removes the need by offering genuinely asynchronous file operations.
M
How does a network card deliver packets to the kernel?

The driver allocates buffers and writes their addresses into a receive descriptor ring in memory. The card DMAs each arriving packet into the next buffer, marks the descriptor done and raises an interrupt (possibly coalesced). The interrupt handler disables further interrupts for that queue and schedules NAPI polling in softirq context, which processes a batch of completed descriptors, hands packets to the network stack, refills the ring with fresh buffers and re-enables interrupts when the ring is empty. Modern cards have many queues, steered by flow hash to different CPUs (receive-side scaling).
M
What does the I/O scheduler do, and why do NVMe drives often use none?

It sits in the block layer between file systems and drivers, merging adjacent requests and reordering them to meet goals: mq-deadline bounds the age of requests, bfq shares bandwidth fairly between processes, kyber targets latency. On spinning disks, ordering requests to reduce seeks mattered hugely. NVMe drives have no seek penalty, many internal parallel channels and up to tens of thousands of hardware queues, so reordering in software mostly adds CPU overhead and latency; the none scheduler passes requests straight to the per-CPU hardware queues.
H
How does io_uring work, and what makes it faster than epoll plus read?

The program and kernel share two ring buffers. The program writes submission entries describing operations (read this file at this offset into this buffer, accept on this socket, send this data) into the submission queue and advances its tail; one io_uring_enter call submits many entries and can also wait for completions. The kernel executes them, inline if possible or with internal workers, and posts results to the completion queue, which the program reads from shared memory without system calls. Savings come from batching many operations per system call, doing the I/O and the copy in one step instead of readiness plus read, supporting files and sockets uniformly, and optional modes: SQPOLL, where a kernel thread polls the submission ring so submissions need no system call at all, and registered files and buffers, which avoid per-operation lookups and page pinning.

Follow-up: Why have some companies disabled io_uring? — It exposes a large, fast-changing kernel attack surface; Google reported in 2023 that most kernel exploits submitted to its bug bounty the previous year targeted io_uring, and restricted it on ChromeOS, Android and its servers. Container runtimes' default seccomp profiles also block it.
H
What is receive livelock and how do modern kernels avoid it?

At very high packet rates, a system that takes one interrupt per packet spends all its CPU entering interrupt handlers and queueing packets that it never gets time to process, so throughput collapses to near zero while the CPU is 100% busy. Mogul and Ramakrishnan described it in 1996. The fixes are to stop interrupting under load: Linux's NAPI disables the receive interrupt and polls the ring in batches while packets keep coming, devices coalesce interrupts, and excess packets are dropped early, at the card, rather than after work has been invested in them.
H
A storage-heavy service shows p99 read latency of 20 ms on NVMe drives that benchmark at 100 µs. How do you investigate?

First separate device time from queueing: iostat -x shows per-device r_await (average read latency including queueing), aqu-sz (average queue depth) and %util. If await is high with high queue depth, the device or its queue is saturated, perhaps by another workload's writes; check whether reads are stuck behind large writes, garbage collection inside the SSD, or write-back bursts from the page cache. If device latency is fine, the delay is above the block layer: page-cache misses on a cold cache, lock contention in the file system, or a thread pool too small for blocking I/O. biolatency and biosnoop (eBPF) give per-I/O latency histograms and the issuing process; perf or off-CPU profiling shows where threads wait. Typical fixes: isolate write bursts (dirty-page limits, cgroup io.max), increase concurrency to use the device's parallelism, or move to O_DIRECT with io_uring for predictable latency.
H
Design the I/O layer for a server that must handle 50,000 mostly idle TLS connections and also read from local files to answer requests.

Use non-blocking sockets with an event loop per core (epoll, or io_uring for sockets as well), with SO_REUSEPORT or a shared listener using EPOLLEXCLUSIVE to spread accepts across loops. Connections are cheap in this model, a few kilobytes of state each plus kernel buffers. File reads must not block a loop: either serve hot files from memory or the page cache and send them with sendfile, or perform file reads through io_uring or a small thread pool with completions posted back to the loop. Bound concurrency for file I/O to the device's useful queue depth, set timeouts on idle connections, and watch event-loop lag as the key health metric.

t: Inter-process communication: pipes, shared memory, message queues, signals and Unix sockets
sum: How isolated processes talk: pipes and FIFOs, Unix domain sockets (including passing file descriptors), POSIX message queues, shared memory with process-shared synchronization, and signals with their delivery rules and pitfalls, plus how to choose between them and the production failures each one causes.
prereq: os2
Processes have separate address spaces; fork copies the file-descriptor table, and exec keeps descriptors open unless they are close-on-exec.
os4
Shared data needs mutual exclusion and condition variables; on Linux these are built on futexes, which work on any shared memory.
os10
File descriptors point to open file descriptions; reads and writes on pipes and sockets go through kernel buffers like files do.
why:
The isolation that os2 and os7 work so hard to provide has a cost: processes cannot simply share variables. Yet real systems are made of cooperating processes everywhere you look. A shell pipeline chains grep, sort and uniq. Chrome splits each tab into a renderer process that talks to the browser process thousands of times a second. PostgreSQL's backends share one buffer pool of gigabytes. A PyTorch training job's data-loader workers hand decoded batches to the main process. Nginx's master process tells its workers to reload configuration. docker on the command line talks to the Docker daemon. Kubernetes tells your container to shut down. Each uses a different inter-process communication (IPC) mechanism, chosen for different reasons.

Choosing badly causes real incidents. A pipeline hangs because a process forgot to close a pipe end. A server dies silently when a client disconnects, killed by a signal nobody handled. A machine-learning job crashes with "Bus error" only inside Docker. A service takes 30 seconds to stop on every deploy and drops requests when it finally does. A shared-memory design corrupts data because two processes wrote without a lock, or deadlocks because one crashed while holding it.

Interviewers ask "what IPC mechanisms do you know and when would you use each?", "how does a pipe work?", "what is a signal?" and "what is async-signal-safe?" in OS rounds, and design questions in senior rounds: "how would two processes on one machine exchange large data with low latency?", "how do you implement graceful shutdown?".

This lesson covers the mechanisms one by one (pipes and FIFOs, Unix domain sockets, message queues, shared memory, signals), how each works inside the kernel, what each costs, and how to choose, then the production failures each one is known for.
primer:
Ways to talk between rooms

Picture processes as people in separate, soundproof rooms of one building (the machine). They cannot hear or see each other. The building (the kernel) offers several ways to communicate:

  • A pneumatic tube from one room to another: whatever one side pushes in comes out the other side in order. That is a pipe: one direction, a stream of bytes, with a limited capacity in the tube.
  • A telephone line between two rooms, which either side can dial by a number listed in the lobby: two-way conversation, and the caller can even hand over a key to a room through it. That is a Unix domain socket.
  • A mailbox where people drop separate letters, possibly marked urgent: each letter arrives whole. That is a message queue.
  • A shared whiteboard visible from both rooms through a window: no need to send anything, but two people writing at once make a mess unless they agree on turns. That is shared memory, plus the synchronization from os4.
  • A doorbell with a few distinct rings: it carries no message beyond "ring number 15", it interrupts whatever you were doing, and if it rings twice while you are answering the first, you may only notice once. That is a signal.

Where the analogy breaks: everything except shared memory actually passes through the kernel, which copies the data from the sender's memory into a kernel buffer and then into the receiver's memory. Those copies are what make these mechanisms safe and simple, and also what limits their speed for large volumes. Shared memory removes the copies and with them the safety.

Four questions before choosing

Almost every IPC decision comes down to four questions. Are the processes related? A parent can hand its children inherited descriptors (pipes, anonymous shared mappings); strangers need something with a name (a FIFO, a socket path, a named shared-memory object) or a broker. Which direction, and what shape? One-way streaming suits a pipe; request and response suits a socket; discrete prioritised messages suit a queue; a big data set both sides read suits shared memory. How much data, how often? At kilobytes per request, two kernel copies are invisible; at gigabytes per second, they cost whole cores. What happens when one side dies? With pipes and sockets the kernel tells the survivor (end-of-file, EPIPE, connection reset); with shared memory nobody tells you anything, and a lock held by the dead process stays held. Most production problems with IPC trace back to an unasked fourth question.

One more distinction runs through the lesson: data versus notification. Pipes, sockets and queues carry data and notify at the same time, because a blocked reader wakes when bytes arrive. Shared memory carries data but notifies nobody, and signals notify but carry no data. Designs that use shared memory therefore always pair it with some notification channel, and designs that use signals pair them with some data channel, such as a configuration file to reread on SIGHUP.
body:
1. Pipes

pipe(fds) creates a kernel buffer and returns two file descriptors: fds[0] for reading and fds[1] for writing. Data written to one end comes out of the other, in order, as a byte stream with no message boundaries. On its own a pipe is useless; its power comes from fork (os2), which copies descriptors into the child, so parent and child share both ends and each closes the end it does not use.

import os
r, w = os.pipe()
if os.fork() == 0:                # child: the writer
    os.close(r)
    os.write(w, b"hello from child\n")
    os._exit(0)
os.close(w)                       # parent: the reader; close its copy of w!
print(os.read(r, 100))            # b'hello from child\n'
print(os.read(r, 100))            # b'' : every writer has closed, so EOF
os.wait()

The rules of a pipe follow from its buffer, 64 KiB by default on Linux (16 pages; adjustable up to /proc/sys/fs/pipe-max-size, 1 MiB by default, with fcntl(F_SETPIPE_SZ)):

  • Full buffer: write() blocks until the reader drains space. This is natural backpressure: a fast producer piped into a slow consumer is slowed down automatically (os5).
  • Empty buffer: read() blocks until data arrives, unless every write end in every process has been closed, in which case it returns 0, end-of-file. Forgetting to close one copy of the write end (in the reader itself, or in a child that inherited it) means EOF never comes and the reader hangs forever.
  • No readers: if every read end is closed, write() raises SIGPIPE in the writer, which kills it by default; if SIGPIPE is ignored, the write fails with EPIPE. That is how yes | head -1 ends: head exits after one line, and yes dies on its next write.
  • Atomicity: a write of at most PIPE_BUF bytes (4,096 on Linux) is atomic: it will not be interleaved with other writers' data. Larger writes from several processes can interleave. That is why many processes can safely write short lines to one shared pipe or log, but not large records.

A named pipe or FIFO (mkfifo /tmp/feed) is a pipe with an entry in the file system. Unrelated processes open it by name, one for reading and one for writing; data still flows through a kernel buffer, never through the disk. Opening one end blocks until the other end is opened too, a frequent source of "my script hangs at open".

2. Unix domain sockets

Unix domain sockets (AF_UNIX) use the socket API from net13 between processes on the same machine. A server binds to a path such as /run/myapp.sock (or, on Linux, an abstract name that exists only in the kernel, written with a leading zero byte), listens and accepts; clients connect to the path. Compared with pipes they are bidirectional, can be connected to by unrelated processes, and come in three types: SOCK_STREAM (a byte stream, like TCP), SOCK_DGRAM (messages with boundaries preserved, and on Unix sockets, unlike UDP, reliable and ordered) and SOCK_SEQPACKET (connection-oriented messages).

They have three abilities TCP lacks, which explain why so much local infrastructure uses them:

  • Permission control by the file system. A socket file's owner and mode decide who can connect. The Docker daemon listens on /var/run/docker.sock, owned by root and the docker group; anyone who can write to it can control containers, which is effectively root access (production section).
  • Peer credentials. getsockopt(SO_PEERCRED) returns the connecting process's PID, user ID and group ID, verified by the kernel. PostgreSQL's peer authentication and systemd's services use this to know who is calling without passwords.
  • Passing file descriptors. With sendmsg() and an SCM_RIGHTS control message, a process can send open file descriptors; the kernel installs new descriptors in the receiver pointing to the same open file descriptions (os10). The receiver gets access to a file, socket or pipe it could not have opened itself.

Because they skip the network stack entirely (no TCP handshake, sequence numbers, checksums, congestion control or routing), Unix sockets have noticeably lower latency and CPU cost than TCP over loopback; benchmarks typically show tens of percent or more better throughput for small messages. Databases, X11 and Wayland, D-Bus, container runtimes (containerd, the kubelet's CRI socket) and local proxies use them.

3. Message queues

A message queue is a kernel-held list of discrete messages. POSIX queues (mq_open("/jobs", ...), mq_send, mq_receive) give each message a priority, deliver the highest-priority oldest message first, block senders when the queue is full and receivers when it is empty, and appear under /dev/mqueue. On Linux a queue descriptor works with select/epoll, and mq_notify can signal a process when a message arrives. Default limits are small (10 messages of 8 KiB per queue unless raised through /proc/sys/fs/mqueue/). System V message queues (msgget, msgsnd) are the older interface, with typed messages.

Their value over a pipe is that message boundaries are preserved: two 100-byte messages arrive as two 100-byte messages, never as one 200-byte read or a 150 + 50 split, so no framing protocol is needed. In practice they are less common than Unix datagram sockets, which offer the same boundary preservation plus credentials and descriptor passing, and than user-space brokers when messages must survive restarts. Note the difference from distributed message queues such as Kafka or SQS: kernel queues are local, in memory, and vanish on reboot.

4. Shared memory

Every mechanism so far copies data twice: from the sender into a kernel buffer, then from the kernel buffer into the receiver. For a few kilobytes that is negligible; for gigabytes per second it consumes cores. Shared memory removes the copies by mapping the same physical pages into both processes' address spaces (os7): a store by one process is visible to a load by the other, with the kernel not involved at all after setup. Three common ways to set it up on Linux:

  • Anonymous shared mapping before fork: mmap(NULL, size, PROT_READ|PROT_WRITE, MAP_SHARED|MAP_ANONYMOUS, -1, 0), then fork; parent and child share it. Note MAP_SHARED: a private mapping would be copy-on-write (os9).
  • POSIX shared memory: shm_open("/frames", O_CREAT|O_RDWR, 0600) creates a named object, really a file in the /dev/shm tmpfs; size it with ftruncate and map it with mmap(MAP_SHARED) in each process. It persists until shm_unlink. Python's multiprocessing.shared_memory wraps this.
  • memfd: memfd_create() makes an anonymous in-memory file with no name; pass its descriptor over a Unix socket and the receiver maps it. It disappears when the last reference closes, so nothing leaks, and seals can make it immutable before sharing.

Synchronizing across processes. Everything in os4 applies, because two processes sharing memory are like two threads sharing memory. A pthread mutex or condition variable placed in the shared region works across processes if initialised with the PTHREAD_PROCESS_SHARED attribute; it is a futex on the shared page, and futexes work on shared mappings. POSIX named semaphores (sem_open) and C11 atomics in the region also work. Two extra hazards: a process can crash while holding a lock, leaving it locked forever (robust mutexes, PTHREAD_MUTEX_ROBUST, report EOWNERDEAD to the next locker so it can repair the data), and memory ordering must be handled exactly as between threads, with acquire and release when publishing data.

PostgreSQL's shared buffers, Chrome's compositor buffers, PyTorch tensors passed between DataLoader workers and the main process, and audio servers' ring buffers all use shared memory, each with its own synchronization protocol on top.

5. Signals

A signal is a small, numbered, asynchronous notification sent to a process (or a specific thread). Sources: the kernel (SIGSEGV for a bad memory access, SIGPIPE for writing to a closed pipe, SIGCHLD when a child exits), the terminal (SIGINT on Ctrl+C, SIGTSTP on Ctrl+Z), and other processes via kill(pid, sig), subject to permission (same user, or privileged). Each signal has a default action:

SignalNumber (x86 Linux)Typical sourceDefault actionCatchable?
SIGHUP1Terminal closed; convention: reload configTerminateYes
SIGINT2Ctrl+CTerminateYes
SIGKILL9kill -9, OOM killerTerminateNo
SIGSEGV11Invalid memory accessTerminate + core dumpYes (rarely useful)
SIGPIPE13Write to pipe/socket with no readerTerminateYes
SIGTERM15kill, docker stop, KubernetesTerminateYes
SIGCHLD17Child stopped or exitedIgnoreYes
SIGSTOP / SIGCONT19 / 18Pause / resume (debuggers, job control)Stop / continueSIGSTOP: no

How delivery works. Sending a signal sets a bit in the target's pending set; it does not run anything immediately. Each thread has a signal mask of blocked signals, which stay pending until unblocked. When the target thread next returns from the kernel to user mode (after a system call, an interrupt, or being scheduled), the kernel checks for pending, unblocked signals and delivers one: either performs the default action, ignores it, or arranges for the thread to run the program's handler, by building a frame on the user stack so the thread "returns" into the handler and, when the handler returns, into a sigreturn system call that restores the interrupted state (os1's deep section). If the thread was blocked in a slow system call, the call is interrupted and either restarted automatically (with SA_RESTART) or fails with EINTR.

Standard signals are not queued. Pending is a bit, not a counter. If three children exit while SIGCHLD is already pending, the parent's handler may run once, so a handler must loop with waitpid(-1, WNOHANG) until no more children are reaped (os2). Real-time signals (SIGRTMIN to SIGRTMAX) are queued and can carry a value, but are rarely used directly.

Handlers are dangerous. A handler can run between any two instructions of the main program, including in the middle of malloc while it holds the allocator lock or halfway through updating a linked list. If the handler calls malloc, printf or almost any library function, it can deadlock or corrupt state. POSIX lists the async-signal-safe functions callable from handlers (write, read, _exit, kill, sigaction and a few dozen more). The robust patterns all reduce the handler to almost nothing:

  • Set a volatile sig_atomic_t flag that the main loop checks.
  • The self-pipe trick: the handler writes one byte to a pipe that the event loop watches with epoll, turning the signal into an ordinary readable event.
  • signalfd (Linux): block the signals, then read them as data from a file descriptor in the event loop; no handler at all.
  • In multithreaded programs: block signals in all threads and dedicate one thread to sigwait().

Higher-level runtimes do this for you. CPython's C-level handler only records that a signal arrived; your Python handler runs later, in the main thread, between bytecodes. asyncio's loop.add_signal_handler uses a self-pipe; Go delivers signals on a channel.

6. Choosing a mechanism

MechanismData modelWho can use itCopiesBest for
PipeOne-way byte streamRelated processes (inherited)2Pipelines, parent-child streaming, child stdout capture
FIFOOne-way byte streamAnyone with file permission2Simple producer-consumer between unrelated scripts
Unix socketTwo-way stream or messagesAnyone with file permission2Local client-server, credentials, passing fds
Message queuePrioritised messagesAnyone with permission2Small typed messages with priorities
Shared memoryRaw memoryProcesses that map it0Large data, high rates, low latency
SignalA number (no data)Same user or privileged-Lifecycle events: stop, reload, child exit
eventfd / futexCounter / wake-upShared descriptor or memory-Doorbells for shared-memory designs

A common combination is a Unix socket for control (connect, authenticate, pass a memfd, exchange small commands) plus shared memory for bulk data, plus an eventfd or futex for "new data is ready" notifications. That is the structure of Wayland compositors, Chrome's GPU process channels, many high-frequency trading feeds and some inference servers.
deep:
Passing descriptors: socket activation and zero-downtime restarts

Descriptor passing enables patterns that would otherwise be impossible. With systemd socket activation, systemd creates and binds a service's listening socket at boot, before the service starts, and passes it to the service as an inherited descriptor (fd 3 onwards, announced in LISTEN_FDS). Connections arriving before the service is ready wait in the socket's accept queue instead of being refused, services can be started on demand, and the socket survives service restarts. Zero-downtime reloads work similarly: nginx re-executes its binary while keeping listening sockets inherited across exec, and proxies such as HAProxy and Envoy hand listening sockets from the old process to the new one over a Unix socket with SCM_RIGHTS, so no connection is ever refused. Because each passed descriptor shares the same open file description, the new process accepts from the very same kernel queue.

eventfd and futexes as doorbells

Shared-memory designs need a way to wake a sleeping consumer without spinning. An eventfd is a descriptor holding a 64-bit counter: write adds to it, read returns and resets it (or decrements by one in semaphore mode), and it is readable in epoll when non-zero, so it slots into event loops. Between threads and processes that share memory, a futex word inside the shared region does the same job with less overhead (os4). A well-designed shared-memory ring only rings the doorbell when the consumer has said it is going to sleep, avoiding a system call per message in the busy case.

Android's Binder and D-Bus

Operating systems often build a higher-level IPC system on top of these primitives. D-Bus, used on Linux desktops and by systemd, is a message bus over Unix sockets with typed method calls, signals (events, not Unix signals) and a central broker that handles naming and access policy. Android's Binder is a kernel driver for object-oriented remote procedure calls between apps and system services: a transaction copies data once, directly from the sender into a buffer mapped by the receiver, carries the caller's identity for permission checks, can pass file descriptors and object references, and integrates with thread pools and priority inheritance. Nearly every Android API call, from opening the camera to showing a notification, is a Binder transaction.

Signals and threads: why they mix badly

Signal dispositions (handlers) are per process, but masks and delivery are per thread, and a process-directed signal goes to an arbitrary thread that does not block it. Libraries that start background threads therefore change where signals land, and a handler can run on a thread holding a lock the handler needs. Combined with async-signal-safety, this is why robust multithreaded programs block all asynchronous signals in every thread at startup (masks are inherited by new threads) and consume them in one dedicated place: a sigwait thread or a signalfd in the event loop. Synchronous signals such as SIGSEGV and SIGFPE still go to the faulting thread, which is what lets runtimes such as the JVM implement null checks and safepoints with deliberate faults on guard pages.

IPC across containers

Containers (os13) isolate IPC as well as files and networks. Each container normally gets its own IPC namespace, which separates System V objects and POSIX message queues, and its own /dev/shm, so two containers cannot see each other's shared memory or queues by name. Each also has its own network namespace, so localhost in one container is not localhost in another, except for containers in one Kubernetes pod, which share a network namespace and can talk over loopback. Unix sockets are files, so they cross container boundaries wherever a directory is shared: a socket in a volume mounted into two containers is how sidecars such as service-mesh proxies, log agents and the kubelet's container-runtime socket communicate. Pods can opt into a shared IPC namespace for shared memory between their containers, and docker run --ipc=container:<name> does the same for two containers.

Copies, splice and vmsplice

Pipes copy data in and out, but Linux can move data between descriptors without user-space copies. splice() moves pages between a pipe and a file or socket by passing page references inside the kernel, and vmsplice() maps user pages into a pipe. tee() duplicates pipe contents without consuming them. Tools such as high-throughput log shippers and proxies use these to forward data between sockets and files with minimal CPU. They are subtle (the user must not modify pages given to vmsplice until consumed), which is why most programs use sendfile (os11) or plain copies.
prod:
SIGPIPE: the silent killer

A C or Go-cgo server that writes to a client which has already disconnected receives SIGPIPE, whose default action kills the whole server, with no log line. Servers therefore ignore SIGPIPE at startup (signal(SIGPIPE, SIG_IGN)) or pass MSG_NOSIGNAL to send(), and handle the resulting EPIPE error per connection. Python ignores SIGPIPE at interpreter startup, so the same situation raises BrokenPipeError; that is why python script.py | head prints a traceback about a broken pipe when head exits early. The usual fix in command-line tools is to catch it and exit quietly, or restore the default disposition so the tool dies like other Unix filters.

/dev/shm in containers

POSIX shared memory lives in /dev/shm, a tmpfs. Docker gives each container its own /dev/shm of only 64 MB by default. Anything that moves large data through shared memory then fails inside containers but works on the host: PyTorch DataLoader workers (which share batch tensors through shared memory) crash with "Bus error" or "unable to write to file", Chrome and Electron renderers crash, and PostgreSQL's parallel queries fail to allocate dynamic shared memory. Fixes: docker run --shm-size=8g, in Kubernetes a emptyDir volume with medium: Memory and a sizeLimit mounted at /dev/shm, or --ipc=host where isolation allows. Remember that tmpfs pages count against the container's memory limit (os9).

Graceful shutdown under orchestration

When Kubernetes deletes a pod, the kubelet sends SIGTERM to the container's PID 1, waits terminationGracePeriodSeconds (30 seconds by default), then sends SIGKILL. Meanwhile, endpoints are removed from load balancers asynchronously, so new requests may still arrive for a few seconds after SIGTERM. A well-behaved service: catches SIGTERM; starts failing its readiness probe; keeps serving for a short drain period (often implemented as a preStop sleep of 5-10 seconds) so in-flight routing updates catch up; stops accepting new connections; finishes in-flight requests within a deadline; flushes buffers; and exits. Common failures: the application is not PID 1 and never receives SIGTERM (a shell entrypoint without exec, os2); the handler exits immediately, dropping in-flight requests; or shutdown takes longer than the grace period and is cut off by SIGKILL.

The Docker socket is root

Mounting /var/run/docker.sock into a container (common for CI agents and monitoring tools) gives that container full control of the Docker daemon, which runs as root: it can start a privileged container with the host's root file system mounted and take over the machine. Unix-socket permissions are the only gate, so membership of the docker group is equivalent to root. Safer alternatives are rootless runtimes, socket proxies that allow only specific API calls, and build tools that do not need a daemon.

Leaks and stale endpoints

IPC objects can outlive their processes. A server that crashes leaves its Unix socket file behind, and the next start fails with "Address already in use" until the stale file is removed (servers commonly unlink the path before bind, carefully, or use abstract names, which vanish with the socket). POSIX shared memory and message queues persist in /dev/shm and /dev/mqueue until unlinked; System V segments, queues and semaphores persist until removed with ipcrm (list them with ipcs). Python's multiprocessing.shared_memory warns about "leaked shared_memory objects" at shutdown for this reason. Leaked segments consume RAM (tmpfs is memory) and count against limits.

Pipe hangs

Two classic hangs come from pipe rules. A reader waiting for EOF that never arrives, because some process still holds a write end (often a child that inherited it, which is one reason to use O_CLOEXEC/close_fds=True, the default in Python's subprocess). And the two-pipe deadlock from os6: a parent writes a large input to a child's stdin while the child, which writes output as it goes, blocks on its full stdout pipe that the parent is not reading. subprocess.run(..., input=...) and communicate() avoid it by reading and writing concurrently.
myths: Shared memory is always the best IPC because it is fastest.

Shared memory avoids copying data through the kernel, which matters for large or very frequent transfers, but it gives you raw memory and nothing else: you must build synchronization, framing, notification and crash recovery yourself, and pointers inside it are meaningless in the other process unless both map it at the same address. For most messages, a pipe or Unix socket is fast enough and far less error-prone.
A signal handler can do anything a normal function can.

A handler can run between any two instructions of the main program, possibly while it holds the malloc lock or is halfway through printf. Calling such functions from the handler can deadlock or corrupt state. POSIX lists the async-signal-safe functions that are allowed (write, _exit and a few dozen others). Safe handlers just set a flag or write a byte to a pipe and let the main loop do the work.
If I send a process five SIGUSR1 signals, its handler runs five times.

Standard signals are not queued: the kernel keeps one pending bit per signal, so signals that arrive while one is already pending are merged. The handler may run once. Real-time signals (SIGRTMIN to SIGRTMAX) are queued and carry a value, and signalfd or a pipe-based design lets programs count events reliably.
Pipes only work between a parent and a child.

Anonymous pipes are inherited through fork, so they connect related processes. Named pipes (FIFOs created with mkfifo) appear in the file system and can be opened by any process with permission. And file descriptors, including pipe ends, can be passed between unrelated processes over a Unix domain socket.
Unix domain sockets are just TCP on localhost.

They share the socket API, but Unix sockets never touch the network stack: no TCP handshake, checksums, congestion control or IP routing, so they have lower latency and higher throughput than loopback TCP. They are protected by file-system permissions, can report the peer's user and process ID, and can carry open file descriptors, none of which TCP can do.
lab:
Compare copying through a pipe with shared memory, and handle SIGTERM gracefully. Linux, WSL or macOS with Python 3.8+.

  1. Save as ipc.py: 
    import os, time, signal
from multiprocessing import shared_memory

N = 200 * 1024 * 1024                         # 200 MB payload
data = os.urandom(1024) * (N // 1024)

# 1. through a pipe: copied into and out of the kernel
r, w = os.pipe()
t = time.perf_counter()
if os.fork() == 0:
    os.close(r); mv = memoryview(data)
    for i in range(0, N, 1 << 20): os.write(w, mv[i:i + (1 << 20)])
    os._exit(0)
os.close(w); got = 0
while chunk := os.read(r, 1 << 20): got += len(chunk)
os.wait()
print(f"pipe:          {got / (time.perf_counter() - t) / 1e9:.2f} GB/s")

# 2. shared memory: child writes in place, parent reads it directly
shm = shared_memory.SharedMemory(create=True, size=N)
t = time.perf_counter()
if os.fork() == 0:
    shm.buf[:N] = data; os._exit(0)
os.wait()
print(f"shared memory: {N / (time.perf_counter() - t) / 1e9:.2f} GB/s (one copy, by the writer)")
print("same bytes:", bytes(shm.buf[:16]) == data[:16])
shm.close(); shm.unlink()

# 3. graceful SIGTERM
stop = False
def on_term(sig, frame):
    global stop; stop = True                  # just set a flag
signal.signal(signal.SIGTERM, on_term)
print("pid", os.getpid(), "- run: kill", os.getpid())
while not stop: time.sleep(0.2)
print("got SIGTERM: finishing in-flight work, flushing, exiting 0")
  2. Run python3 ipc.py, and when it prints its PID, run kill <pid> from another terminal. Then try kill -9 <pid> on a second run.
  3. Pipe behaviour: yes | head -1; echo "exit codes: ${PIPESTATUS[@]}".

What to look for. The pipe moves data at a few GB/s: every byte is copied from the child into the kernel buffer and from there into the parent, in 64 KiB pipe-sized gulps with a context switch whenever the buffer fills or empties. Shared memory is typically several times faster, since the only cost is the writer's own copy into the mapped pages (plus first-touch page faults), and the reader sees the bytes with no transfer at all. With plain kill (SIGTERM), the program prints its shutdown message and exits cleanly; with kill -9, it dies instantly with no message, since SIGKILL cannot be caught. In step 3, PIPESTATUS shows 141 0: yes was killed by SIGPIPE (128 + 13) as soon as head exited.
recap: Processes are isolated by design, so they communicate through mechanisms the kernel provides: byte streams, messages, shared memory and notifications.

A pipe is a one-way byte stream through a kernel buffer of 64 KiB by default; writers block when it is full, readers block when it is empty, readers see end-of-file when all writers close, and writers get SIGPIPE or EPIPE when all readers close.
Named pipes give a pipe a file-system name so unrelated processes can use it.
Unix domain sockets are bidirectional, support stream and datagram modes, are secured by file permissions, can report the peer's credentials and can pass open file descriptors.
POSIX message queues carry discrete messages with priorities; System V queues are an older equivalent.
