Shared memory maps the same physical pages into several processes, so data needs no copying, but processes must synchronize with process-shared mutexes, semaphores or atomics and must not store raw pointers.
Signals are small asynchronous notifications with default actions; handlers run between arbitrary instructions, must only use async-signal-safe functions, and standard signals are not queued.
Modern programs turn signals into ordinary events with signalfd or the self-pipe trick, and handle SIGTERM for graceful shutdown.
Choose by need: pipes for streaming between related processes, Unix sockets for request-response services and descriptor passing, shared memory for large data, signals only for notifications.
glossary: Abstract socket namespace
A Linux feature letting Unix sockets have names that exist only in the kernel, not as files, starting with a zero byte.
Async-signal-safe
A function that can be safely called from a signal handler because it does not depend on state the interrupted code might be modifying.
EOF
End of file: a read returning 0 bytes, meaning the writer side has closed and no more data will come.
eventfd
A file descriptor holding a 64-bit counter, used to send wake-up notifications between threads or processes and usable with epoll.
FIFO (named pipe)
A pipe with a name in the file system, created with mkfifo, that unrelated processes can open.
IPC
Inter-process communication: any mechanism that lets separate processes exchange data or notifications.
IPC namespace
A Linux namespace that isolates System V IPC objects and POSIX message queues between groups of processes (os13).
memfd
An anonymous file living only in memory, created with memfd_create, that can be mapped and passed to other processes.
Message queue
A kernel object holding discrete messages that processes send and receive, preserving message boundaries.
Pipe
A one-way kernel buffer with a read end and a write end, each a file descriptor.
PIPE_BUF
The size (4,096 bytes on Linux) up to which a write to a pipe is guaranteed not to be interleaved with other writers' data.
Process-shared mutex
A pthread mutex initialised with PTHREAD_PROCESS_SHARED and placed in shared memory so threads in different processes can use it.
Robust mutex
A process-shared mutex that, if its owner dies while holding it, reports EOWNERDEAD to the next locker instead of staying locked forever.
SCM_RIGHTS
A control message on Unix sockets that passes open file descriptors to the receiving process.
Self-pipe trick
A signal handler writes a byte to a pipe that the main event loop watches, converting a signal into an ordinary I/O event.
Shared memory
A region of physical memory mapped into more than one process's address space.
SIGCHLD
Sent to a parent when a child stops or exits.
SIGHUP
Originally 'terminal hung up'; conventionally used to ask daemons to reload their configuration.
SIGINT
Sent by Ctrl+C in a terminal; default action terminates the process.
SIGKILL
Terminates a process immediately; cannot be caught, blocked or ignored.
Signal
A small numbered asynchronous notification delivered to a process or thread by the kernel.
Signal mask
The set of signals a thread currently blocks; blocked signals stay pending until unblocked.
signalfd
A Linux file descriptor from which pending signals can be read as data, so they can be handled in an event loop.
SIGPIPE
Sent to a process that writes to a pipe or socket with no reader; default action terminates it.
SIGSEGV
Sent on an invalid memory access; default action terminates with a core dump.
SIGTERM
A polite request to terminate, sent by kill by default and by container runtimes on stop; can be caught for graceful shutdown.
SO_PEERCRED
A socket option returning the process ID, user ID and group ID of the process on the other end of a Unix socket.
Unix domain socket
A socket for communication between processes on the same host, addressed by a file-system path or an abstract name.
drill:
Design: a local inference sidecar

A Python web service (8 worker processes) calls a GPU inference server running as a separate process on the same machine. Each request sends a 2 MB preprocessed tensor and receives a 4 KB result; the target is 2,000 requests per second with p99 under 20 ms. The first version uses HTTP over TCP to localhost with JSON-encoded tensors and reaches only 300 requests per second with high CPU in both processes. Design a better IPC scheme, estimate its data rates, and describe how you would handle a crash of either side and a graceful restart of the inference server.

Answer

Why the first version is slow. JSON-encoding 2 MB tensors inflates them several times and costs heavy CPU to encode and parse; HTTP over loopback TCP adds the network stack, and every byte is copied at least twice through the kernel. At 2,000 requests/s the raw payload is 4 GB/s before any encoding overhead, which a copy-and-encode design cannot sustain on a few cores.

Design. Separate control from data. Control: each web worker connects to the inference server over a Unix domain socket (lower overhead than TCP, permission-protected, and the server can check the caller with SO_PEERCRED). Data: at connection setup, the server creates a memfd shared-memory region per worker, for example a ring of 16 slots of 2 MB plus a header each (about 32 MB per worker, 256 MB total), and passes it with SCM_RIGHTS; both sides map it. A request: the worker writes the tensor in raw binary directly into a free slot (one 2 MB copy, or zero if preprocessing writes straight into the slot), then sends a tiny message on the socket: "slot 5, length, request id". The server reads the slot in place (or DMAs from it to the GPU, ideally from pinned memory), writes the 4 KB result into the slot's result area, and replies "slot 5 done" on the socket. Messages of a few bytes over a Unix socket cost a few microseconds; the socket also acts as the notification mechanism, so no extra eventfd is needed.

Rates. Data crosses memory once per request: 2,000 × 2 MB = 4 GB/s of writer-side memcpy, spread across 8 workers (about 0.5 GB/s each, a small fraction of one core each). Control traffic is about 4,000 small messages per second, negligible. Latency added by IPC is tens of microseconds, leaving the 20 ms budget to the model.

Failures. If the inference server crashes, workers see EOF or ECONNRESET on their sockets, fail in-flight requests (or retry against a restarted server), and reconnect, receiving new memfds; the old memory is freed automatically when the last mapping closes, so nothing leaks. If a worker crashes, the server sees its socket close and reclaims that worker's slots. Slot ownership is tracked by the protocol on the socket (never by locks inside shared memory), so a crash cannot leave a lock held. Graceful restart: the server handles SIGTERM by stopping acceptance of new requests, telling connected workers to pause (a control message), finishing in-flight slots, and exiting; the new server can be started first and listen on a new socket path (or receive the listening socket via descriptor passing) so workers reconnect without a gap. Size /dev/shm is irrelevant here because memfd does not use it, which avoids the container shared-memory limit.
qa: E
Why do processes need special mechanisms to communicate?

Each process has its own address space, so one process cannot read or write another's variables; that isolation is what keeps a crash or bug in one from corrupting another. To cooperate they must use channels the kernel provides and controls: pipes and sockets that copy data through kernel buffers, message queues, shared-memory regions both explicitly map, signals, or files.
E
What is a pipe and how does the shell use it?

A pipe is a one-way byte stream: a kernel buffer with a write end and a read end, each a file descriptor. For ls | wc -l the shell creates a pipe, forks two children, connects the first child's stdout to the write end and the second child's stdin to the read end with dup2, closes the unused ends and execs both programs. ls writes into the pipe, wc reads from it, and neither knows the other exists.
E
What is a signal? Name some common ones.

A signal is a small asynchronous notification sent by the kernel to a process, identified by a number. SIGINT comes from Ctrl+C, SIGTERM politely asks a process to exit, SIGKILL forcibly kills it, SIGHUP traditionally means reload configuration, SIGCHLD tells a parent a child has exited, SIGSEGV reports an invalid memory access and SIGPIPE reports writing to a pipe with no reader. Each has a default action, and all except SIGKILL and SIGSTOP can be caught or ignored.
M
What happens when a pipe's reader exits while the writer keeps writing, and vice versa?

If all read ends are closed, the next write raises SIGPIPE in the writer, whose default action kills it; if SIGPIPE is ignored or handled, write fails with EPIPE instead. That is how yes | head -1 terminates. If all write ends are closed, read returns 0 once the buffer is drained, which the reader treats as end-of-file. A common bug is forgetting to close an unused write end in the reader process, so the reader never sees end-of-file and hangs.
M
Compare pipes, Unix domain sockets and TCP over localhost for local IPC.

Pipes are one-way byte streams, simplest for parent-child streaming. Unix sockets are bidirectional, offer stream and datagram modes, have file-system names so unrelated processes can connect, provide peer credentials and can pass file descriptors; they skip the network stack, so they are faster than loopback TCP. TCP on localhost is only worth it when the same code must also work across machines or the peer is in another network namespace.
M
How does shared memory IPC work and what are its pitfalls?

Two processes map the same physical pages, either with shm_open and mmap, with a MAP_SHARED anonymous mapping created before fork, or with a memfd passed between them. Writes by one are immediately visible to the other with no copying. Pitfalls: you must synchronize access with process-shared mutexes, semaphores or atomics and handle memory ordering; data must not contain raw pointers because each process may map the region at a different address, so use offsets; a process crashing while holding a lock leaves it locked unless you use robust mutexes; and the segment persists until unlinked, so leaks survive process exit.
M
What is async-signal safety and why does it matter?

A signal handler runs asynchronously, interrupting the main program at any instruction. If the program was inside malloc or printf, holding internal locks or with half-updated data structures, and the handler calls malloc or printf too, it can deadlock or corrupt memory. POSIX defines a list of async-signal-safe functions that can be called from handlers, including write, read, _exit, kill and sigaction but not malloc, printf or most library calls. The safe pattern is for the handler to set a volatile sig_atomic_t flag or write a byte to a pipe and return.

Follow-up: How do higher-level languages deal with this? — Python's C handler only records the signal; the Python-level handler runs later in the main thread between bytecodes, which is safe but means a thread blocked in a long C call delays it.
M
How do you implement graceful shutdown on SIGTERM in a server?

Install a handler (or use signalfd or the runtime's signal API) that only marks shutdown as requested and wakes the main loop. The main loop then stops accepting new connections, fails health checks so load balancers drain traffic, finishes in-flight requests up to a deadline, flushes logs and buffers, closes resources and exits with code 0. In Kubernetes, the pod receives SIGTERM, has terminationGracePeriodSeconds (30 seconds by default) to finish, and is then sent SIGKILL. The process must be PID 1 or have its signals forwarded (os2).
M
How can one process give another an open file descriptor?

Over a Unix domain socket, using sendmsg with an SCM_RIGHTS control message containing the descriptor. The kernel installs a new descriptor in the receiver that refers to the same open file description, with the same offset and flags. This is how systemd socket activation hands listening sockets to services, how some servers achieve zero-downtime restarts by passing their listening socket to the new process, and how privilege-separated programs let an unprivileged process use files opened by a privileged helper.
H
How are signals delivered to multithreaded processes?

Each thread has its own signal mask and pending set, and the process has a shared pending set. Signals generated for a specific thread, such as SIGSEGV from its own fault or pthread_kill, go to that thread. Process-directed signals, such as from kill, are delivered to any one thread that does not block them, chosen by the kernel. Handlers and dispositions are per process. A common design is to block all signals in every thread at startup and dedicate one thread to sigwait or signalfd, so signals are handled synchronously in one known place.
H
PyTorch DataLoader workers crash with 'Bus error' or 'unable to write to file /torch_...' inside Docker but not on the host. Why?

DataLoader workers pass batches to the main process through shared memory, which Linux implements as files in /dev/shm, a tmpfs. Docker gives containers their own /dev/shm of only 64 MB by default. Large batches exhaust it; writes fail, or touching a page of a mapped shared-memory file that cannot be backed raises SIGBUS. Fixes are to increase it with docker run --shm-size (or a memory-backed emptyDir mounted at /dev/shm in Kubernetes), use --ipc=host where acceptable, reduce batch size or worker count, or switch the sharing strategy.
H
Design a low-latency channel to stream 1 GB/s of camera frames from a capture process to an inference process on the same machine.

Use shared memory to avoid copying frames through the kernel: allocate a ring of frame slots in a memfd or shm segment mapped by both, with a small header per slot (sequence number, length, ready flag). The producer writes a frame into the next free slot, then publishes it with a release store of the sequence number; the consumer reads with acquire loads, so it never sees a half-written frame. For notification, use an eventfd or futex in the shared region so the consumer can sleep instead of spinning, and decide the overflow policy explicitly, such as dropping the oldest frame, so a slow consumer cannot stall capture. Use a Unix socket for setup, to pass the memfd and exchange control messages, and handle crashes by detecting the peer's disconnect on that socket.

Follow-up: Why not just use a Unix socket for the frames? — At 1 GB/s each frame would be copied twice through the kernel, costing several CPU cores of memcpy and adding latency; shared memory makes the transfer free and leaves only synchronization.
H
What are the trade-offs of System V IPC versus POSIX IPC?

System V (shmget, msgget, semget) is older, identifies objects by integer keys, has its own limits and permissions model, and objects persist until explicitly removed, so crashed programs leak them; ipcs and ipcrm manage them. POSIX IPC (shm_open, mq_open, sem_open) uses names, integrates with file descriptors and the file system (/dev/shm, /dev/mqueue), works with select or poll for message queues, and is generally simpler. Both persist beyond the process. New code usually prefers POSIX, memfd or Unix sockets; System V survives in older databases and software that still uses it.
refs: Pipe capacity, PIPE_BUF atomicity, blocking, EOF and SIGPIPE rules.
Signal list, default actions, delivery, masks, real-time signals and the async-signal-safe function list.
Unix domain sockets: addresses, abstract namespace, SO_PEERCRED and SCM_RIGHTS.
POSIX shared memory: shm_open, mmap and /dev/shm.
POSIX message queues, priorities and limits.
Shared memory blocks between Python processes, and their lifetime rules.
How tensors are shared through shared memory and the /dev/shm requirements.

t: Linux isolation: namespaces, cgroups, capabilities and seccomp
sum: The kernel features that a container is made of: the eight namespaces that control what a process can see, cgroups v2 that control how much it can use, capabilities that split root into pieces, seccomp filters that limit which system calls it can make, overlay file systems, and why containers share a kernel and what that means for security.
prereq: os2
Linux creates processes and threads with clone(), and flags choose what the new task shares; PID 1 has special duties for reaping orphans and handling signals.
os3
cgroup CPU weights set shares under contention and CPU quotas cap usage per period, which causes throttling.
os9
A cgroup that reaches its memory limit reclaims within itself and then OOM-kills a process inside the group.
sc15
Kubernetes runs containers in pods and turns resource requests and limits into kernel settings on each node.
why:
Run docker run -it ubuntu bash and inside you appear to be on a different machine: your shell is PID 1, the host name is a random hex string, ls / shows a fresh Ubuntu file system, ip addr shows a single interface with an unfamiliar address, and you are root. Yet on the host, ps aux shows that same bash as an ordinary process with a PID in the thousands. There is no second kernel and no virtual hardware. Everything that makes it feel like a separate machine comes from a handful of kernel features applied to a normal process.

Understanding those features is what separates using containers from operating them. Why does a container with a 2 GB limit get killed when free inside it shows 200 GB available? Why does a Go service in Kubernetes get throttled although its CPU graph looks fine? Why can a container that mounts the Docker socket take over the host? Why does a container escape vulnerability in the kernel or runc affect every container on the machine? Why can rootless Podman run containers without being root at all? Each answer is one of four mechanisms: namespaces, cgroups, capabilities and seccomp.

These questions come up in infrastructure, platform, SRE and senior backend interviews ("what is a container, really?", "namespaces versus cgroups", "how do Kubernetes limits work under the hood?", "how would you run untrusted code safely?") and in incident reviews. The Kubernetes lesson (sc15) covered containers from the orchestration side; this lesson opens the kernel side.

We will take each mechanism in turn: the eight namespaces and how a container's view is assembled, the overlay file system for images, cgroups v2 and its controllers, capabilities, seccomp filters and security modules, then how they combine, where the boundary is weak, and what stronger sandboxes add.
primer:
Serviced apartments in one building

Imagine a building of serviced apartments, all sharing one foundation, one electrical system and one front desk (the kernel). Each tenant's apartment is set up so that it feels like a whole house. Four separate things make that work:

  • Walls and curtains decide what each tenant can see: their own rooms, their own door number, their own mailbox. That is namespaces, controlling visibility of processes, files, network, host name and user IDs.
  • Meters and fuses decide how much each apartment can draw: electricity, water, heating, with a breaker that trips if a tenant exceeds their allowance. That is cgroups, controlling CPU, memory, I/O and process count.
  • Keys: even a tenant who is "in charge" of their apartment gets only some keys, not the building's master key. That is capabilities, splitting root's powers so a process gets only what it needs.
  • A list of requests the front desk will accept from each apartment: they will deliver parcels but will not let a tenant rewire the building. That is seccomp, filtering which system calls a process may make.

The analogy shows the key weakness too. All tenants share one foundation and one front desk. If the front desk has a flaw that lets a cleverly worded request open any door, every apartment is exposed. In computing terms, all containers share one kernel, so a kernel bug reachable through a permitted system call can break isolation for everyone. Virtual machines are more like separate houses on separate foundations.

Who puts the layers together

No single kernel feature called "container" exists. A stack of user-space software assembles one from the pieces. At the bottom, a low-level runtime such as runc or crun reads a configuration file (the OCI runtime specification: which namespaces, which mounts, which cgroup limits, which capabilities, which seccomp profile) and makes the system calls. Above it, containerd or CRI-O pulls images, unpacks layers and manages container lifecycles; Docker and Podman add the familiar command line; and in a cluster, the kubelet translates pod specs into those configurations through the container runtime interface (CRI). Every Dockerfile option and pod field that touches security or resources (USER, --memory, securityContext, resources.limits) eventually becomes one of a few dozen kernel settings described in this lesson.

That also tells you where to look when something is wrong. If a container cannot see a file, think mount namespace and volumes. If it cannot reach a service, think network namespace and routing. If it is killed or slow, think cgroups. If a call fails with EPERM even as root, think capabilities, seccomp or the security module. Matching the symptom to the mechanism is most of the debugging, and the rest of this lesson gives you the details of each mechanism so you can do that matching quickly.
body:
1. A container is a process with new namespaces

os2 showed that Linux creates every task with clone(), and that flags decide what the new task shares with its parent. A set of extra flags, CLONE_NEWNS, CLONE_NEWPID, CLONE_NEWNET, CLONE_NEWUTS, CLONE_NEWIPC, CLONE_NEWUSER, CLONE_NEWCGROUP and CLONE_NEWTIME (the last applies on the next fork), creates the child in new namespaces instead of its parent's. Three system calls manage them: clone() creates a process in new namespaces, unshare() moves the calling process into new ones, and setns() joins an existing namespace given a file descriptor for it. Every process's namespaces are visible as links in /proc/<pid>/ns/; two processes are in the same namespace exactly when the links point to the same inode number:

$ ls -l /proc/self/ns/
... cgroup -> 'cgroup:[4026531835]'
... mnt    -> 'mnt:[4026531841]'
... net    -> 'net:[4026531840]'
... pid    -> 'pid:[4026531836]'
... uts    -> 'uts:[4026531838]'   (also ipc, user, time)

Container runtimes such as runc and crun are, at their core, programs that call these system calls in the right order, set up the file system, cgroups and security settings, and then exec the container's entrypoint.

2. The namespaces, one by one

NamespaceIsolatesWhat the container seesLinux version
MountThe set of mountsIts own root file system and mount table2.4.19 (2002)
UTSHost name, domain nameIts own hostname2.6.19
IPCSystem V IPC, POSIX message queuesOnly its own queues and segments (os12)2.6.19
PIDProcess-ID numberingIts first process as PID 1; no host processes2.6.24
NetworkInterfaces, addresses, routes, firewall, ports, Unix abstract socketsIts own lo and eth0, its own port 802.6.29
UserUID/GID mappings, capabilities over the namespaceRoot inside, maybe nobody special outside3.8
CgroupVisible cgroup hierarchyIts own cgroup as the root of /sys/fs/cgroup4.6
TimeOffsets of monotonic and boot-time clocksClocks that survive checkpoint and restore5.6

PID namespaces nest: a process has a PID in its own namespace and in every ancestor namespace. The container's shell may be PID 1 inside and PID 48213 on the host. The PID 1 inside inherits init's duties (os2): orphans in the namespace are reparented to it, signals with default actions are ignored unless it installs handlers, and when it exits the kernel kills every other process in the namespace.

Network namespaces start empty except for a down loopback interface. To connect one, the runtime (or a CNI plugin in Kubernetes) creates a veth pair, two virtual interfaces joined like the ends of a cable, moves one end into the container's namespace (renamed eth0) and attaches the other to a bridge or routing setup on the host, then configures addresses, routes and NAT. Each namespace has its own port space, which is why ten containers can all listen on port 80. A Kubernetes pod is a group of containers sharing one network namespace, so they reach each other over localhost.

Mount namespaces give the container its own mount table, and the runtime uses pivot_root to make the image's file system the root, so the host's files simply are not in its tree, except paths deliberately bind-mounted in (volumes).

User namespaces are the most powerful and subtle. They map ranges of user and group IDs: container UID 0 might map to host UID 100000, container UID 1000 to host 101000. Inside, the process is root with all capabilities, but only over resources owned by its user namespace (its own mount, network and other namespaces); toward the host it is an unprivileged user. That is what makes rootless containers (Podman, rootless Docker, and Kubernetes pods with hostUsers: false) possible.

You can build a rough container with one command on Linux or WSL:

$ sudo unshare --uts --ipc --net --pid --fork --mount-proc bash
# hostname sandbox; hostname        → sandbox (host unchanged)
# ps aux                            → only bash (PID 1) and ps
# ip link                           → only lo, and it is DOWN

3. The file system: image layers and OverlayFS

A container image is a stack of layers, each a tarball of files added or changed by one build step. Rather than copy them into one directory per container, runtimes stack them with OverlayFS: the image layers are read-only lower directories, each container gets a writable upper directory, and the merged view shows upper on top of lowers. Reading a file finds the topmost copy. Writing to a file from a lower layer triggers copy-up: the whole file is copied into the upper directory first, then modified. Deleting a lower file creates a whiteout marker in upper. So a hundred containers from one image share one copy of its files on disk and in the page cache (os10), and each container's changes cost only what it writes. Copy-up of large files on first write and the build-up of upper directories are the usual performance and disk-space surprises; databases and other write-heavy data belong in volumes, which bypass the overlay.

4. cgroups v2: limiting and accounting

Control groups organise processes into a tree, mounted at /sys/fs/cgroup, and attach controllers that account for and limit resources of everything in a subtree. cgroups v2, the unified hierarchy, is the default on current distributions and Kubernetes; v1 had a separate tree per controller, which made combined policies such as "throttle I/O caused by memory write-back of this group" impossible. Each cgroup is a directory; its interface is files:

ControllerKey filesMeaning
cpucpu.weight, cpu.maxRelative share under contention (default 100); hard quota per period (os3)
memorymemory.min, memory.low, memory.high, memory.maxProtected minimum; soft protection; throttle-and-reclaim threshold; hard limit with OOM kill (os9)
ioio.weight, io.maxRelative I/O share; bandwidth or IOPS caps per device
pidspids.maxMaximum number of tasks (processes and threads)
cpusetcpuset.cpus, cpuset.memsWhich CPUs and NUMA memory nodes may be used

Each group also exposes accounting: cpu.stat (usage and throttling counts), memory.current and memory.stat (anonymous, file cache, kernel memory), memory.events (how often high and max were hit, OOM kills), io.stat, and pressure stall information (cpu.pressure, memory.pressure, io.pressure). Doing it by hand takes a few commands:

$ sudo mkdir /sys/fs/cgroup/demo
$ echo "50000 100000" | sudo tee /sys/fs/cgroup/demo/cpu.max     # half a CPU
$ echo 100M | sudo tee /sys/fs/cgroup/demo/memory.max
$ echo 64   | sudo tee /sys/fs/cgroup/demo/pids.max
$ echo $$   | sudo tee /sys/fs/cgroup/demo/cgroup.procs           # move this shell in
$ python3 -c "x = bytearray(300_000_000)"                            # → Killed
$ cat /sys/fs/cgroup/demo/memory.events                              # oom_kill 1

How Kubernetes uses it. The kubelet arranges a tree: kubepods.slice for all pods, split by quality-of-service class, then one cgroup per pod and per container. A container's CPU request becomes cpu.weight (proportional to millicores), so CPU is shared by request when the node is busy; a CPU limit becomes cpu.max, with the throttling behaviour from os3; a memory limit becomes memory.max, and exceeding it produces OOMKilled. systemd does the same for services on any Linux host: every unit is a cgroup, and CPUWeight=, MemoryMax=, TasksMax= in a unit file write these files.

5. Capabilities: root in pieces

Traditional Unix had two classes of process: root (UID 0), which bypasses every permission check, and everyone else. That is far too coarse: a web server that only needs to bind port 443 should not also be able to load kernel modules. Linux splits root's power into about forty capabilities. A few important ones:

CapabilityAllows
CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICEBinding to ports below 1024
CAP_NET_ADMINConfiguring interfaces, routes, firewall rules
CAP_NET_RAWRaw sockets (ping, packet crafting)
CAP_DAC_OVERRIDEBypassing file read/write/execute permission checks
CAP_CHOWN, CAP_SETUID, CAP_SETGIDChanging file owners; changing process user and group IDs
CAP_SYS_PTRACETracing and inspecting other processes' memory
CAP_SYS_MODULELoading kernel modules
CAP_SYS_ADMINMounting, many namespace and admin operations: so broad it is nearly root

Each thread has several capability sets: effective (checked by the kernel right now), permitted (the most it may enable), bounding (a ceiling that can only shrink, inherited by children) and others governing what survives execve. Executables can carry file capabilities (setcap cap_net_bind_service=+ep ./server), giving one binary one privilege without running it as root. And the no_new_privs flag ensures that nothing a process execs (setuid binaries, file capabilities) can ever gain more privilege than it has, which container runtimes set.

Docker's default keeps 14 relatively low-risk capabilities (CHOWN, DAC_OVERRIDE, FOWNER, FSETID, KILL, SETGID, SETUID, SETPCAP, NET_BIND_SERVICE, NET_RAW, SYS_CHROOT, MKNOD, AUDIT_WRITE, SETFCAP) and drops the rest, so root in a default container cannot, for example, load modules, change the network configuration of the host or mount file systems. --privileged gives all capabilities back and more (see below). Kubernetes' "restricted" Pod Security Standard requires dropping all capabilities (adding back at most NET_BIND_SERVICE) and running as non-root.

6. seccomp: filtering system calls

Capabilities control privileged operations; they do nothing about the hundreds of unprivileged system calls every process may make, each of which is kernel code an attacker might find a bug in. seccomp (secure computing mode) closes that gap. A process installs a filter, a small program in classic BPF, that the kernel runs on every system call the process makes, looking at the call number and arguments and returning an action:

  • ALLOW: proceed normally.
  • ERRNO: fail the call with a chosen error (often EPERM), without running it.
  • KILL_PROCESS / KILL_THREAD, TRAP (send SIGSYS), LOG, or USER_NOTIF (ask a supervisor process to decide, used by some sandboxes).

Filters are inherited by children and can only be added to, never removed, so a sandboxed process cannot escape its filter. The original 2005 "strict" mode allowed only read, write, exit and sigreturn; the filter mode (seccomp-bpf, 2012) made it practical. Docker's and containerd's default profile allows the few hundred calls ordinary programs need and blocks several dozen dangerous or rarely needed ones, such as kexec_load (load a new kernel), init_module, keyctl and add_key (a historically buggy keyring interface), bpf, userfaultfd, mount without CAP_SYS_ADMIN, and the io_uring calls (os11). Kubernetes uses it when a pod sets seccompProfile: RuntimeDefault, which the restricted Pod Security Standard requires. Chrome's renderers, Android apps, systemd services (SystemCallFilter=) and OpenSSH's pre-authentication process use seccomp too.

7. Security modules and how it all combines

Linux Security Modules add mandatory access control on top: AppArmor (Ubuntu, Debian, SUSE) confines programs with path-based profiles, and SELinux (Red Hat, Android) labels every process and file and enforces a policy over the labels. Docker applies an AppArmor profile docker-default on Ubuntu; on Red Hat systems each container gets a unique SELinux category so that even two root containers cannot touch each other's files.

A container launch, then, applies all of it in a specific order: create namespaces; set up the overlay root, mounts and pivot_root; join the cgroup and apply limits; configure networking; drop capabilities and set no_new_privs; apply the LSM profile; install the seccomp filter (last, because setting things up needs calls the filter will block); switch to the container's user; and exec the entrypoint. --privileged skips most of this: all capabilities, no seccomp filter, no AppArmor confinement, and access to all host devices, which together make it nearly equivalent to running on the host as root.

8. Containers versus virtual machines

ContainergVisor-style sandboxMicroVM / VM
KernelHost kernel, sharedUser-space kernel intercepts calls; small host surfaceOwn guest kernel
BoundarySyscall interface + namespaces, cgroups, caps, seccompgVisor's kernel + filtered host callsHardware virtualisation + minimal device model
Start timeMillisecondsTens of millisecondsAbout 100 ms (Firecracker) to seconds
OverheadNear zeroHigher for syscall- and I/O-heavy codeMemory per guest kernel, some I/O cost
Typical useYour own servicesUntrusted code needing Linux compatibilityMulti-tenant serverless, untrusted workloads

The deciding question is trust. For your own services, container isolation is about resource control and tidiness, and its boundary is good enough with sane settings. For running other people's code (serverless functions, CI jobs from public repositories, notebooks from strangers, AI agents executing generated code), the shared kernel is too large a surface, and platforms add gVisor (Google Cloud Run's first generation, GKE Sandbox) or microVMs (AWS Lambda and Fargate on Firecracker, Kata Containers).
deep:
User namespaces: a security tool and an attack surface

User namespaces let unprivileged users become "root" over their own namespaces, which is exactly what rootless containers need. The catch is that a lot of kernel code that was written assuming only real root could reach it (file-system mounting code, netfilter configuration, many namespace-specific paths) becomes reachable by any local user who creates a user namespace with its own mount or network namespace. A long series of privilege-escalation bugs used this path, including CVE-2022-0185 in file-system context parsing. Distributions responded differently: some disabled unprivileged user namespaces by default for years (Debian historically, via a sysctl), and Ubuntu 23.10 and 24.04 restrict them with AppArmor so that only programs with a profile allowing it can create them. Container runtimes' default seccomp profiles also block unshare and clone with namespace flags inside containers. The trade-off is real: user namespaces make containers safer by removing host root, while making the kernel's exposed surface larger.

Escapes through the runtime

The runtime that sets up a container briefly runs on the host with full privileges, inside and around the container's namespaces, and bugs there are serious. In CVE-2019-5736, a malicious container image could overwrite the host's runc binary: when runc executed inside the container (for docker exec), the container could open /proc/self/exe, which pointed to the host binary, and write to it after runc exited, gaining code execution as root on the next runc invocation. The fix made runc execute from a sealed, read-only memfd copy of itself. In CVE-2024-21626 ("Leaky Vessels"), runc leaked a file descriptor referring to a host directory into the container process; setting the container's working directory to /proc/self/fd/7 gave the container a foothold in the host file system. Both show why runtimes must be patched as promptly as kernels, and why the setup phase is as security-critical as the steady state.

Memory accounting subtleties in cgroups

A cgroup's memory.current includes more than processes' heaps: page cache for files the group read or wrote, tmpfs files (including /dev/shm, os12), kernel memory such as socket buffers, dentries and inodes created on its behalf. That is why a container that only streams files through can hit its limit: its page cache counts until reclaimed. Reclaim within the group usually frees cache before any OOM kill, but a burst of dirty pages that cannot be written back fast enough, or memory pinned by the kernel, can still trigger OOMKilled with a modest heap. Page-cache pages are charged to the first group that touches them, so a shared file read first by one container is charged to it even when others use it. memory.stat breaks usage into anon, file, kernel, sock, shmem and more, and is the first file to read when a limit is hit unexpectedly.

Why /proc lies inside containers

Most of /proc and /sys reflects the whole machine, because the corresponding kernel data is not namespaced: /proc/meminfo, /proc/cpuinfo, /proc/stat, /proc/loadavg and sysconf(_SC_NPROCESSORS_ONLN) (unless a cpuset restricts CPUs). Programs that size themselves from these values in a container limited by cgroup quotas over-commit: a JVM sizing its heap as a quarter of 256 GB, a Go program running 64 scheduler threads under a 2-CPU quota (heavy throttling, os3), a Python process pool with 64 workers. Fixes are container-aware runtimes (modern JVMs; Go 1.25 made GOMAXPROCS respect CPU limits by default; libraries such as automaxprocs before that), explicit configuration from the downward API in Kubernetes, and LXCFS, a FUSE file system that serves cgroup-aware versions of those /proc files to containers.

Network namespace plumbing

A container's packets take a longer path than a host process's: from the container's eth0 across the veth pair into the host namespace, through a bridge or routing, through netfilter rules for NAT and Kubernetes service load balancing, and out of the physical interface. Each hop costs CPU, and the netfilter rules installed by kube-proxy in iptables mode grow linearly with the number of services, which is why large clusters moved to IPVS mode or eBPF-based data planes (Cilium), which replace rule lists with hash-table lookups attached to the interfaces. Pods with hostNetwork: true skip all of it by staying in the host's network namespace, trading isolation for performance and port conflicts.
prod:
Reading a container's cgroup when something goes wrong

Find the container's cgroup (cat /proc/<pid>/cgroup on the host gives the path under /sys/fs/cgroup; inside a container with a cgroup namespace it shows /) and read the files directly. For kills: memory.events (max and oom_kill counts) and memory.stat (what kind of memory). For slowness: cpu.stat (nr_throttled, throttled_usec, os3), memory.pressure and io.pressure (PSI shows whether the group is stalling on memory reclaim or I/O, often the hidden cause of latency under a memory limit set too tight), and io.stat. For fork failures: pids.current versus pids.max (os2). These files are the ground truth behind every container metric your monitoring system shows.

Hardening defaults that matter most

In rough order of value for typical services: run as a non-root user (USER in the Dockerfile, runAsNonRoot: true); never run privileged and never mount /var/run/docker.sock or sensitive host paths (os12); drop all capabilities and add back only what is needed (capabilities: drop: ["ALL"]); set allowPrivilegeEscalation: false (which sets no_new_privs); use seccompProfile: RuntimeDefault; make the root file system read-only and mount writable volumes only where needed; and enforce these with Pod Security Admission or a policy engine. Where available, enable user namespaces for pods (hostUsers: false) so container root maps to an unprivileged host user. Keep kernels and runtimes (runc, containerd, CRI-O) patched, since they are the boundary.

Debugging inside namespaces

Minimal images often lack shells and tools. From the host, nsenter -t <pid> -n runs host tools such as ss, tcpdump and ip inside the container's network namespace only, keeping the host's file system and binaries, which is often the most useful combination. nsenter -t <pid> -a joins all namespaces. In Kubernetes, kubectl debug -it <pod> --image=busybox --target=<container> adds an ephemeral container sharing the target's process namespace, and kubectl debug node/<name> gives a privileged shell on the node. Tools like perf and eBPF profilers (os14) run on the host and see container processes directly, since they are host processes; only symbol resolution needs access to the container's file system (/proc/<pid>/root).

Noisy neighbours that cgroups do not stop

cgroups divide CPU time, memory, block I/O and tasks, but not everything that is shared. Last-level CPU cache and memory bandwidth are shared by all cores (Intel RDT can partition them on supporting hardware); the kernel's own locks, page allocator and network softirq processing are shared; inodes, file descriptors (system-wide limits), conntrack table entries and ephemeral ports are node-wide. A pod opening millions of connections can exhaust the node's conntrack table and break networking for everyone; a pod creating millions of tiny files can exhaust inodes on the node's container storage (os10). Monitoring at node level, not just per pod, is necessary for these.

Version and configuration drift

Behaviour differs between cgroup v1 and v2 hosts (file names, memory accounting, PSI availability), between kernels (EEVDF since 6.6, os3; time namespaces since 5.6), between runtimes (runc versus crun versus gVisor's runsc), and between seccomp profile versions (a new runtime release may start blocking a call your application uses, surfacing as unexpected EPERM). When a container behaves differently on two nodes, compare kernel version, cgroup version (stat -fc %T /sys/fs/cgroup prints cgroup2fs for v2), runtime and profile first.
myths: A container is a lightweight virtual machine.

A virtual machine runs its own kernel on virtual hardware. A container is ordinary processes on the host's kernel, started with namespaces that limit what they can see and cgroups that limit what they can use. ps on the host shows every container's processes. That is why containers start in milliseconds and share memory efficiently, and also why a kernel vulnerability reachable from inside a container can compromise the whole host.
Root inside a container is harmless because it is isolated.

Without a user namespace, UID 0 in a container is UID 0 on the host, held back only by dropped capabilities, seccomp, read-only mounts and security modules. Mount the wrong host path, run with --privileged or add CAP_SYS_ADMIN, and that root can take over the host. Running as a non-root user, or with user namespaces so container root maps to an unprivileged host UID, removes most of this risk.
cgroups and namespaces are the same thing.

They are independent features that containers combine. Namespaces control visibility: which processes, mounts, network interfaces and host name a process sees. cgroups control resources: how much CPU, memory, I/O and how many processes a group may use. A process can be in a new namespace with no resource limits, or limited by a cgroup while seeing the whole host.
Inside a container, /proc/meminfo and nproc show the container's limits.

Most /proc files are not namespaced. A container limited to 2 GB and 2 CPUs still sees the host's 256 GB in /proc/meminfo and, unless a cpuset restricts it, all 64 CPUs in nproc. Programs that size heaps or thread pools from these values over-allocate and get OOM-killed or throttled. Container-aware runtimes read the cgroup files instead (memory.max, cpu.max).
Dropping to a non-root user is enough; seccomp and capabilities are optional extras.

A non-root user removes most capabilities, but the process can still make every system call the kernel offers, and kernel bugs in rarely used calls are a common route to privilege escalation. A seccomp filter that blocks unneeded calls removes that attack surface. Defence in depth means non-root user, no extra capabilities, a seccomp profile, a read-only root file system and an LSM policy together.
lab:
Build a container from kernel primitives and watch a cgroup kill a process. Linux or WSL 2 with root (sudo); WSL 2 on recent Windows uses cgroups v2.

  1. Namespaces with unshare: 
    sudo unshare --uts --ipc --net --pid --fork --mount-proc bash
hostname sandbox && hostname     # new host name, host unaffected
echo $$                           # 1: this shell is PID 1
ps aux                            # only processes in this PID namespace
ip link                           # only a DOWN loopback interface
readlink /proc/self/ns/pid /proc/self/ns/net
exit
    Compare the readlink output with the same command run outside.
  2. A memory-limited cgroup (as root; if memory.max does not appear in the new directory, first run echo "+memory +pids +cpu" > /sys/fs/cgroup/cgroup.subtree_control to enable those controllers for children): 
    cd /sys/fs/cgroup && mkdir demo && cd demo
echo 100M > memory.max; echo 0 > memory.swap.max; echo 32 > pids.max
echo $$ > cgroup.procs            # move this shell into the cgroup
python3 -c "b = bytearray(50_000_000); print('50 MB ok')"
python3 -c "b = bytearray(300_000_000); print('300 MB ok')"
cat memory.events memory.peak
python3 -c "import os; [os.fork() or __import__('time').sleep(30) for _ in range(40)]"
  3. Capabilities: grep Cap /proc/self/status, then capsh --decode=<CapEff value> as a normal user and as root, and (if Docker is installed) inside docker run --rm alpine grep Cap /proc/self/status.
  4. Clean up: open a new shell, echo <demo shell PID> > /sys/fs/cgroup/cgroup.procs or exit it, then rmdir /sys/fs/cgroup/demo.

What to look for. In step 1 the shell is PID 1, sees only its own processes, has only a loopback interface, and its namespace links show different inode numbers from the host's: a container without an image. In step 2, the 50 MB allocation succeeds and the 300 MB one is "Killed": memory.events shows oom_kill 1 and memory.peak is about 100 MB, the limit. The fork loop fails with BlockingIOError: [Errno 11] once the cgroup reaches 32 tasks: the pids controller at work (os2). In step 3, a normal user's effective set is empty, root's decodes to every capability, and a default Docker container's is a much shorter list (the 14 defaults).
recap: A container is a set of ordinary processes on the host kernel, isolated by namespaces, limited by cgroups, and restricted by capabilities, seccomp and security modules.

Namespaces give a process its own view of one kind of resource: mount (file-system tree), PID (process IDs), network (interfaces, routes, ports), UTS (host name), IPC, user (UID and GID mappings), cgroup and time.
Namespaces are created with clone or unshare and joined with setns; nsenter uses this to step into a running container.
The container's root file system is usually an overlay of read-only image layers plus a writable layer, with pivot_root making it the new root.

cgroups v2 organise processes in one hierarchy and apply controllers: cpu (weight and max), memory (min, low, high, max), io, pids and cpuset; Kubernetes requests become weights and limits become maxima.
Capabilities split root's powers into about forty separate privileges; Docker keeps only 14 by default, and CAP_SYS_ADMIN is so broad it is nearly equivalent to root.
seccomp attaches a BPF filter to a process that allows, rejects or kills on each system call; container runtimes block dozens of rarely needed and dangerous calls by default.
User namespaces map container root to an unprivileged host user, enabling rootless containers, at the cost of exposing more kernel code to unprivileged users.
Because containers share the kernel, kernel and runtime vulnerabilities can lead to escapes; sandboxes such as gVisor and microVMs such as Firecracker add a stronger boundary for untrusted code.
glossary: AppArmor / SELinux
Linux security modules that enforce mandatory access-control policies on files, network and capabilities, beyond normal permissions.
Capability
One of about forty separate privileges that together make up root's power, such as CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE or CAP_SYS_ADMIN.
CAP_SYS_ADMIN
A very broad capability covering mounts, namespaces and many administrative operations; effectively close to full root.
cgroup (control group)
A kernel grouping of processes to which resource controllers apply limits, weights and accounting.
cgroups v2
The unified cgroup hierarchy, mounted at /sys/fs/cgroup, now the default on modern distributions and Kubernetes.
CNI
Container Network Interface: the plugin standard Kubernetes uses to set up pod networking.
Container runtime
Software such as runc or crun that creates namespaces and cgroups and starts the container's first process; higher layers such as containerd manage images and lifecycle.
cpu.max / cpu.weight
cgroup v2 CPU controls: a hard quota per period, and a relative share under contention.
CRI
Container Runtime Interface: the API the kubelet uses to ask a runtime such as containerd or CRI-O to run containers.
gVisor
A sandbox that intercepts a container's system calls with a user-space kernel, so the host kernel is exposed to far fewer calls.
LSM
Linux Security Module: a hook framework in the kernel that AppArmor, SELinux and others use to enforce extra access checks.
memory.max / memory.high
cgroup v2 memory controls: the hard limit that triggers OOM kills, and a softer limit above which the group is throttled and reclaimed.
MicroVM
A minimal virtual machine (Firecracker, Kata Containers) started per container or function to give it its own kernel.
Mount namespace
A namespace giving a process its own set of mounts, and so its own file-system tree.
Namespace
A kernel feature that gives a group of processes their own isolated instance of a global resource, such as process IDs or network interfaces.
Network namespace
A namespace with its own network interfaces, IP addresses, routing table, firewall rules and port numbers.
no_new_privs
A per-process flag guaranteeing that nothing it execs can gain privileges, such as through setuid binaries or file capabilities.
nsenter
A tool that runs a command inside the namespaces of an existing process, for debugging containers from the host.
OCI
Open Container Initiative: the standards for container image format and runtime configuration that runc, containerd and others implement.
OverlayFS
A union file system that stacks read-only lower directories under a writable upper directory, used for container image layers.
PID namespace
A namespace with its own process-ID numbering, in which the first process is PID 1.
pids.max
The cgroup v2 limit on the number of processes and threads in a group, used to stop fork bombs.
pivot_root
A system call that makes a new directory the root of the mount namespace and moves the old root aside, used when starting containers.
Privileged container
A container run with all capabilities, no seccomp filter and access to host devices; nearly equivalent to root on the host.
PSI
Pressure stall information: per-cgroup statistics of time lost waiting for CPU, memory or I/O.
Rootless container
A container started by an unprivileged user using a user namespace, so container root has no special power on the host.
seccomp
Secure computing mode: a kernel feature that filters a process's system calls with a BPF program.
unshare
A system call and command that moves the caller into new namespaces.
User namespace
A namespace that maps user and group IDs, so a process can be root inside it while being an ordinary user outside.
UTS namespace
A namespace with its own host name and domain name.
veth pair
Two virtual network interfaces connected back to back, used to link a container's network namespace to the host.
drill:
Review: a pod spec for running user-submitted code

Your team is launching a feature that runs short Python scripts written by customers (data transformations) inside the company's Kubernetes cluster. A first draft creates one pod per job with this container spec: image python:3.12, securityContext: {privileged: true} "because some scripts needed to install system packages", no resource limits "to keep scripts fast", the job's input data mounted from a host path, and the cluster's default service-account token mounted. Review it as a security and reliability reviewer: list the risks in terms of this lesson's mechanisms and propose a design.

Answer

Risks. (1) privileged: true gives all capabilities (including CAP_SYS_ADMIN and CAP_SYS_MODULE), no seccomp filter, no AppArmor confinement and access to host devices: a customer script can mount the host's disk, load a kernel module or otherwise take over the node, and with it every other tenant's pods on that node. (2) Even unprivileged, root in a container shares the host kernel; untrusted code calling obscure system calls is exactly the scenario where a kernel bug becomes an escape. (3) No limits: a script can allocate all node memory (OOM-killing other pods, os9), burn every CPU, fork-bomb the node's PID space (os2) or fill the disk; the only cgroup protection left is whatever the QoS class gives. (4) A hostPath mount gives direct access to the node's file system, and if writable, to other jobs' data or system files. (5) The service-account token lets the script call the Kubernetes API with the pod's permissions, possibly listing secrets or creating pods. (6) No network restrictions: scripts can reach internal services and the cloud metadata endpoint, which can hand out node credentials.

Design. Treat customer code as hostile. Run jobs in a sandboxed runtime, gVisor (runtimeClassName: gvisor) or Kata/Firecracker microVMs, on a dedicated node pool with taints so only these jobs land there. In the pod: run as a non-root user, allowPrivilegeEscalation: false, drop all capabilities, seccompProfile: RuntimeDefault (gVisor adds its own), read-only root file system with a small emptyDir for scratch, and hostUsers: false if supported. Set requests and limits for CPU and memory, a pod PID limit and ephemeral-storage limits, plus a hard job timeout (activeDeadlineSeconds). Do not mount host paths; deliver input through an object-store download with short-lived, job-scoped credentials. Disable the service-account token (automountServiceAccountToken: false). Apply a NetworkPolicy denying all egress except the object store, and block the metadata endpoint. Preinstall common packages in a curated image instead of allowing system package installation. Finally, enforce all of this with an admission policy so a later change cannot quietly reintroduce privileged.
qa: E
What is a container, in terms of Linux kernel features?

A container is one or more ordinary processes running on the host kernel, started in new namespaces so they see their own file-system tree, process IDs, network stack and host name, and placed in a cgroup that limits CPU, memory, I/O and process count. Runtimes also drop capabilities, apply a seccomp filter and an AppArmor or SELinux profile, and give it a root file system built from image layers with an overlay file system. There is no separate kernel and no hardware virtualisation.
E
What is the difference between namespaces and cgroups?

Namespaces control what a process can see: its own view of process IDs, mounts, network interfaces, host name, IPC objects, user IDs, cgroup tree and clocks. cgroups control how much a group of processes can use: CPU share and quota, memory limits, I/O bandwidth, number of processes, which CPUs and memory nodes. Containers need both, but they are independent mechanisms.
E
Name the Linux namespaces and what each isolates.

Mount isolates the set of mounted file systems; PID isolates process-ID numbering; network isolates interfaces, addresses, routes, firewall rules and ports; UTS isolates the host name; IPC isolates System V objects and POSIX message queues; user isolates user and group ID mappings and capabilities; cgroup isolates the visible cgroup hierarchy; time isolates the offsets of the monotonic and boot-time clocks. Each is visible as a link in /proc/PID/ns/.
M
How do Kubernetes resource requests and limits map onto cgroups?

On a cgroup v2 node, the kubelet creates a cgroup per pod and container. The CPU request becomes cpu.weight, a relative share used only when CPUs are contended. The CPU limit becomes cpu.max, a quota of CPU time per 100 ms period, enforced by throttling. The memory limit becomes memory.max, and exceeding it triggers an OOM kill inside the container; the memory request is used for scheduling and, with the newer memory QoS feature, can set memory.min or memory.low. Pod quality-of-service classes also set oom_score_adj.
M
What are Linux capabilities and why do they matter for containers?

Capabilities split the all-powerful root privilege into about forty pieces: binding to ports below 1024 (CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE), changing network configuration (CAP_NET_ADMIN), bypassing file permissions (CAP_DAC_OVERRIDE), tracing other processes (CAP_SYS_PTRACE), mounting and many administrative operations (CAP_SYS_ADMIN). A process needs only the ones it uses. Docker keeps 14 low-risk capabilities by default and drops the rest, so root in a container is much weaker than root on the host. Hardened deployments drop all capabilities and add back only the needed ones.
M
What does seccomp do and what does Docker's default profile block?

seccomp lets a process install a BPF filter that the kernel runs on every system call, deciding to allow it, return an error, kill the process, or notify a supervisor, based on the call number and arguments. The filter is inherited and cannot be removed. Docker's default profile allows the few hundred calls ordinary programs need and blocks several dozen dangerous or rarely needed ones, such as kexec_load, mount without privileges, keyctl, add_key, bpf, perf_event_open without privileges, and the io_uring calls. It reduces the kernel attack surface reachable from a container.
M
What is a user namespace and how does it enable rootless containers?

A user namespace has its own mapping of user and group IDs to IDs outside it. A process can be UID 0 inside the namespace, with full capabilities over resources owned by that namespace, while being mapped to an unprivileged UID such as 100000 on the host. A non-root user can therefore create a user namespace and, inside it, mount, network and PID namespaces, which is how Podman and rootless Docker run containers without host root. If the container breaks out, it is just an unprivileged user on the host.
M
Why does a Java or Go program inside a container sometimes use too many threads or too much memory?

It sizes itself from what it sees. /proc/meminfo and the CPU count from sysconf show the host's resources, not the container's cgroup limits, unless a cpuset restricts CPUs. Older runtimes therefore created thread pools for 64 cores and heaps for 256 GB inside a container limited to 2 CPUs and 4 GB, leading to CPU throttling and OOM kills. Modern JVMs read cgroup limits (container support has been on by default since JDK 10, backported to 8u191), and Go 1.25 made GOMAXPROCS respect CPU limits; with older versions, set them explicitly.
M
How do you get a shell in a running container's environment from the host, and how does it work?

Find the container's main PID (docker inspect or crictl inspect) and run nsenter -t PID -m -u -i -n -p with the namespaces you need; or use docker exec or kubectl exec, which do the same through the runtime, or kubectl debug to attach an ephemeral debugging container sharing the pod's namespaces. Underneath, the tool opens /proc/PID/ns/* and calls setns() to join each namespace, then execs a shell, which therefore sees the container's file system, processes and network.
H
How have container escapes happened in practice?

Through the shared kernel and the runtime. Kernel bugs reachable from inside, such as CVE-2022-0185, a heap overflow in file-system context parsing exploitable by a user who could create a user namespace, let attackers gain host root. Runtime bugs matter too: CVE-2019-5736 let a malicious container overwrite the host's runc binary through /proc/self/exe while runc was executing in it, and CVE-2024-21626 ('Leaky Vessels') let a container start with its working directory in a file descriptor runc had leaked, giving access to the host file system. Misconfiguration is the most common route: privileged containers, the Docker socket mounted inside, host paths mounted writable, or CAP_SYS_ADMIN granted.

Follow-up: How do you reduce exposure? — Patch kernels and runtimes quickly, run as non-root with user namespaces, drop capabilities, use the runtime's default seccomp and an LSM profile, forbid privileged pods with admission policies, and use gVisor or microVMs for untrusted code.
H
Walk through building a minimal container by hand with Linux primitives.

Unpack an image's root file system into a directory (or stack layers with overlayfs). Call unshare or clone with new mount, PID, UTS, IPC, network and optionally user namespaces. In the child, set the host name, make the mounts private, bind-mount the new root, mount proc, sys and dev inside it, and pivot_root into it, unmounting the old root. Create a cgroup directory, write the child's PID into cgroup.procs and set memory.max, cpu.max and pids.max. Set up networking by creating a veth pair, moving one end into the namespace and configuring addresses and routes. Drop capabilities, set no_new_privs, install a seccomp filter, switch to an unprivileged user, and exec the application as PID 1. runc does essentially this from an OCI configuration file.
H
Compare containers, gVisor and microVMs for running untrusted code.

Plain containers share the host kernel, so the security boundary is the full system-call interface plus the runtime; they are the cheapest and fastest. gVisor interposes a user-space kernel (the Sentry, written in Go) that implements most Linux system calls itself, so the application talks to gVisor and gVisor uses a small, filtered set of host calls; isolation is much stronger, at a cost in system-call-heavy and I/O-heavy performance and some compatibility. MicroVMs such as Firecracker (used by AWS Lambda and Fargate) and Kata Containers give each workload its own guest kernel behind hardware virtualisation, with a minimal device model and startup in about a hundred milliseconds; isolation is VM-grade with more memory overhead per workload. Multi-tenant platforms running customer code typically use one of the latter two.
H
A node runs out of PIDs and new pods fail to start, although each pod looks healthy. How do cgroups help diagnose and prevent this?

Every thread counts as a task against kernel.pid_max and threads-max. One pod leaking threads or forking processes can exhaust them for the whole node, failing even system services. The pids controller tracks and limits tasks per cgroup: pids.current shows usage per pod, so walking /sys/fs/cgroup/kubepods.slice or using crictl stats finds the offender. Prevention is setting pids.max per pod (kubelet's podPidsLimit) and reserving PIDs for system daemons, so a runaway pod hits its own limit, its forks fail with EAGAIN, and the node and other pods are unaffected.
